blocks.text:
A gym accepts members aged 18 to 65. Apply 2-value BVA to the boundaries of the valid partition.

Boundary values of the valid partition: 18 and 65.
Closest neighbour of 18 in the adjacent partition: 17. Closest neighbour of 65 in the adjacent partition: 66.

Coverage items: 17, 18, 65, 66. Four items, so four test cases.

Notice that 17 and 66 are themselves the boundary values of the two invalid partitions. That is why the syllabus can say that in 2-value BVA all coverage items are boundary values.

blocks.title: Worked example 2: the same range, 3-value, and coverage
blocks.text:
Same gym, 3-value BVA on the boundaries of the valid partition.

For 18: 17, 18, 19. For 65: 64, 65, 66.
Coverage items: 17, 18, 19, 64, 65, 66. Six items.

A tester has run ages 17, 18, 40, 65 and 66. For 3-value BVA, the items hit are 17, 18, 65 and 66: four of six, so coverage is 66.7%. The value 40 is not a coverage item and adds nothing. For 2-value BVA the same tests hit four of four items: 100%.

Why bother with the extra values? Take a rule with one boundary: "a senior discount applies up to age 65", coded by mistake as "age = 65". The 2-value tests for this boundary, 65 and 66, both behave correctly, so 2-value BVA sees nothing. Age 64, which only 3-value BVA tests, wrongly gets no discount.

blocks.title: Worked example 3: all partitions of a closed range
blocks.text:
An exam score from 0 to 100 gives "fail" for 0 to 39, "pass" for 40 to 69 and "distinction" for 70 to 100. Scores outside 0 to 100 cannot be entered.

Now the question is about the boundaries of all partitions. Boundary values: 0, 39, 40, 69, 70, 100.

2-value BVA: each boundary value plus its closest neighbour in the adjacent partition. The neighbour of 39 is 40 and the neighbour of 40 is 39, and both are already on the list. The values 0 and 100 have no adjacent partition, because nothing outside the range can be entered. Coverage items: 0, 39, 40, 69, 70, 100. Six items.

3-value BVA: add both neighbours of every boundary value, as long as they can be entered. Coverage items: 0, 1, 38, 39, 40, 41, 68, 69, 70, 71, 99, 100. That is 12 items. There is no -1 and no 101.

If the system could accept and reject out-of-range scores, there would be two more partitions (below 0 and above 100), and their boundary values -1 and 101 would join the 2-value list. The 3-value list would gain -2 and 102 as well, as neighbours of the new boundary values.

blocks.title: Common traps
blocks.text:
- Answering for all partitions when the question says "the valid partition", or the reverse. For 18 to 65, 3-value BVA on the valid partition gives six values. Across all partition boundaries (17, 18, 65 and 66 are all boundary values then) it gives eight: 16, 17, 18, 19, 64, 65, 66, 67. Both are correct answers to different questions.
- Giving the 3-value set when asked for 2-value. The 3-value set contains the 2-value set, so it "covers" it, but it is not "exactly the coverage items".
- Testing only inside the range (18, 19, 64, 65). 2-value BVA needs the neighbour in the adjacent partition, which is outside.
- Adding a middle value. It is an equivalence partitioning value and counts for nothing in BVA coverage.
- Using the wrong step, such as 17 instead of 17.99 for money.
- Applying BVA to data with no order, such as colours or countries. It cannot be done.

blocks.title: Exercise
blocks.text:
A lift accepts a load of 50 to 900 kg in whole kilograms. Lighter loads are treated as empty and heavier loads are refused.

a) Give the 2-value coverage items for the boundaries of the valid partition.
b) Give the 3-value coverage items for the boundaries of the valid partition.
c) Tests were run with 49, 50, 51 and 900. What is the 3-value coverage?

blocks.title: Worked solution
blocks.text:
a) 49, 50, 900, 901
b) 49, 50, 51, 899, 900, 901
c) The tests hit 49, 50, 51 and 900: four of six items, 66.7%. The items 899 and 901 are still missing.

blocks.title: Syllabus reference
blocks.text: CTFL syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.2.2; learning objective FL-4.2.2 (K3). K3 means you must be able to apply the technique to a new situation, so practise until you can do each step without looking at this page.

lessons.title: Lab · Decision tables
lessons.summary: Build the table, drop impossible columns, turn columns into test cases and calculate coverage.

blocks.title: The method
blocks.text:
Decision tables fit requirements in which combinations of conditions lead to different outcomes, such as business rules.

1. List the conditions (the inputs to the decision) and the actions (what the system does).
2. Count the columns. A full table for Boolean conditions has one column, called a rule, for every combination: 2 conditions give 4 rules, 3 give 8, 4 give 16. The number doubles with each condition.
3. Fill in the condition entries. A simple pattern avoids gaps: the first condition is T for the first half of the columns and F for the second half; the next alternates in quarters, and so on.
4. Fill in the actions for each rule from the requirement. An X means the action happens.
5. Delete columns whose combination cannot occur (infeasible).
6. Optionally merge two columns that have the same actions and differ in one condition only. That condition is then shown as "–", meaning it does not matter.
7. Write one test case per column: choose inputs that make the conditions true or false as the column says, and take the actions as the expected result.

Coverage = columns exercised ÷ feasible columns, as a percentage. The coverage items are the feasible columns.

Notation to know: T and F for conditions, "–" for irrelevant, N/A for infeasible, X for an action that occurs, blank for one that does not. In a limited-entry table everything is Boolean; an extended-entry table allows other values such as ranges.

blocks.title: Worked example 1: two conditions
blocks.text:
Rule: "Members get free delivery. Non-members get free delivery only on baskets of £50 or more."

Conditions: Member? Basket ≥ £50?
Action: Free delivery.

blocks.title: Decision table: free delivery
blocks.text: Conditions are the upper rows and actions the lower rows. Each column is one rule. X means the action occurs.

blocks.title: Reading the table
blocks.text:
Four rules, all feasible. Four test cases give 100% coverage, for example: member with £60; member with £20; non-member with £60; non-member with £20 (expected: delivery is charged).

After running R1 and R4 only, coverage is 2 ÷ 4 = 50%.

R1 and R2 have the same action and differ only in the basket, so they can be merged into one column "Member = T, Basket = –". The minimised table has three columns.

blocks.title: Worked example 2: three conditions and a test case
blocks.text:
A bank pre-screens loans. Conditions: Income verified? Credit score ≥ 650? Existing customer?
Actions: approve if income is verified and the score is high enough; manual review if income is verified, the score is too low and the applicant is an existing customer; otherwise reject.

blocks.title: Using the table
blocks.text:
2 × 2 × 2 = 8 rules.

Test case: income verified, score 610, existing customer. Translate: T, F, T. That is R3, so the expected result is manual review.

If R1, R3 and R8 have been tested, coverage is 3 ÷ 8 = 37.5%.

blocks.title: Worked example 3: infeasible combinations
blocks.text:
A burglar alarm reacts when a door opens. Conditions: Armed? Entry delay running? Valid code entered?

The entry delay can only run while the alarm is armed. So every column with Armed = F and Entry delay = T is infeasible. There are two of them (code entered T or F).

Full table: 8 columns. Feasible columns: 8 − 2 = 6.

So 100% decision table coverage needs 6 test cases, not 8. If four of them have been run, coverage is 4 ÷ 6 = 66.7%, not 4 ÷ 8.

The denominator is always the feasible columns. This is the most common calculation slip in this technique.

blocks.title: Common traps
blocks.text:
- Counting rules as 2 × the number of conditions (6 for three conditions) instead of 2 to the power of that number (8).
- Dividing by the full table when some columns are infeasible.
- Merging columns that have the same action but differ in two conditions, or that differ in one condition but have different actions. Both must hold: same actions, exactly one differing condition.
- Mixing up the test input with the condition. "Basket of £49.99" means the condition "Basket ≥ £50" is F. Translate carefully, especially at limits.
- Reading "–" as false. It means the condition does not affect the outcome.
- Forgetting what the technique is good at: it finds combinations that were overlooked, and gaps or contradictions in the requirements. With many conditions the rules grow exponentially, so a minimised table or a risk-based selection is used.

blocks.title: Exercise
blocks.text:
A cinema sells a discounted ticket when the visitor is a student or the showing is before 17:00. A visitor who is a student and comes before 17:00 also gets free popcorn.

a) How many rules does the full table have?
b) Write the table.
c) Which rule does "non-student at 15:30" exercise, and what is expected?
d) Tests exist for "student at 20:00" and "non-student at 20:00". What is the coverage?

blocks.title: Worked solution
blocks.text:
a) Two conditions (Student? Before 17:00?), so 4 rules.
b) See the table below.
c) F, T is R3: discount, no popcorn.
d) Those tests are R2 and R4: 2 ÷ 4 = 50%.

blocks.title: Syllabus reference
blocks.text: CTFL syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.2.3; learning objective FL-4.2.3 (K3). K3 means you must be able to apply the technique to a new situation, so practise until you can do each step without looking at this page.

lessons.title: Lab · State transition testing
lessons.summary: Read a state model, write tests as event sequences, and calculate the three kinds of coverage.

blocks.title: The method
blocks.text:
A state model shows the states a system can be in and the valid transitions between them. A transition is started by an event, may be restricted by a guard condition, and may cause an action. The label syntax is: event [guard condition] / action.

A state table shows the same model with one row per state and one column per event. Each cell holds the target state. Empty cells are the invalid transitions, which a diagram does not show.

A test case is a sequence of events from the initial state. One test case usually covers several transitions.

1. List the states and the valid transitions. Number the transitions.
2. For a given test, walk through the model event by event and tick the transitions and states you pass.
3. Calculate the coverage that is asked for:
   - All states coverage = states visited ÷ all states.
   - Valid transitions coverage (also called 0-switch coverage) = valid transitions exercised ÷ all valid transitions. This is the most widely used criterion.
   - All transitions coverage = valid transitions exercised plus invalid transitions attempted ÷ all cells of the state table. Test one invalid transition per test case, so that one defect cannot hide another (defect masking).

Strength order: all transitions is stronger than valid transitions, which is stronger than all states. 100% valid transitions coverage guarantees 100% all states coverage, but not the other way round.

blocks.title: Worked example 1: coverage of one test
blocks.text:
An order has these valid transitions, starting in "New":
1. New — pay → Paid
2. New — cancel → Cancelled
3. Paid — ship → Shipped
4. Paid — refund → Cancelled
5. Shipped — deliver → Delivered

Test 1: pay, ship, deliver. It exercises transitions 1, 3 and 5.
Valid transitions coverage: 3 ÷ 5 = 60%.
States visited: New, Paid, Shipped, Delivered. All states coverage: 4 ÷ 5 = 80%.

Adding Test 2 (cancel) brings transitions to 4 ÷ 5 and states to 5 ÷ 5. All states are covered, yet transition 4 (refund) has never been tested. That is why all states coverage is the weakest criterion.

blocks.title: Worked example 2: how many test cases are needed?
blocks.text:
Same order model. What is the minimum number of test cases for 100% valid transitions coverage, if every test starts in "New"?

Look for states with no way out: Cancelled and Delivered. A test that reaches one of them is finished. Then count the different ways to end:
- pay, ship, deliver (transitions 1, 3, 5)
- pay, refund (transitions 1, 4)
- cancel (transition 2)

Three test cases, and it cannot be fewer: transitions 2, 4 and 5 each lead into a dead end, so no single test can contain two of them. Minimum = 3.

Compare a music player: Stopped — play → Playing; Playing — pause → Paused; Paused — play → Playing; Playing — stop → Stopped; Paused — stop → Stopped. No state is a dead end, so one long test can cover everything: play, pause, play, stop, play, pause, stop. Minimum = 1.

Rule of thumb: dead ends and branches that cannot be revisited force extra test cases; loops let one test continue.

blocks.title: Worked example 3: invalid transitions from the state table
blocks.text:
A door with a badge reader: Locked — badge → Unlocked; Unlocked — open → Open; Open — close → Unlocked; Unlocked — timeout → Locked.

States: Locked, Unlocked, Open (3). Events: badge, open, close, timeout (4).

blocks.title: State table: door with a badge reader
blocks.text: Rows are states and columns are events. A cell holds the state reached; "–" marks an invalid transition.

blocks.title: Counting from the state table
blocks.text:
The table has 3 × 4 = 12 cells. Four hold a valid transition, so 8 cells are invalid transitions.

For 100% all transitions coverage you exercise the 4 valid transitions and attempt each of the 8 invalid ones, such as "badge while Open". Each invalid attempt goes in its own test case. A sensible expected result for an invalid transition is that the event is ignored or rejected and the state does not change.

A sequence such as badge, close is not a valid test of valid transitions: after badge the door is Unlocked, and "close" has no transition from Unlocked.

blocks.title: Common traps
blocks.text:
- Counting an event twice. Coverage counts different transitions, however often you pass them.
- Confusing events with transitions. "play" appears on two different transitions of the player (from Stopped and from Paused); they are two coverage items.
- Forgetting that the initial state counts as visited.
- Reporting all states coverage when valid transitions coverage is asked, or the reverse. Underline the criterion in the question.
- Calculating invalid transitions as states × events without subtracting the valid ones.
- Putting several invalid transitions into one test case.
- Walking a sequence without tracking the current state. Write the state after every event.

blocks.title: Exercise
blocks.text:
A support ticket: Open — assign → In progress; Open — reject → Closed; In progress — resolve → Resolved; Resolved — reopen → In progress; Resolved — confirm → Closed. The initial state is Open.

a) Test A is: assign, resolve, confirm. What are its valid transitions coverage and its all states coverage?
b) What is the minimum number of test cases for 100% valid transitions coverage?
c) How many invalid transitions does the state table show?

blocks.title: Worked solution
blocks.text:
The model has 5 transitions, 4 states (Open, In progress, Resolved, Closed) and 5 events.
a) Test A exercises assign, resolve and confirm: 3 ÷ 5 = 60%. It visits all four states: 100%.
b) 2. Closed is a dead end reached by reject and by confirm, so two tests are needed: "reject", and "assign, resolve, reopen, resolve, confirm".
c) 4 × 5 = 20 cells, minus 5 valid transitions: 15.

blocks.title: Syllabus reference
blocks.text: CTFL syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.2.4; learning objective FL-4.2.4 (K3). K3 means you must be able to apply the technique to a new situation, so practise until you can do each step without looking at this page.

lessons.title: 4.3 · White-box coverage
lessons.summary: Calculate statement and branch coverage and explain what structural percentages leave unresolved.

blocks.title: Understand
blocks.text: Statement coverage is executed executable statements divided by total executable statements. Branch coverage is executed control-flow branches divided by total branches. Use the model given in the question to identify branches; conditional decisions generally have both true and false outcomes. Full branch coverage implies full statement coverage for the modeled executable structure, but full statement coverage can miss a branch. Structural coverage can expose untested implementation and support useful checks, but it cannot reveal behavior that was never implemented merely by reaching code.

blocks.title: Worked example
blocks.text: Pseudocode: if member then applyDiscount; printTotal. A member test executes both statements, achieving full statement coverage, but misses the false outcome of the decision. Adding a non-member test exercises that branch. If four of five executable statements run, statement coverage is 4/5 × 100 = 80%.

blocks.title: Common exam trap
blocks.text: Do not infer branch coverage from a statement percentage. Even 100% coverage does not establish correctness or complete requirements coverage.

blocks.title: Self-check and solution
blocks.text: A model has eight branches; six run. Coverage is 6/8 × 100 = 75%. What additional evidence is needed before calling the product correct? Assertions against expected behavior, requirements and risk-based tests beyond structural reachability.

blocks.title: Count implementation items before interpreting coverage
blocks.text: Statements are executable items, not automatically comments or declarations. Branch items are control-flow transfers, including unconditional branches when present in the specified model. Simplified questions may explicitly count true/false decision outcomes. Full branch coverage implies full statement coverage; the reverse is false. Neither metric establishes defect removal, requirements completeness or every possible path. Structural evidence needs meaningful checks of the executed behavior and complementary evidence from the specification.

blocks.title: Worked case: an optional surcharge
blocks.text: Use this simplified model with four executable statements: total = base; if express then total = total + 5; receipt = total; save(receipt). Count the surcharge assignment as the second statement and the two decision outcomes as branch items. An express case executes all four statements but only one decision outcome: 100% statement coverage and 50% branch coverage in this model. A non-express case reaches the other outcome. A missing tax requirement can still escape these checks.

blocks.title: Exercise
blocks.text: A stated model has ten executable statements and six branch items. Eight statements and four branches execute. Calculate both percentages. Does this establish that 80% of requirements are satisfied?

blocks.title: Worked solution
blocks.text: Statement coverage is 8/10=80%; branch coverage is 4/6, about 66.7%. Requirements have a different denominator and need traceability. Reached code can contain defects, so interpret the result with assertions, outcomes and specification-derived evidence.

blocks.title: Syllabus details to know
blocks.text:
A branch is a transfer of control between two nodes of the control flow graph. It can be unconditional (straight-line code) or conditional (a decision outcome: true or false of an IF, a case of a switch, or continuing or exiting a loop). Branch coverage counts both kinds and subsumes statement coverage, but not the reverse. 100% statement coverage executes every executable statement, but can miss data-dependent defects such as division by zero and need not exercise all branches. Branch coverage can miss defects that need a specific path.
White-box strengths: the whole implementation is considered, so defects can be found even when the specification is vague, outdated or incomplete; it gives an objective coverage measure that black-box testing alone cannot. Weakness: defects of omission. White-box techniques also work statically, in dry runs of code not yet ready to execute and in reviews of pseudocode or other logic modeled as a control flow graph.

blocks.title: Syllabus references
blocks.text: CTFL syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.3 (starts on p. 42). Learning objectives: FL-4.3.1 (K2), FL-4.3.2 (K2), FL-4.3.3 (K2). Read the full section and the chapter keyword list alongside this lesson.

blocks.title: Statement and branch coverage on one piece of code
blocks.text:
1  read price, member
2  if member then
3      price = price * 0.9
4  end if
5  if price > 100 then
6      print "free delivery"
7  end if
8  print price

blocks.title: Working out the coverage
blocks.text:
Executable statements: lines 1, 2, 3, 5, 6 and 8, so six. Each "if" has two outcomes, true and false, so there are four conditional branches. This example counts these decision outcomes, as exam questions on branch coverage normally do.

Test A: price 200, member = true. Line 2 is true, so line 3 runs; the price becomes 180; line 5 is true, so line 6 runs. All six statements are executed: 100% statement coverage with a single test.
Branches taken by test A: 2-true and 5-true. That is two of four: 50% branch coverage.

Test B: price 50, member = false. Both decisions are false. Together, A and B take all four outcomes: 100% branch coverage.

What this shows:
- 100% statement coverage does not give 100% branch coverage. The false outcomes, which skip code, have no statements of their own.
- 100% branch coverage always gives 100% statement coverage. Branch coverage subsumes statement coverage.
- Even 100% branch coverage is not proof of correctness. If line 5 should read "price ≥ 100", tests A and B both pass, because neither uses exactly 100. Coverage tells you what was executed, not whether the right values were tried.

blocks.title: What white-box testing is good and bad at
blocks.text:
Strength: the whole implementation is taken into account, so defects can be found even when the specification is vague, outdated or incomplete. Coverage is measured objectively, and the measurement shows exactly which tests to add.

Weakness: a requirement that was never implemented leaves no code behind. White-box testing may not detect such defects of omission.

White-box techniques also work in static testing, for example in a dry run of code, pseudocode or other logic that can be drawn as a control flow graph. And black-box testing alone gives no measure of actual code coverage.

lessons.title: 4.4 · Experience-based techniques
lessons.summary: Turn experience into fault attacks, focused exploratory charters and maintained checklists.

blocks.title: Understand
blocks.text: Error guessing uses knowledge of typical mistakes and previous defects to propose tests. Exploratory testing combines learning, design and execution as the tester responds to observations; it is often organized into time-boxed sessions with charters, notes and debriefs. Checklist-based testing uses a maintained list of conditions to guide consistent checking while allowing judgment in the detailed cases. All three can complement systematic techniques, particularly where specifications are incomplete. Their effectiveness depends on relevant expertise and on documenting enough evidence to communicate results.

blocks.title: Worked example
blocks.text: A tester guesses that a copied discount rule might mishandle a zero amount. In an exploratory session with a “recover after payment interruption” charter, observations guide the next checks. A release checklist reminds the team to verify keyboard access, validation messages and recovery from network loss.

blocks.title: Common exam trap
blocks.text: Exploratory testing is not unrecorded random clicking. A checklist guides coverage but is not automatically a detailed executable procedure.

blocks.title: Self-check and solution
blocks.text: Which technique best fits a 45-minute investigation where each result informs the next experiment? Exploratory testing. How can the session remain accountable? Use a charter, record observations and summarize coverage and findings.

blocks.title: Give experience a mission and preserve evidence
blocks.text: Error guessing turns knowledge of likely faults into checks, such as missing inputs, incorrect operators and interface mismatches. Fault attacks organize possible faults into a list and derive revealing tests. Exploratory testing combines learning, design and execution; observations guide the next check. A charter defines a mission, a timebox bounds the session, and notes and debrief preserve useful information. Checklists supply reusable conditions while leaving detailed cases to judgment. Update them when risks and knowledge change.

blocks.title: Worked case: interrupted checkout
blocks.text: Charter: investigate resuming checkout after network interruption. In a 30-minute session, vary interruption around address save, authorization and confirmation. Record build, account, inputs, observations and unexplored questions. If a retry duplicates authorization, investigate related timing. Prior incidents suggest stale sessions; a checklist reminds the tester to check persistence and messages. The session has a purpose while adapting to discoveries.

blocks.title: Exercise
blocks.text: Improve the note “clicked around checkout; seemed fine.” Explain what to do if retry creates a second authorization.

blocks.title: Worked solution
blocks.text: Add charter, build/environment, explored conditions and inputs, results, supporting evidence and unresolved scope. Investigate reproduction and related retry conditions, then report the observed behavior. Exploratory work adapts while preserving enough evidence for follow-up; random click count does not measure its value.

blocks.title: Syllabus details to know
blocks.text:
Error guessing draws on how the application behaved before, typical developer errors and failures in similar applications. Areas: input (valid input rejected, parameters wrong or missing), output (wrong format or result), logic (missing cases, wrong operator), computation (wrong operand or calculation), interfaces (parameter mismatch, incompatible types) and data (wrong initialization or type). A fault attack implements error guessing from a list of possible errors, defects and failures.
Exploratory testing designs, executes and evaluates tests at the same time as the tester learns. Session-based testing uses a time box, a test charter with objectives, test session sheets for steps and discoveries, and a debriefing with interested stakeholders. It suits few or inadequate specifications and time pressure, and works best with experienced testers who have domain knowledge. It can use other techniques such as EP.
Checklist-based testing covers test conditions from a checklist built from experience, user priorities or how software fails. Items are often questions that can be checked separately and directly. Leave out items that can be checked automatically, items that belong in entry or exit criteria, and items that are too general. Update checklists from defect analysis as entries lose effect, but keep them short. High-level checklists give more variability: potentially greater coverage, less repeatability.

blocks.title: Syllabus references
blocks.text: CTFL syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.4 (starts on p. 43). Learning objectives: FL-4.4.1 (K2), FL-4.4.2 (K2), FL-4.4.3 (K2). Read the full section and the chapter keyword list alongside this lesson.

blocks.title: Three experience-based techniques side by side
blocks.text:
Error guessing anticipates errors, defects and failures from what the tester knows: how the application worked in the past, the mistakes these developers tend to make, and failures seen in similar applications. Typical areas are input, output, logic, computation, interfaces and data. A fault attack makes it methodical: build or obtain a list of possible errors, defects and failures, and design a test to expose each one.

Exploratory testing designs, executes and evaluates tests at the same time, while the tester learns about the test object. It suits few or inadequate specifications and time pressure, and it complements more formal techniques. In session-based testing it runs in a time box, guided by a test charter with test objectives, and is followed by a debriefing with stakeholders; test session sheets record the steps and discoveries. It works best with an experienced tester who has domain knowledge, and it can use other techniques, such as equivalence partitioning, inside a session.

Checklist-based testing designs, implements and executes tests to cover the test conditions of a checklist. Items are often questions, and each must be checkable separately and directly. A checklist should not contain items that can be checked automatically, items that are really entry or exit criteria, or items that are too general. Checklists wear out as developers learn, so they are updated from defect analysis, without letting them grow too long. High-level checklists give more coverage and less repeatability.

blocks.title: Good and bad checklist items
blocks.text:
Good: "Does every mandatory field show an error message when left empty?" Specific, and checkable on its own.
Bad: "Is the code formatted according to the standard?" A tool can check that automatically.
Bad: "Is the test environment available?" That is an entry criterion.
Bad: "Is the user interface good?" Too general to check directly.

lessons.title: 4.5 · Collaborative acceptance testing
lessons.summary: Clarify acceptance rules collaboratively and derive positive, negative and boundary examples.

blocks.title: Understand
blocks.text: User stories describe a user, a need and its value. The card is a starting point for conversation; confirmation is captured in acceptance criteria. Business representatives, developers and testers develop a shared understanding through examples. Acceptance criteria may be scenario-oriented, such as Given/When/Then, or rule-oriented, such as a checklist of constraints. Criteria define what must be met and should support unambiguous evaluation. ATDD derives acceptance tests collaboratively before implementation; include positive, negative and relevant non-functional cases and resolve inconsistent examples early.

blocks.title: Worked example
blocks.text: Story: “As a subscriber, I want to pause renewals so I can avoid unwanted charges.” Criterion: Given an active subscription, when the user pauses before the renewal cutoff, then no renewal charge is made. Tests should cover a timely pause, a request after cutoff, an already paused account and resumption according to agreed rules.

blocks.title: Common exam trap
blocks.text: A story is not complete simply because its card exists. Acceptance criteria describe behavior; they need not prescribe implementation details.

blocks.title: Self-check and solution
blocks.text: Criterion: purchases of at least 50 qualify for free delivery. An ATDD case uses a total of 50 and expects zero delivery charge; a negative case uses 49.99 and expects the specified paid-delivery amount. Agree that amount before automating the case.

blocks.title: Resolve examples before implementing rules
blocks.text: A story identifies who needs a capability, what is needed and why. The card starts a conversation; confirmation captures acceptance criteria. Developers, testers and business representatives contribute complementary perspectives. Scenario-oriented criteria describe a concrete situation and outcome; rule-oriented criteria list constraints. ATDD derives acceptance tests before implementation, including positive, negative and relevant quality cases. Conflicting examples expose a need for clarification rather than a reason to choose an arbitrary implementation.

blocks.title: Worked case: parcel locker
blocks.text: A code must match the parcel, be unexpired and belong to an uncollected parcel. Agree a positive example and expect the assigned door to open. Isolate negative cases for a wrong code, expiry, and reuse after collection. Clarify the expiry boundary: strictly before 18:00 implies rejection at 18:00. Agree time precision and timezone. If opening speed matters, define an observable response-time criterion rather than “quickly.”

blocks.title: Exercise
blocks.text: A ticket is refundable when unused and requested at least 48 hours before departure. Give an accepted case, two rejected cases isolating different rules, and a boundary question.

blocks.title: Worked solution
blocks.text: Accept unused/60 hours. Reject used/60 hours to isolate usage and unused/47 hours to isolate time. Ask how exactly 48 hours is interpreted and which timestamps, timezone and precision apply. “At least” suggests inclusion, but examples should confirm shared understanding before implementation.

blocks.title: Syllabus details to know
blocks.text:
Collaboration-based approaches also aim at avoiding defects. A user story has 3 C's: Card (the medium), Conversation (how the software will be used) and Confirmation (the acceptance criteria). Format: 'As a [role], I want [goal], so that I can [business value]'. Brainstorming and mind mapping combine business, development and testing perspectives. INVEST: Independent, Negotiable, Valuable, Estimable, Small, Testable. If a stakeholder cannot say how to test a story, it may be unclear or not valuable to them.
Acceptance criteria define story scope, build consensus, describe positive and negative scenarios, are the basis for acceptance testing and support planning and estimation. Formats: scenario-oriented (Given/When/Then) and rule-oriented (verification lists or tabulated input-output mappings); custom formats work if unambiguous.
ATDD: a specification workshop analyzes and writes the story and criteria, resolving gaps; test cases follow, written by the team or the tester, as examples. Order: positive cases first, then negative cases, then non-functional characteristics. Tests cover every characteristic of the story without going beyond it, no two describe the same characteristic, and they are understandable to stakeholders. Automated, they become executable requirements.

blocks.title: Syllabus references
blocks.text: CTFL syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.5 (starts on p. 45). Learning objectives: FL-4.5.1 (K2), FL-4.5.2 (K2), FL-4.5.3 (K3). Read the full section and the chapter keyword list alongside this lesson.

blocks.title: From user story to acceptance criteria
blocks.text:
A user story describes a feature of value to a user or purchaser. Its three critical aspects are the 3 C's: the Card (the medium that carries the story), the Conversation (how the software will be used, written or spoken) and the Confirmation (the acceptance criteria).

The usual format is: "As a [role], I want [goal], so that I can [business value]", followed by the acceptance criteria.

Writing the story together, with techniques such as brainstorming and mind mapping, gives the team a shared vision from three perspectives: business, development and testing.

A good story is INVEST: Independent, Negotiable, Valuable, Estimable, Small and Testable. If a stakeholder cannot say how to test a story, the story may be unclear, it may not be valuable to them, or they may just need help with testing.

Acceptance criteria are the conditions the implementation must meet to be accepted. They are, in effect, the test conditions. They define the scope of the story, help stakeholders reach consensus, describe positive and negative scenarios, are the basis for acceptance testing, and allow accurate planning and estimation.

blocks.title: The same criterion in both formats
blocks.text:
Story: "As a customer, I want free delivery on larger orders, so that I can save money."

Scenario-oriented (Given/When/Then, as in BDD):
Given a basket worth £60, when the customer chooses standard delivery, then the delivery charge is £0.
Given a basket worth £40, when the customer chooses standard delivery, then the delivery charge is £4.

Rule-oriented, as a bullet-point verification list:
- Standard delivery is free for baskets of £50 or more.
- Express delivery is never free.

Rule-oriented criteria can also be a table that maps input to output, as below. Any other format is acceptable too, as long as the criteria are well-defined and unambiguous.

lessons.title: Lab · Deriving tests with ATDD
lessons.summary: Turn a user story and its acceptance criteria into the right set of test cases, in the right order.

blocks.title: The method
blocks.text:
Acceptance test-driven development (ATDD) is a test-first approach: the test cases are written before the user story is implemented. They are created by people with different perspectives, typically a customer or business representative, a developer and a tester.

1. Hold a specification workshop. The team analyses and discusses the user story and its acceptance criteria, and writes the criteria if they do not exist yet. Gaps, ambiguities and defects in the story are resolved here.
2. Create the test cases from the acceptance criteria. The team can do this together, or the tester alone. The tests are examples of how the software works, so "example" and "test" mean the same thing here.
3. Follow the usual order:
   - first positive test cases: correct behaviour, no exceptions or error conditions, everything goes as expected;
   - then negative test cases: error conditions and refusals;
   - finally non-functional characteristics, such as performance efficiency or usability.
4. Write each test so that stakeholders can understand it: natural-language sentences with preconditions (if any), inputs and postconditions. Given/When/Then is a common way to do this.
5. Check the set against three rules:
   - it covers all characteristics of the user story;
   - it does not go beyond the story;
   - no two test cases describe the same characteristic.
6. If the tests are written in a format a test automation framework supports, developers automate them while implementing the story. The acceptance tests then become executable requirements.

Test techniques from the rest of chapter 4 can be used while designing the tests, for example boundary values for a limit in a criterion.

blocks.title: Worked example 1: first test, next test, last test
blocks.text:
Story: "As a customer, I want to return an item online so that I get my money back."
Criteria: (1) returns are possible within 30 days of delivery; (2) a return label is e-mailed; (3) "final sale" items cannot be returned; (4) the refund goes to the original payment method.

Positive (written first):
Given an item delivered 10 days ago that is not final sale, when the customer requests a return, then a label is e-mailed and the refund goes to the original payment method.

Negative (written next):
Given an item delivered 31 days ago, when the customer requests a return, then the request is refused.
Given a final-sale item delivered 5 days ago, when the customer requests a return, then the request is refused.

Non-functional (written last, and only for what the story asks). Suppose the team adds criterion 5, "the label arrives within one minute":
Given a return request, when it is approved, then the label e-mail arrives within one minute.

If a question asks "which test case is written first?", choose the one in which nothing goes wrong.

blocks.title: Worked example 2: checking a set of tests against the criteria
blocks.text:
Story: "As an accountant, I want to export the monthly invoices as a spreadsheet."
Criteria: (1) every invoice of the chosen month is exported; (2) amounts keep two decimals; (3) a month without invoices gives a file with headings only; (4) only the Finance role can export.

Proposed tests:
T1 export March (12 invoices), all 12 present
T2 export April (3 invoices), all 3 present
T3 the amount 19.50 is exported as 19.50
T4 a user without the Finance role cannot export
T5 the export can be sent by e-mail from the app

Make a small table: criterion 1 is covered by T1 and T2; criterion 2 by T3; criterion 3 by nothing; criterion 4 by T4. T5 traces to no criterion.

Findings: T1 and T2 describe the same characteristic, so one should go. Criterion 3 has no test. T5 goes beyond the story: remove it, or raise it as a new story.

blocks.title: Worked example 3: a gap found in the workshop
blocks.text:
Story: "As a diner, I want to book a table online."
Criterion 1: "A table can be booked for 1 to 8 guests."

The tester asks: what happens with 9 guests? The criterion does not say. The developer assumes an error message; the product owner wants a note "please phone us for larger groups".

In ATDD this is settled in the specification workshop, before any code exists. The criterion is completed, and a negative test is written:
Given 9 guests, when the diner tries to book, then the message "please phone us for larger groups" is shown and no booking is made.

This is not "going beyond the story". The acceptance criteria may detail issues described in the story; what is forbidden is testing behaviour that neither the story nor its criteria contain, such as paying a deposit.

The limit also invites boundary values: 1 and 8 as positive tests, 0 and 9 as negative ones.

blocks.title: Common traps
blocks.text:
- Choosing a negative or a performance test as the "first" test. Positive comes first.
- Thinking negative tests are not part of ATDD. They are the second step.
- Calling a test that clarifies a criterion "beyond the story". Beyond means outside the story and all of its criteria.
- Accepting two tests for the same characteristic because the data differs. Different months with invoices are the same characteristic; a month without invoices is a different one.
- Believing the tests are written after coding, or by the developer alone. They come first and involve several perspectives.
- Writing tests in technical jargon. Stakeholders must be able to read them.
- Thinking automation ends manual testing. ATDD test cases may be executed manually or automated.

blocks.title: Exercise
blocks.text:
Story: "As a registered user, I want to reset my password by e-mail."
Criteria: (1) a reset link is sent to the registered address; (2) the link works once and for 30 minutes; (3) the new password must differ from the last three.

Tests drafted: A) a user requests a reset and sets a new password with a fresh link; B) a link opened after 45 minutes is refused; C) a link opened a second time is refused; D) the user changes the e-mail address in the profile.

a) Which test is written first?
b) Which test goes beyond the story?
c) Name a negative test that is still missing.

blocks.title: Worked solution
blocks.text:
a) A, the positive case.
b) D. Changing the e-mail address is not in the story or its criteria.
c) B and C are the negative tests for the two parts of criterion 2 (time limit and single use). Criterion 3 has none: "a new password equal to one of the last three is rejected". Criterion 1 could have one too: "a reset request for an unregistered address sends no link".

blocks.title: Syllabus reference
blocks.text: CTFL syllabus v4.0.1, section 4.5.3; learning objective FL-4.5.3 (K3). K3 means you must be able to apply the technique to a new situation, so practise until you can do each step without looking at this page.

lessons.title: 5.1 · Planning, estimates and priorities
lessons.summary: Connect plans and criteria with effort estimates, coverage priorities, pyramids and quadrants.

blocks.title: Understand
blocks.text: A test plan states objectives, scope, approach, resources, schedule, responsibilities and criteria. Testers contribute to release and iteration planning by identifying risks, testability concerns and effort. Entry criteria describe conditions for starting an activity; exit criteria describe conditions for completion. Estimate effort from relevant historical ratios, extrapolation, expert consensus or three-point estimates. In the three-point formula used here, E = (optimistic + 4 × most likely + pessimistic) / 6. State assumptions and uncertainty. Prioritize by risk, coverage or requirements importance, then account for dependencies and resources. A test pyramid favors many small fast checks and fewer broad slower checks. Testing quadrants organize technology/business focus and support/critiquing purpose: Q1 component checks, Q2 business-facing examples supporting work, Q3 business-facing evaluation, Q4 technology-facing quality evaluation. A related three-point uncertainty estimate is SD=(pessimistic−optimistic)/6; for O=6 and P=18 days, SD=2 days. This is distinct from expected effort.

blocks.title: Worked example
blocks.text: For O=4, M=7 and P=16 hours, E=(4+28+16)/6=8 hours. If execution of a high-risk payment test requires account setup, setup must run first. A coverage-based order starts with the case covering the most items; additional-coverage ordering then chooses cases covering the most still-uncovered items.

blocks.title: Common exam trap
blocks.text: An estimate is not a commitment without uncertainty. Highest priority does not override a prerequisite. Quadrants are not chronological phases or fixed test levels.

blocks.title: Self-check and solution
blocks.text: Three teams report 10, 14 and 18 hours. Can their arithmetic mean alone remove uncertainty? No: discuss assumptions. If T1 covers A,B,C; T2 covers B,C; T3 covers D,E, additional-coverage order is T1,T3,T2.

blocks.title: Connect planning, criteria and uncertainty
blocks.text: A plan communicates scope, objectives, basis, risks, approach, responsibilities, data, environments, budget and schedule. Release planning spans iterations; iteration planning refines immediate tasks. Entry criteria identify prerequisites; exit criteria identify completion expectations. Deadline expiry does not turn unmet criteria into satisfied criteria: report the gap and seek an informed decision. Estimates can use historical ratios, extrapolation, expert consensus or three points. State assumptions. The pyramid suggests many fast isolated checks and fewer broad checks; quadrants classify focus and purpose rather than sequence.

blocks.title: Worked case: estimates and prioritization
blocks.text:
A historical test/development ratio of 0.4 with 50 developer-days suggests 20 tester-days if context is comparable. With O=4, M=7, P=16 days, E=(4+4x7+16)/6=8 days and SD=(16-4)/6=2 days.
T1 covers A,B,C; T2 A,B; T3 D,E. Total coverage places T1 first. After T1, additional coverage prefers T3 because it adds two items while T2 adds none. Dependencies can constrain the execution order.

blocks.title: Exercise
blocks.text: Calculate E and SD for O=3, M=6, P=15 days. T2 covers Q,R,S and is selected; T1 covers P,Q and T3 T,U. Which adds more? Classify component checks, guiding acceptance examples, user exploration and load evaluation into quadrants.

blocks.title: Worked solution
blocks.text: E=(3+24+15)/6=7 days; SD=(15-3)/6=2 days. T1 adds P; T3 adds T,U, so prefer T3 for additional coverage. Component support is Q1; business examples guiding development Q2; user-focused critique Q3; technology-focused load critique Q4. These models support decisions but do not prescribe a single fixed execution sequence.

blocks.title: Syllabus details to know
blocks.text:
A test plan documents means and schedule, helps meet criteria, communicates with stakeholders and shows adherence to, or deviation from, the test policy and test strategy. Content: context (scope, objectives, basis), assumptions and constraints, stakeholders, communication, risk register, test approach (levels, types, techniques, deliverables, entry and exit criteria, independence, metrics, data and environment requirements, deviations), budget and schedule.
Release planning: testers write testable stories and acceptance criteria, join risk analyses, estimate effort for stories, determine the test approach and plan release testing. Iteration planning: detailed story risk analysis, testability, breaking stories into testing tasks, estimating task effort and refining functional and non-functional aspects.
Entry criteria: available resources, available testware and an initial quality level such as passed smoke tests. Exit criteria: thoroughness measures (coverage, unresolved defects, defect density, failed tests) and yes/no criteria (planned tests run, static testing done, defects reported, regression tests automated). Running out of time or budget can be a valid exit if stakeholders accept the risk. Agile terms: Definition of Done (exit) and Definition of Ready (entry).
Estimation: decompose large tasks. Ratios: a 3:2 development-to-test ratio with 600 person-days of development gives 400. Extrapolation: for example the average of the last three iterations. Wideband Delphi: experts estimate in isolation, discuss estimates outside agreed boundaries and re-estimate until consensus; Planning Poker is a variant. Three-point: E = (a + 4m + b)/6, SD = (b - a)/6; a=6, m=9, b=18 gives 10 ± 2.
Prioritization: risk-based, coverage-based (including additional coverage) and requirements-based, adjusted for dependencies and for the availability of resources such as tools, environments or people. Test pyramid: higher layers have lower granularity, lower isolation and longer execution times (for example unit, service and UI tests). Quadrants: Q1 component and component integration tests, automated in CI; Q2 functional tests, examples, story tests, UX prototypes, API testing and simulations; Q3 exploratory, usability and user acceptance testing; Q4 smoke tests and non-functional tests except usability.

blocks.title: Syllabus references
blocks.text: CTFL syllabus v4.0.1, section 5.1 (starts on p. 48). Learning objectives: FL-5.1.1 (K2), FL-5.1.2 (K1), FL-5.1.3 (K2), FL-5.1.4 (K3), FL-5.1.5 (K3), FL-5.1.6 (K1), FL-5.1.7 (K2). Read the full section and the chapter keyword list alongside this lesson.

blocks.title: Entry criteria, exit criteria and their Agile names
blocks.text:
Entry criteria are the preconditions for starting an activity. If they are not met, the activity is likely to be harder, slower, costlier and riskier. Typical examples: resources are available (people, tools, environments, test data, budget, time); testware is available (test basis, testable requirements, user stories, test cases); and the test object has an initial quality level, for example all smoke tests have passed.

Exit criteria say what must be achieved to call the activity complete. Typical examples: measures of thoroughness (coverage achieved, number of unresolved defects, defect density, number of failed test cases) and yes/no criteria (planned tests executed, static testing performed, all defects found are reported, all regression tests automated).

Running out of time or budget can also be a valid exit criterion, if the stakeholders have reviewed and accepted the risk of going live without further testing.

In Agile development, the entry criteria a user story must meet before work starts are the Definition of Ready, and the exit criteria for a releasable item are the Definition of Done.

Quick test for a question: is it something you need before you can begin (entry), or something you measure to decide you can stop (exit)?

blocks.title: The test pyramid and the testing quadrants
blocks.text:
The test pyramid shows that tests have different granularity, and it supports decisions on test automation and effort allocation. Bottom layer: small, isolated, fast tests that each check a small piece of functionality, so many are needed. Top layer: complex, high-level, end-to-end tests that are slower and each check a large piece, so few are needed. The higher the layer, the lower the granularity and isolation and the longer the execution time. The original model has unit, service and UI tests; another common version has unit (component), integration and end-to-end tests.

The testing quadrants group test levels, test types, activities and work products in Agile development. Two questions define them: is the test business facing or technology facing, and does it support the team (guide development) or critique the product (measure it against expectations)?

The table below lists the four quadrants. Memory aid: Q1 and Q2 support the team; Q2 and Q3 are business facing.

blocks.title: The four testing quadrants
rows: Component tests and component integration tests
Functional tests, examples, user story tests, user experience prototypes, API testing, simulations
Manual or automated; check the acceptance criteria
Exploratory testing, usability testing, user acceptance testing
Smoke tests and non-functional tests except usability tests

lessons.title: Lab · Estimating test effort
lessons.summary: Calculate with ratios, extrapolation and three-point estimation, and know how Wideband Delphi and Planning Poker run.

blocks.title: The four techniques
blocks.text:
Estimation predicts the effort needed for the testing. It rests on assumptions and is always subject to error; estimates for small tasks are usually more accurate than for large ones, so large tasks are broken down first.

1. Estimation based on ratios. Use figures from earlier, similar projects to derive a standard ratio, then apply it. If development to test effort was 3:2 and development is now estimated at 600 person-days, testing is 600 × 2 ÷ 3 = 400 person-days.

2. Extrapolation. Measure as early as possible in the current project and project forward. A team may take the test effort of the next iteration to be the average of the last three iterations.

3. Wideband Delphi. Experts estimate alone. The results are collected; if they deviate beyond the agreed range, the experts discuss their reasons and then estimate again alone. This repeats until consensus. Planning Poker is a variant used in Agile teams, with cards showing the effort size.

4. Three-point estimation. Experts give three values: the most optimistic (a), the most likely (m) and the most pessimistic (b).
   Estimate E = (a + 4m + b) ÷ 6
   Standard deviation SD = (b − a) ÷ 6
   The result is reported as E ± SD.

Ratios and extrapolation are metrics-based: they use data. Wideband Delphi and three-point estimation are expert-based.

blocks.title: Worked example 1: ratio
blocks.text:
In the last three releases of a billing system, development and test effort were in the ratio 5:3. Development of the next release is estimated at 450 person-days.

Set it up as "3 test for every 5 development":
Test effort = 450 × 3 ÷ 5 = 270 person-days.

Check the direction: the test share (3) is smaller than the development share (5), so the answer must be smaller than 450. The upside-down calculation, 450 × 5 ÷ 3 = 750, fails that check.

If the question gives the total instead ("the project is 800 person-days in total"), split by parts: 800 × 3 ÷ 8 = 300 for testing.

blocks.title: Worked example 2: extrapolation
blocks.text:
a) Average of recent iterations. Test effort in the first five iterations was 52, 40, 44, 46 and 48 person-hours. The team extrapolates with the average of the last three:
(44 + 46 + 48) ÷ 3 = 46 person-hours for iteration six. The first two values are ignored, even though 52 is the largest.

b) Rate so far. 60 of 200 requirements have been tested in 45 person-days. The rate is 45 ÷ 60 = 0.75 person-days per requirement. Remaining: 140 requirements, so 140 × 0.75 = 105 person-days.

Read whether the question asks for the remaining effort (105) or the total effort (200 × 0.75 = 150).

blocks.title: Worked example 3: three-point estimation with a range
blocks.text:
The team estimates a regression test: optimistic 10, most likely 14, pessimistic 24 person-hours.

E = (10 + 4 × 14 + 24) ÷ 6 = (10 + 56 + 24) ÷ 6 = 90 ÷ 6 = 15 person-hours.

Now a = 12, m = 18, b = 30:
E = (12 + 72 + 30) ÷ 6 = 114 ÷ 6 = 19
SD = (30 − 12) ÷ 6 = 3
Reported as 19 ± 3 person-hours, that is between 16 and 22.

Order of work that avoids slips: multiply m by 4 first, add the three numbers, divide by 6 last. The most likely value does not appear in the SD formula at all.

blocks.title: Common traps
blocks.text:
- Taking the plain average (a + m + b) ÷ 3. For 10, 14, 24 that gives 16, not 15. The most likely value counts four times, and the divisor is 6.
- Dividing by 4 or 5 instead of 6.
- Using m in the standard deviation, or dividing (b − a) by 2 or 3.
- Turning a ratio upside down. Always sanity-check which side should be larger.
- Averaging all iterations when the method says "the last three".
- Giving the total when the remaining effort is asked, or the reverse.
- Describing Wideband Delphi as "take the average of the experts" or "take the highest". The point is the repeated cycle: estimate alone, discuss the differences, estimate again, until consensus.
- In Planning Poker, dropping the outlier. The people with the extreme cards explain first; then everyone plays again.

blocks.title: Exercise
blocks.text:
a) Optimistic 4, most likely 7, pessimistic 16 person-days. Give E and SD.
b) Development to test ratio 7:2, development 840 person-days. Test effort?
c) 120 of 300 test cases were run in 80 person-hours. Remaining effort?
d) Four experts estimate 30, 34, 36 and 70 person-hours alone. What happens next in Wideband Delphi?

blocks.title: Worked solution
blocks.text:
a) E = (4 + 28 + 16) ÷ 6 = 48 ÷ 6 = 8 person-days. SD = (16 − 4) ÷ 6 = 2. Report 8 ± 2.
b) 840 × 2 ÷ 7 = 240 person-days.
c) 80 ÷ 120 per test case, times 180 remaining = 120 person-hours.
d) The experts discuss why they differ, especially the 70, and then each estimates again alone. This repeats until they agree.

blocks.title: Syllabus reference
blocks.text: CTFL syllabus v4.0.1, section 5.1.4; learning objective FL-5.1.4 (K3). K3 means you must be able to apply the technique to a new situation, so practise until you can do each step without looking at this page.

lessons.title: Lab · Prioritizing test cases
lessons.summary: Order tests by risk, by coverage and by requirement priority, and handle dependencies correctly.

blocks.title: The three strategies and the dependency rule
blocks.text:
Once test cases and procedures exist, they are put into a test execution schedule. The order matters because testing may stop early: the most important tests should already have run.

1. Risk-based prioritization. The order follows the results of risk analysis. Tests covering the most important risks run first.

2. Coverage-based prioritization. The order follows coverage, for example statement coverage. Tests achieving the highest coverage run first. In the variant called additional coverage prioritization, the test with the highest coverage runs first, and each following test is the one that adds the most coverage not yet achieved.

3. Requirements-based prioritization. The order follows the priorities of the requirements, which stakeholders define. Tests for the most important requirements run first.

The dependency rule. Ideally tests run in priority order. But if a test with a higher priority depends on a test with a lower priority, the lower-priority test must run first. The availability of resources, such as a test tool, an environment or a person who is only there at certain times, can change the order too.

Method for any ordering question:
1. Work out the pure priority order first.
2. Go down that list. Before placing a test, place everything it depends on (and whatever those depend on).
3. Never place a test twice.

blocks.title: Worked example 1: risk-based order
blocks.text: Each test covers one risk. Risk level = likelihood × impact, both on a scale of 1 to 5.

blocks.title: The order
blocks.text:
Highest level first: TC2, TC1, TC3, TC4.

Ordering by likelihood alone would put TC4 first, although its risk level is the lowest. Ordering by impact alone would put TC1 first. Always calculate the level.

blocks.title: Worked example 2: additional coverage
blocks.text:
Four tests cover these requirements:
TC1: 1, 2, 3, 4
TC2: 5, 6, 7, 8, 10
TC3: 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 11
TC4: 1, 2, 9

Step 1: highest total coverage is TC3 (6 requirements). Covered so far: 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 11.
Step 2: what does each remaining test add? TC1 adds 1, 2, 3, 4 (four new). TC2 adds only 10 (one new). TC4 adds 1, 2 (two new). Take TC1.
Step 3: covered now 1 to 9 and 11. TC2 adds 10 (one new). TC4 adds nothing. Take TC2, then TC4.

Order: TC3, TC1, TC2, TC4.

Plain "total coverage" ordering would be TC3, TC2, TC1, TC4, because TC2 covers five requirements. But four of TC2's five are already covered by TC3. Additional coverage recounts after every choice; that recount is the whole technique.

blocks.title: Worked example 3: priorities with dependencies
blocks.text:
Five tests, priority 1 is highest:
TC1: priority 2, can only run after TC2
TC2: priority 5
TC3: priority 1, can only run after TC4
TC4: priority 4
TC5: priority 3

Pure priority order: TC3, TC1, TC5, TC4, TC2.

Go down the list:
- TC3 needs TC4 first. Place TC4, then TC3.
- TC1 needs TC2 first. Place TC2, then TC1.
- TC5 has no dependency. Place TC5.
- TC4 and TC2 are already placed.

Order: TC4, TC3, TC2, TC1, TC5.

TC4 and TC2 have the lowest priorities and still run early, because important tests wait for them. A prerequisite is pulled forward to just before the test that needs it, not to the very start of the schedule.

blocks.title: Common traps
blocks.text:
- Ignoring dependencies and answering with the pure priority order. It is always offered as a wrong option.
- Running all prerequisites first and then everything else by priority. Pull each prerequisite forward only as far as needed.
- Missing a chain: if A needs B and B needs C, the order is C, B, A.
- In additional coverage, ordering once by total coverage and stopping. Recount what is new after each pick.
- Ordering risks by likelihood or impact alone.
- Reading the priority scale backwards. Check whether 1 is the highest or the lowest; in these questions 1 is normally the highest.

blocks.title: Exercise
blocks.text:
a) Risk levels: TC1 likelihood 5, impact 2; TC2 likelihood 3, impact 5; TC3 likelihood 4, impact 3; TC4 likelihood 2, impact 2. Give the order.
b) Priorities: TC1 = 3, TC2 = 1, TC3 = 4, TC4 = 2. TC2 can only run after TC3. Give the order.
c) Coverage: TC1 covers 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6; TC2 covers 4, 5, 6, 7, 8; TC3 covers 9, 10, 12; TC4 covers 7, 8, 9, 10, 11. Give the additional coverage order.

blocks.title: Worked solution
blocks.text:
a) Levels 10, 15, 12, 4: TC2, TC3, TC1, TC4.
b) Pure order TC2, TC4, TC1, TC3. TC2 needs TC3 first: TC3, TC2, TC4, TC1.
c) TC1 first (six). Then TC4 adds five (7 to 11), TC2 would add two, TC3 three: take TC4. Then TC3 adds one (12) and TC2 adds none: TC1, TC4, TC3, TC2.

blocks.title: Syllabus reference
blocks.text: CTFL syllabus v4.0.1, section 5.1.5; learning objective FL-5.1.5 (K3). K3 means you must be able to apply the technique to a new situation, so practise until you can do each step without looking at this page.

lessons.title: 5.2 · Risk management
lessons.summary: Assess project and product risks, choose mitigation and monitor remaining exposure.

blocks.title: Understand
blocks.text: A risk is an uncertain event with possible adverse consequences. Risk level combines likelihood and impact, often by multiplication of agreed scales. Project risks threaten delivery, such as staff loss or unavailable environments. Product risks threaten product quality, such as wrong payments or insecure access. Product risk analysis identifies and assesses risks; it guides scope, effort, techniques, coverage and priority. Possible responses include mitigation, acceptance, transfer and contingency planning. Testing reduces uncertainty and can reduce the probability of delivering defects, but residual risk remains and must be communicated.

blocks.title: Worked example
blocks.text: Risk A has likelihood 2 and impact 5, level 10; risk B has likelihood 4 and impact 2, level 8. Under that model A ranks higher. Delayed environment delivery is a project risk; incorrect transaction totals are a product risk. More thorough checks may be allocated to totals because financial consequences are severe.

blocks.title: Common exam trap
blocks.text: Risk likelihood is not impact. Multiplying ordinal ratings is a prioritization convention, not a precise probability of loss. A passing suite does not erase residual risk.

blocks.title: Self-check and solution
blocks.text: A release contains an untested authentication change. What should a status report include? The affected risk, missing evidence, consequences and proposed actions so the decision-maker can make an informed acceptance or mitigation decision.

blocks.title: Use risk assessment to choose actions
blocks.text: Identification lists adverse events; assessment considers likelihood, impact and priority. Project risks threaten schedule, resources or scope; product risks threaten delivered quality. Quantitative levels can multiply likelihood and impact; qualitative matrices use agreed categories. Ordinal scores are not calibrated probabilities. Risk-based testing uses the analysis to select levels, types, techniques, coverage and effort. Mitigation implements actions; monitoring checks their effectiveness and emerging exposure. Acceptance, transfer and contingency planning are other responses.

blocks.title: Worked case: invoice priorities
blocks.text: On a 1-5 scale, incorrect tax has likelihood 3 and impact 5, score 15; cosmetic alignment has 4 and 1, score 4. Prioritize tax-rule review, boundaries, combinations and regression. Separately, an unavailable test service threatens schedule: arrange controlled substitution and later real-interface evidence. Report remaining financial risk if needed data cannot be tested. These scores support comparison, not exact forecasts of failure rates.

blocks.title: Exercise
blocks.text: Authorization checks and tests mitigate invoice-access risk. What evidence should be monitored, and why is a falling overall defect count insufficient?

blocks.title: Worked solution
blocks.text: Monitor relevant role/ownership coverage, denied-access outcomes, unresolved findings and new paths introduced by changes. Reassess the risk using this evidence. A falling count can reflect less testing or fewer cosmetic findings; it does not establish effective mitigation of unauthorized access.

blocks.title: Syllabus details to know
blocks.text:
Risk management has two parts: risk analysis (identification and assessment) and risk control (mitigation and monitoring). Risk-based testing selects, prioritizes and manages test activities from them. Risk likelihood is a probability greater than zero and less than one; impact is the harm.
Project risks: organizational (late deliveries, inaccurate estimates, cost cutting), people (skills, conflicts, communication, staff shortage), technical (scope creep, poor tool support) and supplier (third-party delivery failure, bankruptcy). They affect schedule, budget or scope. Product risks relate to quality characteristics: missing or wrong functionality, incorrect calculations, runtime errors, poor architecture, inefficient algorithms, slow response, poor user experience, security vulnerabilities. Possible consequences: user dissatisfaction, lost revenue, trust or reputation, damage to third parties, high maintenance costs, help desk overload, criminal penalties, and in extreme cases physical damage, injury or death.
Identification uses brainstorming, workshops, interviews or cause-effect diagrams. Assessment categorizes risks, determines likelihood, impact and level, prioritizes and proposes responses, quantitatively (likelihood × impact) or qualitatively (risk matrix). Results determine test scope, levels and types, techniques and coverage, effort, prioritization, and other risk-reducing activities.
Responses: mitigation by testing, acceptance, transfer or a contingency plan. Mitigation by testing: suitably skilled testers, appropriate independence, reviews and static analysis, suitable techniques and coverage, suitable test types, and dynamic and regression testing. Monitoring checks that mitigation works, improves assessment and finds emerging risks.

blocks.title: Syllabus references
blocks.text: CTFL syllabus v4.0.1, section 5.2 (starts on p. 51). Learning objectives: FL-5.2.1 (K1), FL-5.2.2 (K2), FL-5.2.3 (K2), FL-5.2.4 (K2). Read the full section and the chapter keyword list alongside this lesson.

blocks.title: Risk, step by step
blocks.text:
A risk is a potential event whose occurrence causes an adverse effect. It has a likelihood and an impact, and together they give the risk level. In the quantitative approach, risk level = likelihood × impact; in the qualitative approach a risk matrix is used.

Project risks concern the management and control of the project. They threaten schedule, budget or scope. Categories: organisational issues (late deliveries, inaccurate estimates, cost cutting), people issues (insufficient skills, conflicts, communication problems, staff shortage), technical issues (scope creep, poor tool support) and supplier issues (a third party fails to deliver or goes bankrupt).

Product risks concern the quality characteristics of the product: missing or wrong functionality, incorrect calculations, runtime errors, poor architecture, inefficient algorithms, inadequate response time, poor user experience, security vulnerabilities. Their consequences fall on users and the business: dissatisfaction, loss of revenue, trust or reputation, damage to third parties, high maintenance costs, an overloaded help desk, criminal penalties and, in extreme cases, injury or death.

Quick test: "would it hurt the project plan?" is a project risk; "would it hurt someone using the product?" is a product risk.

Risk management has two parts. Risk analysis is risk identification (a comprehensive list, from brainstorming, workshops, interviews or cause-effect diagrams) followed by risk assessment (categorise, determine likelihood, impact and level, prioritise, propose handling). Risk control is risk mitigation (carrying out the proposed actions) followed by risk monitoring (checking that mitigation works, improving the assessment, spotting emerging risks).

Product risk analysis shapes the testing: the scope, the test levels and types, the techniques and coverage, the effort per task, and the order, so that critical defects are found as early as possible.

Responses to an analysed risk: mitigation by testing, acceptance, transfer, or a contingency plan. Mitigation by testing means choosing testers with the right experience, the right level of independence, reviews and static analysis, suitable techniques and coverage levels, test types for the affected characteristics, and dynamic testing including regression testing.

lessons.title: 5.3 · Monitoring, control and communication
lessons.summary: Interpret metric denominators and report scope, blockers and consequences for decisions.

blocks.title: Understand
blocks.text: Monitor progress, coverage, defects, effort, cost and quality signals against the plan. Metrics need context: counts of executed tests say little without scope, results and risk. Control actions may change priorities, resources, schedule or scope in response to evidence. Progress reports support ongoing decisions; completion reports summarize achieved objectives, results, deviations and unresolved risks at a milestone. Tailor detail and format to the audience. Developers may need reproducible findings; managers need consequences and decisions; distributed teams benefit from clear written records in addition to discussion.

blocks.title: Worked example
blocks.text: A report says 80 of 100 tests ran, with 12 failures concentrated in checkout and 20 security cases blocked by an environment issue. A manager sees release exposure, while engineers receive failure details. A control action restores the environment and brings high-risk security checks forward.

blocks.title: Common exam trap
blocks.text: A high pass percentage can conceal missing high-risk coverage. Reports should distinguish what was tested from what remains unknown.

blocks.title: Self-check and solution
blocks.text: The plan expects 90 executions, but 45 are complete. Identifying the deviation is monitoring; deciding to reallocate engineers is control. For a release meeting, include residual risk and decision requests rather than only raw logs.

blocks.title: Give metrics a denominator and a decision
blocks.text: Monitoring gathers progress, quality, defect, coverage, cost and risk evidence. Control changes priorities, resources, scope or schedule in response. Completion consolidates evidence and reusable testware at milestones. Progress reports support ongoing control; completion reports summarize achieved objectives, deviations and remaining issues. Tailor detail to the audience. Record build and scope, distinguish failed, blocked and unexecuted cases, and state the denominator. A developer needs reproduction evidence; a sponsor needs release implications.

blocks.title: Worked case: interpret pass rate
blocks.text: Of 120 planned cases, 80 passed, 10 failed, 20 are blocked and 10 unexecuted. Executed-case pass rate is 80/90, about 88.9%; planned-case pass percentage is 80/120, about 66.7%; execution progress is 90/120=75%. None establishes risk coverage. If blocked cases concern settlements, restore that environment or communicate the gap rather than simply running more already-covered checks.

blocks.title: Exercise
blocks.text: A release has completed 95% of cases, but the remaining 5% concerns deletion and retention of personal data. Outline a useful stakeholder update.

blocks.title: Worked solution
blocks.text: State the build and completed scope, the untested scenarios and consequences, the blocker, owner and expected resolution. Identify unmet exit criteria and residual risk. Request a decision about further testing or an explicit exception. A percentage without the high-impact gap can mislead stakeholders.

blocks.title: Syllabus details to know
blocks.text:
Test monitoring gathers information to assess progress and exit criteria. Test control issues control directives, for example reprioritizing when a risk becomes an issue, re-evaluating entry or exit criteria after rework, adjusting the schedule for a late environment, or adding resources. Test completion happens when a level, iteration, project (completed or cancelled), release or maintenance release ends.
Metric categories: project progress (task completion, resource use, effort); test progress (implementation and environment progress, run/not run, passed/failed, execution time); product quality (availability, response time, mean time to failure); defect (number and priority found or fixed, defect density, defect detection percentage); risk (residual risk level); coverage (requirements, code); and cost (cost of testing, cost of quality).
Progress reports, produced regularly, contain the testing period, progress and notable deviations, impediments and workarounds, metrics, new and changed risks, and testing planned for the next period. Completion reports contain a summary, evaluation against the plan's objectives and exit criteria, deviations from the plan, impediments, metrics, unmitigated risks and unfixed defects, and lessons learned. Reporting within the team is frequent and informal; completion reporting follows a template and occurs once. ISO/IEC/IEEE 29119-3 calls progress reports test status reports.
Communication options: verbal, dashboards (CI/CD dashboards, task boards, burn-down charts), email or chat, online documentation and formal reports. Distributed teams may need more formal communication, and content should be tailored to each stakeholder.

blocks.title: Syllabus references
blocks.text: CTFL syllabus v4.0.1, section 5.3 (starts on p. 53). Learning objectives: FL-5.3.1 (K1), FL-5.3.2 (K2), FL-5.3.3 (K2). Read the full section and the chapter keyword list alongside this lesson.

blocks.title: Monitoring, control, completion and their reports
blocks.text:
Test monitoring gathers information to assess progress and to see whether the exit criteria are being met. Test control uses that information to issue control directives: reprioritising tests when a risk becomes an issue, re-evaluating entry or exit criteria after rework, adjusting the schedule when the environment is late, adding resources. Test completion collects experience, testware and other information at a milestone.

Metric categories, with one example each: project progress (task completion), test progress (test cases run, passed, failed), product quality (mean time to failure), defect (defect density), risk (residual risk level), coverage (requirements coverage) and cost (cost of testing).

A test progress report is produced regularly during testing and supports control. It contains: the testing period; progress, including notable deviations; impediments and workarounds; test metrics; new and changed risks; and testing planned for the next period.

A test completion report is produced once, at completion. It contains: a test summary; an evaluation of testing and product quality against the original test plan; deviations from the plan; impediments and workarounds; test metrics; unmitigated risks and unfixed defects; and lessons learned.

How to tell them apart in a question: "planned for next period" belongs only to the progress report; "lessons learned" and "evaluation against the original plan" belong only to the completion report.

Status can be communicated verbally, through dashboards (CI/CD dashboards, task boards, burn-down charts), through electronic channels such as e-mail and chat, in online documentation or in formal reports. Tailor it to the audience, and prefer more formal communication for distributed teams.

lessons.title: 5.4 · Configuration management
lessons.summary: Preserve versioned configurations and baselines so results remain reproducible.

blocks.title: Understand
blocks.text: Configuration management identifies, versions, controls and relates items needed for reproducible testing. Relevant items include requirements, builds, tests, data, environment configuration and results. A baseline is an agreed set of versions that can be referenced consistently. Traceability plus version control helps determine which result applies to which product and test basis. Controlled changes make impact analysis and investigation more reliable.

blocks.title: Worked example
blocks.text: A test result links application build 82, requirement revision 4, test suite 11 and data set 6. When a failure cannot be reproduced on build 83, the team can restore the original baseline and compare the change.

blocks.title: Common exam trap
blocks.text: A test result detached from its build and environment may be misleading even if the test passed. Versioning source code alone does not control all test dependencies.

blocks.title: Self-check and solution
blocks.text: Which information makes a data-dependent failure reproducible? The product version, procedure, environment and data version, as well as actual and expected results. “It failed last week” is insufficient.

blocks.title: Preserve the configuration behind observations
blocks.text: Configuration management identifies and controls basis, build, cases, data, environment settings, tools and results. A baseline is an agreed configuration that can be referenced consistently. Traceability relates items; versions distinguish revisions. A result without its build and data revision may become uninterpretable after a change. Preserve controlled changes and status information to support reproduction, impact analysis and understanding which configurations have actually been evaluated.

blocks.title: Worked case: different currency totals
