Entry and exit criteria for each test level
The risk register for product and project risks
Defect reports raised during execution

questions.explanation: Typical test plan content includes the context of testing, assumptions and constraints, stakeholders, communication, the risk register, the test approach with its entry and exit criteria, and budget and schedule. Actual results and defect reports come from execution, and lessons learned belong to test completion. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.1.1 (p. 48); FL-5.1.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: In which testing quadrant does the syllabus place smoke tests?

options.text: Q3: business facing, critique the product
Q4: technology facing, critique the product
Q2: business facing, support the team
Q1: technology facing, support the team

questions.explanation: Quadrant Q4, technology facing and critiquing the product, contains smoke tests and non-functional tests other than usability, which are often automated. Q1 holds component and component integration tests, Q2 functional tests and examples, and Q3 exploratory, usability and user acceptance testing. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.1.7 (p. 51); FL-5.1.7 (K2).

questions.prompt: A team writes API tests and simulations that check acceptance criteria while a feature is being developed. Which quadrant fits these tests?

options.text: Q4
Q3
Q2
Q1

questions.explanation: Q2, business facing and supporting the team, contains functional tests, examples, user story tests, user experience prototypes, API testing and simulations that check acceptance criteria. Q1 contains component tests, Q3 user-oriented critique and Q4 technology-facing critique. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.1.7 (p. 51); FL-5.1.7 (K2).

questions.prompt: Select TWO kinds of testing that belong to quadrant Q3 (business facing, critique the product).

options.text: API testing
Component integration testing
User acceptance testing
Usability testing
Performance testing

questions.explanation: Q3 contains exploratory testing, usability testing and user acceptance testing, which are user-oriented and often manual. Component integration tests belong to Q1, API tests to Q2 and performance tests to Q4. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.1.7 (p. 51); FL-5.1.7 (K2).

questions.prompt: A company buys insurance against losses caused by failures of a new payment feature. Which response to product risk is this?

options.text: Risk acceptance
Contingency plan
Risk mitigation
Risk transfer

questions.explanation: Shifting the financial consequences to an insurer transfers the risk. Mitigation reduces the risk level, for example through testing; acceptance takes the risk knowingly; and a contingency plan prepares actions for when the risk occurs. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.2.4 (p. 53); FL-5.2.4 (K2).

questions.prompt: Which of the following is a project risk rather than a product risk?

options.text: Security vulnerabilities in login
Scope creep in the requirements
Poor user experience in checkout
Inefficient algorithms in the search

questions.explanation: Scope creep is a technical issue among project risks, which affect schedule, budget or scope. Inefficient algorithms, poor user experience and security vulnerabilities relate to product quality characteristics and are product risks. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.2.2 (p. 52); FL-5.2.2 (K2).

questions.prompt: Product risk analysis rates the payment module as the highest risk. Which use of this result is consistent with the syllabus?

options.text: Postponing payment tests until the final iteration
Reducing reviews because testing will find the defects
Choosing more rigorous techniques and higher coverage there
Assigning equal effort to all modules for fairness

questions.explanation: Product risk analysis results determine test scope, levels, types, techniques, coverage, effort and priority, so the highest-risk area gets more rigorous techniques and higher coverage and is tested early. Reducing reviews, equal effort and postponement ignore the analysis. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.2.3 (p. 52); FL-5.2.3 (K2).

questions.prompt: Which item typically appears in a test progress report and is absent from a test completion report?

options.text: Unmitigated risks and defects not fixed
Lessons learned that are relevant to testing
Testing planned for the next period
Final evaluation against the exit criteria

questions.explanation: Progress reports support ongoing control and include the testing period, progress, impediments, metrics, new and changed risks, and testing planned for the next period. Lessons learned, the final evaluation against exit criteria, and unmitigated risks with unfixed defects belong to the completion report. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.3.2 (p. 54); FL-5.3.2 (K2).

questions.prompt: How does test reporting within the team typically differ from test completion reporting?

options.text: It omits test metrics and impediments
It is written for external auditors alone
It is produced once, using a set template
It is frequent and informal rather than templated

questions.explanation: Test progress reporting to others in the same team is often frequent and informal, while test completion reporting follows a set template and occurs once. Different audiences need different information, formality and frequency. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.3.2 (p. 54); FL-5.3.2 (K2).

questions.prompt: A test team is distributed across three time zones. Which way of communicating test status is most appropriate?

options.text: No status communication until test completion
Identical detailed logs for every stakeholder
Verbal updates at a daily meeting in one office
More formal communication, such as written reports

questions.explanation: More formal communication may be more appropriate for distributed teams, where direct face-to-face communication is not always possible because of distance or time differences. Office-only verbal updates exclude remote members, and communication should be ongoing and tailored to stakeholders. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.3.3 (p. 55); FL-5.3.3 (K2).

questions.prompt: A test environment has been approved for testing and has become a baseline. How can it be changed afterwards?

options.text: It can never be changed after approval
Only through a formal change control process
By any tester who needs a different setting
By replacing it with the newest component versions

questions.explanation: Once a configuration item is approved for testing it becomes a baseline and can only be changed through a formal change control process. Uncontrolled edits or silently taking newer versions break reproducibility, and baselines can change, just not informally. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.4 (p. 56); FL-5.4.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: A defect report states that a failure occurred on last month's build. How does configuration management help the team investigate it?

options.text: It removes the need to record the test environment
It ensures that later builds behave identically
It allows reverting to a previous baseline to reproduce results
It replaces the defect workflow with version numbers

questions.explanation: Configuration management records changed items when a new baseline is created, making it possible to revert to a previous baseline and reproduce earlier test results. It still requires environments to be recorded, does not make builds behave identically, and complements defect management. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.4 (p. 56); FL-5.4.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: What does configuration management ensure in order to support testing?

options.text: Test cases are executed in order of their risk
Items are uniquely identified and version controlled
Results are reported to stakeholders daily
Defects are fixed before each new baseline

questions.explanation: Configuration management ensures that configuration items, including test items, are uniquely identified, version controlled, tracked for changes and related for traceability, and that testware references them unambiguously. Prioritization, defect fixing and daily reporting are other activities. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.4 (p. 56); FL-5.4.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: In a comparable previous project, the development-to-test effort ratio was 5:2. Development effort for the new project is estimated at 750 person-days. Using estimation based on ratios, what is the test effort estimate?

options.text: 300 person-days
1875 person-days
450 person-days
375 person-days

questions.explanation: With a development-to-test ratio of 5:2, test effort is 2/5 of development effort: 750 × 2 / 5 = 300 person-days. 1875 inverts the ratio, 450 uses 3/5 and 375 halves the development effort. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.1.4 (p. 49); FL-5.1.4 (K3).

questions.prompt: Test effort in the last three iterations was 24, 30 and 33 person-days. The team extrapolates the next iteration as the average of the last three. What is the estimate?

options.text: 33 person-days
30 person-days
29 person-days
87 person-days

questions.explanation: Extrapolating as the average of the last three iterations gives (24 + 30 + 33) / 3 = 29 person-days. 33 uses only the latest value, 30 is the median and 87 the total. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.1.4 (p. 49); FL-5.1.4 (K3).

questions.prompt: Experts estimate a test task as a = 4, m = 10 and b = 22 person-hours. Using three-point estimation with E = (a + 4m + b) / 6 and SD = (b − a) / 6, what is the estimate?

options.text: 11 ± 3 person-hours
10 ± 3 person-hours
11 ± 18 person-hours
12 ± 3 person-hours

questions.explanation: E = (4 + 4 × 10 + 22) / 6 = 66 / 6 = 11 and SD = (22 − 4) / 6 = 3, so the estimate is 11 ± 3 person-hours, that is 8 to 14. 10 is only the most likely value, 12 is the simple average of the three estimates, and 18 is b − a without dividing by 6. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.1.4 (p. 49); FL-5.1.4 (K3).

questions.prompt: In a Wideband Delphi estimation, three experts estimate 8, 9 and 20 days. The agreed boundary requires every estimate to lie within 25% of the median. What happens next?

options.text: The most experienced expert chooses the value
The average of 12.3 days becomes the estimate
The experts discuss, then each re-estimates in isolation
The highest estimate is accepted to be safe

questions.explanation: The median is 9 days, so 20 lies outside the agreed boundary of 6.75 to 11.25 days. In Wideband Delphi the experts then discuss their estimates and each makes a new estimate in isolation, repeating until consensus. Averaging, deferring to one expert or taking the maximum skips this feedback cycle. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.1.4 (p. 49); FL-5.1.4 (K3).

questions.prompt:
Test cases cover these requirements:
T1: R1, R2
T2: R2, R3, R4
T3: R1, R5
T4: R4
T5: R3, R4
Using additional coverage prioritization, which test case is executed second?

options.text: T1
T4
T5
T3

questions.explanation: T2 covers the most requirements (R2, R3, R4) and runs first. Additional coverage then counts only uncovered items: T3 adds R1 and R5, T1 adds R1, and T4 and T5 add nothing. T3 is therefore second, although T5 has the same total coverage as T3. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.1.5 (p. 50); FL-5.1.5 (K3).

questions.prompt: Test cases have these risk-based priorities: TC1 high, TC2 medium, TC3 high, TC4 low. TC3 needs a test environment that is available on day 2 alone; the others can run on day 1. Each day, all available test cases run in priority order. What is the execution order?

options.text: TC1, TC3, TC2, TC4
TC1, TC2, TC3, TC4
TC3, TC1, TC2, TC4
TC1, TC2, TC4, TC3

questions.explanation: On day 1 the available test cases run by priority: TC1 (high), TC2 (medium), TC4 (low). TC3 has high priority, but its environment is available only on day 2, so it runs last. The execution order must take the availability of resources into account. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.1.5 (p. 50); FL-5.1.5 (K3).

questions.prompt:
Statements covered by each test case:
T1: S1, S2, S3, S4
T2: S3, S4, S5, S6, S7, S8
T3: S1, S9
T4: S2, S10, S11
Using additional coverage prioritization, what is the execution order?
questions.explanation: T2 covers six statements and runs first. Of the uncovered S1, S2, S9, S10 and S11, T4 adds three, then T3 adds S1 and S9, and finally T1 adds nothing new. Ordering by total coverage instead would give T2, T1, T4, T3. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.1.5 (p. 50); FL-5.1.5 (K3).

questions.prompt: In release 3.2, applying voucher SAVE10 to a cart totalling 80.00 shows 88.00 where 72.00 is expected. Which defect report title is best?

options.text: Voucher SAVE10 raises cart total instead of reducing it
Voucher code contains a sign error in the discount calculation
Voucher SAVE10 does not work for some customers
Critical: vouchers must be fixed before the 3.2 release

questions.explanation: A title should give a short summary of the anomaly: what happens under which conditions. The vague title does not identify the anomaly, the sign-error title states an unverified cause, and the critical title expresses priority instead of describing the failure. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.5 (p. 56); FL-5.5.1 (K3).

questions.prompt: A defect report contains a unique ID, title, date and author, test object and environment, context with the test case and data, steps to reproduce with logs, actual result, severity, priority, status and a reference to the test case. Which essential element is missing?

options.text: The expected result
A summary of other test results
A proposed root cause
The configuration management plan

questions.explanation: A defect report should include both expected and actual results so readers can see why the behavior is an anomaly. A proposed cause is not required and may be wrong, and summaries of other results and configuration management plans are not defect report contents. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.5 (p. 56); FL-5.5.1 (K3).

questions.prompt: A developer fixes a reported defect and deploys the fix to the test environment. Which status should the defect report now have?

options.text: Deferred to a later release
Awaiting confirmation testing
Re-opened for further analysis
Closed as resolved by the developer

questions.explanation: After a fix is deployed, the report waits for confirmation testing, and it is closed only when that test passes. Deferred means that the fix is postponed, and re-opening applies when a confirmation test fails. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.5 (p. 56); FL-5.5.1 (K3).

questions.prompt: Analysis of a reported anomaly shows that the test's expected result was wrong and the software behaves correctly. How should the report be handled?

options.text: Reopen it as a high-severity defect
Defer it to the next planned release
Reject it as a false positive and fix the test
Close it as fixed after a confirmation test

questions.explanation: Reported anomalies may turn out to be something other than defects, such as false-positive results, and the workflow decides a suitable response: here, rejecting the report and correcting the test. Closing as fixed, deferring or reopening treats it as a real product defect. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.5 (p. 56); FL-5.5.1 (K3).

questions.prompt: A team uses containers to create identical test environments on demand for every pipeline run. To which tool category does this belong?

options.text: Scalability and deployment standardization tools
Test execution and test coverage tools
Non-functional testing tools for load and stress
Test design and test implementation tools

questions.explanation: Virtual machines and containerization tools support scalability and deployment standardization. Test design and implementation tools generate cases, data and procedures, execution and coverage tools run tests and measure coverage, and non-functional tools test characteristics such as performance under load. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 6.1 (p. 59); FL-6.1.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: A tool generates test data and test procedures from a model of the system. Which category of test tool is this?

options.text: Test design and test implementation tools
Test execution and coverage tools
Test management tools for tracking tests
DevOps tools for build pipelines

questions.explanation: Test design and implementation tools facilitate the generation of test cases, test data and test procedures. Management tools track tests, defects and requirements, DevOps tools support the delivery pipeline, and execution tools run tests and measure coverage. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 6.1 (p. 59); FL-6.1.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: A team uses a spreadsheet to record test conditions and their status. How does the syllabus classify the spreadsheet?

options.text: As a test execution tool
As a static analysis tool for documents
As no tool at all, since it is office software
As a test tool, because it assists in testing

questions.explanation: Any tool that assists in testing is a test tool; the syllabus notes that a spreadsheet is a test tool in the context of testing. It does not analyze work products statically or execute tests. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 6.1 (p. 59); FL-6.1.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: Which tool category supports the delivery pipeline, workflow tracking, automated builds and CI/CD?

options.text: DevOps tools
Test management tools
Static testing tools
Collaboration tools

questions.explanation: DevOps tools support the DevOps delivery pipeline, workflow tracking, automated build processes and CI/CD. Collaboration tools facilitate communication, test management tools manage tests and defects, and static testing tools support reviews and static analysis. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 6.1 (p. 59); FL-6.1.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: Which is a potential benefit of test automation?

options.text: Independence from the tool vendor's support
More objective assessment, such as coverage
Replacement of critical thinking by testers
No need for maintenance of test scripts

questions.explanation: Automation can provide more objective assessment, such as coverage, and measures too complicated for humans to determine. Scripts still need maintenance, dependency on a vendor is a risk, and relying on a tool instead of critical thinking is a risk. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 6.2 (p. 59); FL-6.2.1 (K1).

questions.prompt: Which is a risk of using an open-source test tool?

options.text: It cannot be used for regression testing
It costs more than comparable commercial tools
It removes the need to train the testers
It may be abandoned and receive no further updates

questions.explanation: A listed risk is that open-source software may be abandoned, so no further updates are available, or that its components need frequent updates. Higher cost, unsuitability for regression testing and removing the need for training are not risks the syllabus names. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 6.2 (p. 59); FL-6.2.1 (K1).

questions.prompt: Select TWO potential risks of test automation.

options.text: A tool that breaches regulatory or safety standards
Reduced test execution times and faster feedback
Easier access to statistics about test progress
A tool incompatible with the development platform
More time for testers to design deeper tests

questions.explanation: Risks include an automation tool that is not compatible with the development platform and choosing an unsuitable tool that does not comply with regulatory requirements or safety standards. Faster feedback, easier access to test information and more time for deeper tests are benefits. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 6.2 (p. 59); FL-6.2.1 (K1).

questions.prompt: Which is a potential benefit of test automation for test management and reporting?

options.text: Elimination of manual testing
Easier access to test progress statistics
Removal of the need for a test plan
Automatic acceptance of residual risks

questions.explanation: Automation gives easier access to information that supports test management and reporting, such as statistics, graphs and aggregated data about progress, failure rates and execution duration. It does not replace planning, decide on risk acceptance or remove the need for manual testing. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 6.2 (p. 59); FL-6.2.1 (K1).

questions.prompt: A lender's application form asks for the loan term in whole months. Terms of 6 to 12 months are handled as "Short", 13 to 36 months as "Medium" and 37 to 84 months as "Long". A term below 6 months or above 84 months is rejected with an error message. A tester wants 100% equivalence partition coverage of the term with the fewest test cases. Which set of input values achieves this?
questions.explanation: There are 5 partitions and each needs one value: 3 is in "Rejected: too short"; 9 is in "Short"; 24 is in "Medium"; 60 is in "Long"; 96 is in "Rejected: too long". The other sets either put two values in one partition and miss another, or cover every partition with more test cases than necessary. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.2.1 (p. 39); FL-4.2.1 (K3).

questions.prompt: A greenhouse controller reads the air temperature in whole degrees Celsius. Below 5 °C it raises a frost alarm, from 5 to 18 °C it switches the heating on, from 19 to 24 °C it stays idle, from 25 to 40 °C it switches the fans on, and above 40 °C it raises an overheat alarm. A tester wants 100% equivalence partition coverage of the temperature with the fewest test cases. Which set of input values achieves this?
questions.explanation: There are 5 partitions and each needs one value: -3 is in "Frost alarm"; 11 is in "Heating on"; 21 is in "Idle"; 33 is in "Fans on"; 47 is in "Overheat alarm". The other sets either put two values in one partition and miss another, or cover every partition with more test cases than necessary. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.2.1 (p. 39); FL-4.2.1 (K3).

questions.prompt: A fitness watch classifies the resting pulse it measures, in whole beats per minute. Below 40 it shows "Low alarm", from 40 to 59 "Low", from 60 to 100 "Normal", from 101 to 150 "Elevated" and above 150 "High alarm". A tester wants 100% equivalence partition coverage of the pulse with the fewest test cases. Which set of input values achieves this?
questions.explanation: There are 5 partitions and each needs one value: 32 is in "Low alarm"; 48 is in "Low"; 75 is in "Normal"; 130 is in "Elevated"; 170 is in "High alarm". The other sets either put two values in one partition and miss another, or cover every partition with more test cases than necessary. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.2.1 (p. 39); FL-4.2.1 (K3).

questions.prompt: A cinema website sets the ticket type from the visitor's age in whole years. Ages 0 to 3 get a "Free" ticket, 4 to 12 a "Child" ticket, 13 to 64 an "Adult" ticket and 65 to 120 a "Senior" ticket. An age above 120 is rejected as a typing mistake, and the field does not accept negative numbers. A tester has run test cases with these age values: 2, 3, 8, 35, 40. What equivalence partition coverage has been achieved?
questions.explanation: Coverage is the partitions exercised divided by the partitions identified. There are 5 partitions and the values fall into 3 of them (2 is in "Free"; 3 is in "Free"; 8 is in "Child"; 35 is in "Adult"; 40 is in "Adult"), so coverage is 3/5 = 60%. Several values in the same partition count once. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.2.1 (p. 39); FL-4.2.1 (K3).

questions.prompt: A sign-up page rates a new password by its length in characters. A password of 0 to 7 characters is rejected as too short, 8 to 11 characters is rated "Weak", 12 to 19 "Good" and 20 to 64 "Strong". Anything longer than 64 characters is rejected as too long. A tester has run test cases with these password length values: 4, 9, 10, 30. What equivalence partition coverage has been achieved?
questions.explanation: Coverage is the partitions exercised divided by the partitions identified. There are 5 partitions and the values fall into 3 of them (4 is in "Rejected: too short"; 9 is in "Weak"; 10 is in "Weak"; 30 is in "Strong"), so coverage is 3/5 = 60%. Several values in the same partition count once. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.2.1 (p. 39); FL-4.2.1 (K3).

questions.prompt: A training portal converts a final score from 0 to 100 into a result. Scores 0 to 39 give "Fail", 40 to 59 "Pass", 60 to 79 "Merit" and 80 to 100 "Distinction". A score above 100 is rejected as invalid, and negative scores cannot be typed. The existing test cases use these score values: 20, 50, 90, 105. Which one additional value brings equivalence partition coverage to 100%?
questions.explanation: The existing values cover every partition except "Merit". Only 60 lies in that partition; each other value repeats a partition that is already covered and adds no coverage. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.2.1 (p. 39); FL-4.2.1 (K3).

questions.prompt: A roadside camera in a 50 km/h zone decides what happens from the measured speed in whole km/h. Up to 50 nothing happens, from 51 to 60 a warning letter is sent, from 61 to 80 a fine is issued, and above 80 the case goes to court. The existing test cases use these speed values: 42, 70, 95. Which one additional value brings equivalence partition coverage to 100%?
questions.explanation: The existing values cover every partition except "Warning letter". Only 51 lies in that partition; each other value repeats a partition that is already covered and adds no coverage. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.2.1 (p. 39); FL-4.2.1 (K3).

questions.prompt: A wholesaler's shop applies a discount from the ordered quantity. Orders of 1 to 9 items get no discount, 10 to 49 items get 5%, 50 to 199 items get 10% and 200 to 999 items get 15%. An order of 1,000 items or more is not priced online but passed to the sales team. A reviewer checks a list of proposed test inputs for redundancy. Which pair of quantity values belongs to the same equivalence partition, so that testing both adds no equivalence partition coverage?

options.text: 49 and 50
9 and 10

questions.explanation: Both 50 and 199 lie in the "10% discount" partition, so the system should treat them the same way. The other pairs sit on either side of a partition border: they look close together but belong to different partitions. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.2.1 (p. 39); FL-4.2.1 (K3).

questions.prompt: An insurer's quote engine is tested with equivalence partitioning. The parameters and their partitions are: Driver age: 18 to 25, 26 to 60, 61 to 80; Vehicle: car, van, motorcycle, lorry; Cover: third party, comprehensive. Any combination of partitions is allowed. What is the minimum number of test cases that achieves Each Choice coverage?
questions.explanation: Each Choice coverage needs every partition of every parameter in at least one test case, and ignores combinations. One test case uses one partition from each parameter, so the parameter with the most partitions sets the minimum: 4. Adding the partitions (9) or multiplying them (24) answers different questions. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.2.1 (p. 39); FL-4.2.1 (K3).

questions.prompt: A railway booking service is tested with equivalence partitioning. The parameters and their partitions are: Passenger: adult, child, senior; Class: standard, first; Payment: card, wallet, voucher, invoice, cash; Seat: window, aisle. Any combination of partitions is allowed. What is the minimum number of test cases that achieves Each Choice coverage?
questions.explanation: Each Choice coverage needs every partition of every parameter in at least one test case, and ignores combinations. One test case uses one partition from each parameter, so the parameter with the most partitions sets the minimum: 5. Adding the partitions (12) or multiplying them (60) answers different questions. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.2.1 (p. 39); FL-4.2.1 (K3).

questions.prompt: A wholesaler's shop applies a discount from the ordered quantity. Orders of 1 to 9 items get no discount, 10 to 49 items get 5%, 50 to 199 items get 10% and 200 to 999 items get 15%. An order of 1,000 items or more is not priced online but passed to the sales team. Test cases already exist for these quantity values: 5, 120, 1500. Which TWO additional values are needed to reach 100% equivalence partition coverage? Select TWO options.
questions.explanation: The existing values leave two partitions untested: "5% discount" and "15% discount". The values 10 and 200 fall into them. The remaining options repeat partitions that already have a test. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.2.1 (p. 39); FL-4.2.1 (K3).

questions.prompt: A hotel chain sets a guest's loyalty level from the nights stayed in the last year. A guest with 0 to 4 nights is "Basic", 5 to 19 nights "Silver", 20 to 49 nights "Gold" and 50 to 365 nights "Platinum". The system cannot record fewer than 0 or more than 365 nights, so there are no other partitions. What is the minimum number of test cases needed for 100% equivalence partition coverage of the number of nights? Enter a whole number only.
questions.explanation: Each partition needs at least one value and one test case can only use one number of nights, so the minimum equals the number of partitions: 4 (Basic, Silver, Gold, Platinum). Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.2.1 (p. 39); FL-4.2.1 (K3).

questions.prompt: A florist's checkout chooses the delivery method from the distance in whole kilometres. Distances of 1 to 10 km go by bicycle, 11 to 40 km by van and 41 to 300 km by overnight courier. A distance of 0 km means collection in the shop, and anything above 300 km is refused. What is the minimum number of test cases needed for 100% equivalence partition coverage of the distance? Enter a whole number only.
questions.explanation: Each partition needs at least one value and one test case can only use one distance, so the minimum equals the number of partitions: 5 (Collection in shop, Bicycle, Van, Overnight courier, Refused). Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.2.1 (p. 39); FL-4.2.1 (K3).

questions.prompt: A lender's application form asks for the loan term in whole months. Terms of 6 to 12 months are handled as "Short", 13 to 36 months as "Medium" and 37 to 84 months as "Long". A term below 6 months or above 84 months is rejected with an error message. Test cases have been run with these term values: 3, 9, 12, 96. What percentage of equivalence partition coverage do they achieve? Enter a whole number only.
questions.explanation: The values fall into 3 of the 5 partitions (3 is in "Rejected: too short"; 9 is in "Short"; 12 is in "Short"; 96 is in "Rejected: too long"), so coverage is 3/5 = 60%. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.2.1 (p. 39); FL-4.2.1 (K3).

questions.prompt: A car park charges by the length of stay in whole minutes. A stay of 0 to 15 minutes is free, 16 to 60 minutes costs tariff A, 61 to 180 minutes costs tariff B, and 181 to 1,440 minutes costs the day rate. The barrier never records a stay longer than 1,440 minutes. Test cases have been run with these length of stay values: 10, 45, 50, 600. What percentage of equivalence partition coverage do they achieve? Enter a whole number only.
questions.explanation: The values fall into 3 of the 4 partitions (10 is in "Free"; 45 is in "Tariff A"; 50 is in "Tariff A"; 600 is in "Day rate"), so coverage is 3/4 = 75%. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.2.1 (p. 39); FL-4.2.1 (K3).

questions.prompt: A hotel chain sets a guest's loyalty level from the nights stayed in the last year. A guest with 0 to 4 nights is "Basic", 5 to 19 nights "Silver", 20 to 49 nights "Gold" and 50 to 365 nights "Platinum". The system cannot record fewer than 0 or more than 365 nights, so there are no other partitions. Test cases have been run with these number of nights values: 2, 12, 30, 100. What percentage of equivalence partition coverage do they achieve? Enter a whole number only.
questions.explanation: The values fall into 4 of the 4 partitions (2 is in "Basic"; 12 is in "Silver"; 30 is in "Gold"; 100 is in "Platinum"), so coverage is 4/4 = 100%. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.2.1 (p. 39); FL-4.2.1 (K3).

questions.prompt: A training portal converts a final score from 0 to 100 into a result. Scores 0 to 39 give "Fail", 40 to 59 "Pass", 60 to 79 "Merit" and 80 to 100 "Distinction". A score above 100 is rejected as invalid, and negative scores cannot be typed. Match each test input to the equivalence partition it exercises. One partition is left over.

options.text: Rejected
Pass
Distinction
Fail
Merit

questions.explanation: Each input is placed by comparing it with the partition borders in the specification: Score 5 gives "Fail"; Score 59 gives "Pass"; Score 79 gives "Merit"; Score 100 gives "Distinction". Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.2.1 (p. 39); FL-4.2.1 (K3).

questions.prompt: A roadside camera in a 50 km/h zone decides what happens from the measured speed in whole km/h. Up to 50 nothing happens, from 51 to 60 a warning letter is sent, from 61 to 80 a fine is issued, and above 80 the case goes to court. Match each test input to the equivalence partition it exercises. One partition is left over.

options.text: Fine
Warning letter
No action
Court

questions.explanation: Each input is placed by comparing it with the partition borders in the specification: Speed 30 km/h gives "No action"; Speed 60 km/h gives "Warning letter"; Speed 110 km/h gives "Court". Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.2.1 (p. 39); FL-4.2.1 (K3).

questions.prompt: A fitness watch classifies the resting pulse it measures, in whole beats per minute. Below 40 it shows "Low alarm", from 40 to 59 "Low", from 60 to 100 "Normal", from 101 to 150 "Elevated" and above 150 "High alarm". Match each test input to the equivalence partition it exercises. One partition is left over.

options.text: Normal
Low
Low alarm
High alarm
Elevated

questions.explanation: Each input is placed by comparing it with the partition borders in the specification: Pulse 25 bpm gives "Low alarm"; Pulse 100 bpm gives "Normal"; Pulse 150 bpm gives "Elevated"; Pulse 200 bpm gives "High alarm". Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.2.1 (p. 39); FL-4.2.1 (K3).

questions.prompt: A print service is tested with equivalence partitioning. The parameters and their partitions are: Paper: A3, A4, A5; Colour: mono, colour; Sides: single, double; Quality: draft, normal, high, photo. Any combination is allowed. How many test cases are needed, at minimum, for Each Choice coverage? Enter a whole number only.
questions.explanation: A test case exercises one partition per parameter. The largest set has 4 partitions, so 4 test cases are enough and fewer cannot cover that set. All combinations would need 48 test cases, but Each Choice coverage does not ask for combinations. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.2.1 (p. 39); FL-4.2.1 (K3).

questions.prompt: A booking form accepts between 1 and 8 seats per order (whole numbers). Any other number of seats is rejected. A tester applies 2-value boundary value analysis to the boundaries of the valid partition. Which set contains exactly the coverage items for the number of seats?
questions.explanation: The boundary values of the valid partition are 1 and 8. 2-value BVA takes each boundary value and its closest neighbour in the adjacent partition, here 0 and 9. The values 2 and 7 are only needed by 3-value BVA. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.2.2 (p. 40); FL-4.2.2 (K3).

questions.prompt: A travel insurer sells a policy to applicants aged 18 to 75 (whole years). Younger and older applicants are refused. A tester applies 2-value boundary value analysis to the boundaries of the valid partition. Which set contains exactly the coverage items for the age?
questions.explanation: The boundary values of the valid partition are 18 and 75. 2-value BVA takes each boundary value and its closest neighbour in the adjacent partition, here 17 and 76. The values 19 and 74 are only needed by 3-value BVA. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.2.2 (p. 40); FL-4.2.2 (K3).

questions.prompt: A vaccine fridge accepts a setpoint from 2 to 8 whole degrees Celsius. A setpoint outside this range is refused and an error tone sounds. A tester applies 3-value boundary value analysis to the boundaries of the valid partition. Which set contains exactly the coverage items for the setpoint?
questions.explanation: 3-value BVA takes each boundary value of the valid partition (2 and 8) together with both of its neighbours: 1, 2, 3 and 7, 8, 9. Leaving out 3 and 7 gives the 2-value set instead. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.2.2 (p. 40); FL-4.2.2 (K3).

questions.prompt: A tyre inflator accepts a target pressure from 180 to 320 whole kilopascals. Other targets are rejected. A tester applies 3-value boundary value analysis to the boundaries of the valid partition. Which set contains exactly the coverage items for the target pressure?
questions.explanation: 3-value BVA takes each boundary value of the valid partition (180 and 320) together with both of its neighbours: 179, 180, 181 and 319, 320, 321. Leaving out 181 and 319 gives the 2-value set instead. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.2.2 (p. 40); FL-4.2.2 (K3).

questions.prompt: A banking app accepts a transfer amount from 10 to 2,500 whole euros. Amounts outside this range are rejected. Using 2-value boundary value analysis on the valid partition, a tester has run test cases with these values for the amount: 10, 11, 2500, 2501, 1200. What boundary value coverage has been achieved?
questions.explanation: The 2-value coverage items are 9, 10, 2500, 2501. The tests exercise 3 of them (10, 2500, 2501), so coverage is 3/4 = 75%. Values that are not coverage items add nothing to boundary value coverage. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.2.2 (p. 40); FL-4.2.2 (K3).

questions.prompt: A room booking tool accepts a meeting length from 15 to 240 whole minutes. Shorter and longer meetings are refused. Using 2-value boundary value analysis on the valid partition, a tester has run test cases with these values for the meeting length: 14, 15, 16, 120. What boundary value coverage has been achieved?
questions.explanation: The 2-value coverage items are 14, 15, 240, 241. The tests exercise 2 of them (14, 15), so coverage is 2/4 = 50%. Values that are not coverage items add nothing to boundary value coverage. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.2.2 (p. 40); FL-4.2.2 (K3).

questions.prompt: A forum accepts user names that are 5 to 20 characters long. Shorter and longer names are rejected. Using 3-value boundary value analysis on the valid partition, a tester has run test cases with these values for the name length: 4, 5, 6, 20, 21. What boundary value coverage has been achieved?
questions.explanation: The 3-value coverage items are 4, 5, 6, 19, 20, 21. The tests exercise 5 of them (4, 5, 6, 20, 21), so coverage is 5/6 = 83.3%. Values that are not coverage items add nothing to boundary value coverage. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.2.2 (p. 40); FL-4.2.2 (K3).

questions.prompt: A car park charges by the length of stay in whole minutes. A stay of 0 to 15 minutes is free, 16 to 60 minutes costs tariff A, 61 to 180 minutes costs tariff B, and 181 to 1,440 minutes costs the day rate. The barrier never records a stay longer than 1,440 minutes. The partitions fill the whole input range, and values outside it cannot be entered. Which set contains exactly the coverage items of 2-value boundary value analysis for the length of stay?
questions.explanation: Every partition contributes its smallest and its largest value: 0, 15, 16, 60, 61, 180, 181, 1440. For each boundary value, the closest neighbour in the adjacent partition is that partition's own boundary value, so no further values are needed. Values outside the range cannot be entered, so they are not coverage items here. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.2.2 (p. 40); FL-4.2.2 (K3).

questions.prompt: A hotel chain sets a guest's loyalty level from the nights stayed in the last year. The system cannot record fewer than 0 or more than 365 nights, so there are no other partitions. The partitions fill the whole input range, and values outside it cannot be entered. Which set contains exactly the coverage items of 2-value boundary value analysis for the number of nights?
questions.explanation: Every partition contributes its smallest and its largest value: 0, 4, 5, 19, 20, 49, 50, 365. For each boundary value, the closest neighbour in the adjacent partition is that partition's own boundary value, so no further values are needed. Values outside the range cannot be entered, so they are not coverage items here. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.2.2 (p. 40); FL-4.2.2 (K3).

questions.prompt: An infusion pump accepts a dose from 5 to 40 whole millilitres. A dose outside this range is rejected and the pump does not start. For 2-value boundary value analysis of the valid partition, test cases already exist for the values 5 and 41. Which TWO further values are needed to reach 100% boundary value coverage? Select TWO options.
questions.explanation: The 2-value coverage items are 4, 5, 40, 41. With 5 and 41 already tested, 4 and 40 remain. The values 6 and 39 belong to 3-value BVA, and 22 is not a boundary value at all. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.2.2 (p. 40); FL-4.2.2 (K3).

questions.prompt: A print dialog must accept from 1 to 250 copies. The requirement for the upper limit is "accept the job if copies ≤ 250", but the developer coded the check as "copies < 250". The tester applies 2-value boundary value analysis to the upper boundary. Which test input reveals the defect?
questions.explanation: With the faulty check, 250 copies are rejected although the requirement says they must be accepted, so the test with the boundary value 250 fails. For 249 the result is "accepted" and for 251 and 252 it is "rejected" under both the requirement and the faulty code, so those tests pass and hide the defect. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.2.2 (p. 40); FL-4.2.2 (K3).

questions.prompt: An online shop gives free delivery when the basket holds at most 70 items. The requirement is "free delivery if items ≤ 70", but the developer coded "free delivery if items = 70". A tester who used 2-value boundary value analysis ran the values 70 and 71, and both tests passed. Which value, added by 3-value boundary value analysis, reveals the defect?
questions.explanation: For 70 and 71 the faulty code happens to give the required result, so 2-value BVA misses the defect. 3-value BVA also tests both neighbours of the boundary value 70, which adds 69. With 69 items the requirement gives free delivery but the code does not, so that test fails. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.2.2 (p. 40); FL-4.2.2 (K3).

questions.prompt: A goods lift accepts a load from 50 to 900 whole kilograms. Lighter loads are treated as empty and heavier loads are refused. Using 2-value boundary value analysis on the valid partition, a tester has run test cases with these values for the load: 49, 50, 900. What percentage of boundary value coverage has been achieved? Enter a whole number only.
questions.explanation: The 2-value coverage items are 49, 50, 900, 901. The tests exercise 3 of them (49, 50, 900), so coverage is 3/4 = 75%. Values that are not coverage items add nothing to boundary value coverage. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.2.2 (p. 40); FL-4.2.2 (K3).

questions.prompt: A print dialog accepts from 1 to 250 copies. Any other number is rejected. questions.explanation: The 3-value coverage items are 0, 1, 2, 249, 250, 251. The tests exercise 4 of them (0, 1, 250, 251), so coverage is 4/6 = 66.7%. Values that are not coverage items add nothing to boundary value coverage. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.2.2 (p. 40); FL-4.2.2 (K3).

questions.prompt: An infusion pump accepts a dose from 5 to 40 whole millilitres. A dose outside this range is rejected and the pump does not start. questions.prompt: A team works on this user story: "As a customer, I want to return an item online so that I get my money back." The acceptance criteria are: (1) an item can be returned within 30 days of delivery; (2) a return label is e-mailed to the customer; (3) an item marked "final sale" cannot be returned; (4) the refund goes to the original payment method. Following ATDD, the team writes the positive test cases first. Which test case should be written first?

options.text: Given an item delivered 45 days ago, when the customer requests a return, then the request is refused because the return period has ended
Given an item delivered 10 days ago that is not final sale, when the customer requests a return, then a label is e-mailed and the refund is made
Given an item marked "final sale" delivered 10 days ago, when the customer requests a return, then the request is refused with an explanation
Given 500 customers requesting returns at the same moment, when the requests are processed, then every label is e-mailed and every refund is made within one minute

questions.explanation: In ATDD the first test cases are positive: they confirm the correct behaviour without exceptions or error conditions. The refused returns are negative test cases that come next, and the load test addresses a non-functional characteristic, which comes last. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.5.3 (p. 46); FL-4.5.3 (K3).

questions.prompt: A team works on this user story: "As a registered user, I want to reset my password by e-mail so that I can sign in again." The acceptance criteria are: (1) a reset link is sent to the registered e-mail address; (2) the link works once and for 30 minutes; (3) the new password must differ from the last three passwords; (4) an unknown e-mail address shows the same neutral message as a known one. The team has written positive test cases for criteria 1 and 2. Which test case is a negative test that should be added next?

options.text: Given a valid reset link opened after 10 minutes, when the user sets a new password, then the password is changed
Given a reset link that was already used once, when the user opens it a second time, then the link is rejected and no password can be set
Given a known e-mail address, when the user requests a reset, then a link is sent to that address
Given a valid reset link, when the user sets a new password that was never used before, then the user can sign in with it

questions.explanation: After the positive test cases, ATDD adds negative test cases that cover error conditions. Opening a link for the second time violates the "works once" part of criterion 2. The other three test cases describe expected, successful use and are positive tests. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.5.3 (p. 46); FL-4.5.3 (K3).

Given a party of 8 guests, when the diner books a free slot, then the booking is accepted
Given an existing booking, when the diner pays a deposit by card, then the deposit is shown on the booking

questions.explanation: ATDD test cases must cover all characteristics of the user story but should not go beyond it. Neither the story nor its acceptance criteria mention deposits or payment, so that test case describes behaviour outside the story. The other three trace to criteria 1, 2 and 4. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.5.3 (p. 46); FL-4.5.3 (K3).
