The test cases are then created before implementation. Deciding in code or after release loses the test-first benefit. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.5.3 (p. 46); FL-4.5.3 (K3).

questions.prompt: A team works on this user story: "As a registered user, I want to reset my password by e-mail so that I can sign in again." The acceptance criteria are: (1) a reset link is sent to the registered e-mail address; (2) the link works once and for 30 minutes; (3) the new password must differ from the last three passwords; (4) an unknown e-mail address shows the same neutral message as a known one. The positive and negative functional test cases are complete. Which test case would the team typically add last in ATDD?

options.text: Given a correct e-mail address, when the user requests a reset, then the e-mail with the link arrives within 60 seconds
Given a new password equal to the previous password, when the user submits it, then it is rejected
Given an expired link, when the user opens it, then a message explains that the link is no longer valid
Given an unknown e-mail address, when a reset is requested, then the neutral message is shown

questions.explanation: ATDD typically starts with positive test cases, continues with negative test cases and finishes with test cases for non-functional quality characteristics such as performance efficiency or usability. The 60-second delivery time is a performance expectation; the other three are functional test cases. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.5.3 (p. 46); FL-4.5.3 (K3).

questions.prompt: A team works on this user story: "As an accountant, I want to export the monthly invoices as a spreadsheet so that I can check them offline." The acceptance criteria are: (1) the export contains every invoice dated in the chosen month; (2) amounts keep two decimal places; (3) a month without invoices produces a file with headings only; (4) only users with the "Finance" role can export. A tester writes this test case for criterion 4: "Verify role-based access control matrix RBAC-7 denies EXPORT_INV to principals lacking FIN scope." Why does this test case need rework in ATDD?

options.text: It covers an acceptance criterion instead of the user story itself
It was written before the code exists, so it cannot be executed
It is not expressed in a way the stakeholders can understand
It is a negative test case, and ATDD only uses positive test cases

questions.explanation: ATDD test cases must be understandable for the stakeholders, typically as natural-language sentences with preconditions, inputs and postconditions. The test case is correct in content but written in internal jargon. Negative tests are part of ATDD, and writing tests before the code is its purpose. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.5.3 (p. 46); FL-4.5.3 (K3).

questions.prompt: A team works on this user story: "As a diner, I want to book a table online so that I do not have to phone the restaurant." The acceptance criteria are: (1) a table can be booked for 1 to 8 guests; (2) bookings are possible up to 60 days ahead; (3) the diner receives a confirmation by text message; (4) a time slot that is already full is not offered. The team has test cases for: a booking for 4 guests 10 days ahead with a confirmation text; a booking attempt for 0 guests; a booking attempt 61 days ahead. Which acceptance criterion has no test case yet?

options.text: Criterion 2
Criterion 3
Criterion 1
Criterion 4

questions.explanation: The first test case covers the positive side of criteria 1, 2 and 3, the 0-guest case covers the negative side of criterion 1 and the 61-day case the negative side of criterion 2. No test case uses a full time slot, so criterion 4 is uncovered. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.5.3 (p. 46); FL-4.5.3 (K3).

questions.prompt: A team works on this user story: "As a customer, I want to return an item online so that I get my money back." The acceptance criteria are: (1) an item can be returned within 30 days of delivery; (2) a return label is e-mailed to the customer; (3) an item marked "final sale" cannot be returned; (4) the refund goes to the original payment method. The test cases are written in a format that the team's test automation framework supports. What follows from this in ATDD?

options.text: Only developers can run the test cases, because testers do not work with the framework
Developers can automate them while implementing the story, making them executable requirements
The test cases replace the acceptance criteria, which can then be deleted from the user story
Manual execution of the test cases is no longer allowed once they have been automated

questions.explanation: When ATDD test cases are captured in a format supported by a test automation framework, developers can automate them by writing supporting code as they implement the feature. The acceptance tests then act as executable requirements. They do not replace the criteria or forbid manual testing. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.5.3 (p. 46); FL-4.5.3 (K3).

questions.prompt: A team works on this user story: "As an accountant, I want to export the monthly invoices as a spreadsheet so that I can check them offline." The acceptance criteria are: (1) the export contains every invoice dated in the chosen month; (2) amounts keep two decimal places; (3) a month without invoices produces a file with headings only; (4) only users with the "Finance" role can export. A tester drafts five test cases. Which TWO go beyond the user story and should be removed or raised as new stories? Select TWO options.

options.text: Given March with 12 invoices, when the accountant exports, then the file contains 12 rows
Given an exported file, when the accountant uploads a corrected copy, then the invoices are updated
Given an invoice of 250.00, when the accountant exports, then the amount reads 250.00
Given a user with only the "Sales" role, when that user tries to export, then the export is refused
Given March with 12 invoices, when the accountant exports, then the file is e-mailed to the auditor

questions.explanation: ATDD test cases must cover the characteristics of the story without going beyond it. Sending the file to an auditor and uploading corrections are not in the story or in any of its four acceptance criteria. The other three test cases trace to criteria 1, 2 and 4. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.5.3 (p. 46); FL-4.5.3 (K3).

questions.prompt: A team works on this user story: "As a registered user, I want to reset my password by e-mail so that I can sign in again." The acceptance criteria are: (1) a reset link is sent to the registered e-mail address; (2) the link works once and for 30 minutes; (3) the new password must differ from the last three passwords; (4) an unknown e-mail address shows the same neutral message as a known one. Which TWO statements describe how the team should create the test cases for this story in ATDD? Select TWO options.

options.text: The test cases are based on the acceptance criteria and serve as examples of how the software behaves
The test cases are created before the user story is implemented
The test cases should also cover features that may be added to the story later
The test cases are created by the developer alone after the unit tests pass
Each acceptance criterion should be covered by several test cases that repeat the same characteristic

questions.explanation: ATDD is a test-first approach: test cases are created before implementation, based on the acceptance criteria, and are seen as examples of how the software works. They are created by the team as a whole or by the tester, must not repeat a characteristic and must not go beyond the story. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.5.3 (p. 46); FL-4.5.3 (K3).

questions.prompt: Put these ATDD activities for a user story in the order in which they are typically done.

options.text: Implement the user story so that the test cases pass
Write negative test cases for error conditions
Write positive test cases that confirm the expected behaviour
Analyse and discuss the user story and its acceptance criteria in a specification workshop
Write test cases for non-functional quality characteristics

questions.explanation: ATDD starts with a specification workshop, then creates the test cases: first positive ones, then negative ones and finally those for non-functional characteristics. Because ATDD is test-first, the implementation follows the test cases. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.5.3 (p. 46); FL-4.5.3 (K3).

questions.prompt: A team works on this user story: "As a diner, I want to book a table online so that I do not have to phone the restaurant." The acceptance criteria are: (1) a table can be booked for 1 to 8 guests; (2) bookings are possible up to 60 days ahead; (3) the diner receives a confirmation by text message; (4) a time slot that is already full is not offered. The team has drafted the test cases below. Put them in the order in which ATDD typically creates them.

options.text: Given 9 guests, when the diner tries to book, then the booking is refused
Given 200 diners browsing at once, when they search for a table, then free slots are shown within 2 seconds
Given 4 guests and a free slot 10 days ahead, when the diner books, then the booking is confirmed by text message

questions.explanation: The successful booking is the positive test case and comes first. The refused booking for 9 guests is a negative test case and follows. The response time under load addresses a non-functional characteristic and is typically created last. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.5.3 (p. 46); FL-4.5.3 (K3).

questions.prompt: A team works on this user story: "As a customer, I want to return an item online so that I get my money back." The acceptance criteria are: (1) an item can be returned within 30 days of delivery; (2) a return label is e-mailed to the customer; (3) an item marked "final sale" cannot be returned; (4) the refund goes to the original payment method. Match each test case to the acceptance criterion it is derived from. One criterion is left over.

options.text: Criterion 4: refund to original payment method
Criterion 1: return within 30 days
Criterion 3: final-sale items cannot be returned
Criterion 2: return label by e-mail

slots.text: An item delivered 31 days ago cannot be returned
After a return is approved, the customer finds a label in the inbox
An item paid with a credit card is refunded to that credit card

questions.explanation: The 31-day case tests the limit of the return period (criterion 1), the inbox case tests the e-mailed label (criterion 2) and the credit card case tests the refund route (criterion 4). No listed test case uses a final-sale item. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.5.3 (p. 46); FL-4.5.3 (K3).

questions.prompt: A team works on this user story: "As a registered user, I want to reset my password by e-mail so that I can sign in again." The acceptance criteria are: (1) a reset link is sent to the registered e-mail address; (2) the link works once and for 30 minutes; (3) the new password must differ from the last three passwords; (4) an unknown e-mail address shows the same neutral message as a known one. Match each test case to its type in ATDD. One type is left over.

options.text: Test case that goes beyond the user story
Test case for a non-functional characteristic
Positive test case
Negative test case

slots.text: A user requests a reset and sets a new password with a fresh link
A user opens a link that is 45 minutes old and is refused
A user with a screen reader can complete the reset form

questions.explanation: The successful reset is the positive case. The 45-minute-old link breaks the 30-minute rule, an error condition, so it is a negative case. Completing the form with a screen reader concerns usability and accessibility, a non-functional characteristic. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.5.3 (p. 46); FL-4.5.3 (K3).

questions.prompt: A team works on this user story: "As an accountant, I want to export the monthly invoices as a spreadsheet so that I can check them offline." The acceptance criteria are: (1) the export contains every invoice dated in the chosen month; (2) amounts keep two decimal places; (3) a month without invoices produces a file with headings only; (4) only users with the "Finance" role can export. The team has these test cases: an export of a month with 7 invoices that checks all 7 are present; an export that checks 0.50 stays 0.50; an export by a user without the "Finance" role that is refused. How many acceptance criteria have no test case yet? Enter a whole number only.
questions.explanation: The first test case covers criterion 1, the second criterion 2 and the third criterion 4. Only criterion 3, the month without invoices, is left without a test case, so the answer is 1. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.5.3 (p. 46); FL-4.5.3 (K3).

questions.prompt: A team works on this user story: "As a diner, I want to book a table online so that I do not have to phone the restaurant." The acceptance criteria are: (1) a table can be booked for 1 to 8 guests; (2) bookings are possible up to 60 days ahead; (3) the diner receives a confirmation by text message; (4) a time slot that is already full is not offered. A tester drafts six test cases: (a) 2 guests, free slot, confirmed; (b) 8 guests, free slot, confirmed; (c) 9 guests refused; (d) full slot not offered; (e) diner cancels a booking and gets a refund; (f) diner rates the restaurant after the meal. How many of these test cases go beyond the user story? Enter a whole number only.
questions.explanation: Test cases (a) to (d) trace to the acceptance criteria. Cancelling with a refund (e) and rating the restaurant (f) are not part of the story or its criteria, so two test cases go beyond the story and should be removed or turned into new stories. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.5.3 (p. 46); FL-4.5.3 (K3).

questions.prompt: A team works on this user story: "As a registered user, I want to reset my password by e-mail so that I can sign in again." The acceptance criteria are: (1) a reset link is sent to the registered e-mail address; (2) the link works once and for 30 minutes; (3) the new password must differ from the last three passwords; (4) an unknown e-mail address shows the same neutral message as a known one. The team has drafted five test cases: (a) a user requests a reset and sets a new password with a fresh link; (b) a link opened after 45 minutes is refused; (c) a link opened a second time is refused; (d) a new password equal to the previous password is rejected; (e) the reset e-mail arrives within 60 seconds. How many of these five are negative test cases? Enter a whole number only.
questions.explanation: Test cases (b), (c) and (d) check error conditions: an expired link, a reused link and a repeated password. Test case (a) is the positive case and (e) checks performance efficiency, a non-functional characteristic. So three of the five are negative test cases. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.5.3 (p. 46); FL-4.5.3 (K3).

questions.prompt: Match each ATDD term to its description. One description is left over.

options.text: The team analyses, discusses and writes the user story and its acceptance criteria
A test derived from the code structure after implementation
Confirms correct behaviour without exceptions or error conditions
An acceptance test automated in a framework while the feature is implemented

questions.explanation: In the specification workshop the team clarifies the story and its criteria. Positive test cases confirm the expected flow when everything goes well. Automated acceptance tests act as executable requirements. Deriving tests from finished code is not part of ATDD. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.5.3 (p. 46); FL-4.5.3 (K3).

questions.prompt: A tester estimates the effort to test a new payment page. The optimistic estimate is 4 person-days, the most likely estimate is 7 person-days and the pessimistic estimate is 16 person-days. Using three-point estimation, what is the estimated effort?

options.text: 8.5 person-days
8 person-days
7 person-days
9 person-days

questions.explanation: Three-point estimation weights the most likely value four times: E = (a + 4m + b) / 6 = (4 + 4 × 7 + 16) / 6 = 8 person-days. A plain average of the three values would give 9, which ignores the weighting. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.1.4 (p. 49); FL-5.1.4 (K3).

questions.prompt: A team estimates the regression test of a booking system after a database upgrade. The optimistic estimate is 10 person-hours, the most likely estimate is 14 person-hours and the pessimistic estimate is 24 person-hours. Using three-point estimation, what is the estimated effort?

options.text: 16 person-hours
15.5 person-hours
15 person-hours
14 person-hours

questions.explanation: Three-point estimation weights the most likely value four times: E = (a + 4m + b) / 6 = (10 + 4 × 14 + 24) / 6 = 15 person-hours. A plain average of the three values would give 16, which ignores the weighting. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.1.4 (p. 49); FL-5.1.4 (K3).

questions.prompt: A test manager estimates the system test of a small reporting module. The optimistic estimate is 12 person-days, the most likely estimate is 18 person-days and the pessimistic estimate is 30 person-days. Using three-point estimation, what is the estimated effort?

options.text: 19.5 person-days
19 person-days
18 person-days
20 person-days

questions.explanation: Three-point estimation weights the most likely value four times: E = (a + 4m + b) / 6 = (12 + 4 × 18 + 30) / 6 = 19 person-days. A plain average of the three values would give 20, which ignores the weighting. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.1.4 (p. 49); FL-5.1.4 (K3).

questions.prompt: A team estimates the acceptance test of a warehouse app. The estimates are: optimistic 20 person-hours, most likely 26 person-hours, pessimistic 50 person-hours. The team uses three-point estimation, where the standard deviation is (b − a) / 6. How should the result be reported as E ± SD?

options.text: 32 ± 5 person-hours
29 ± 5 person-hours
26 ± 7.5 person-hours
29 ± 15 person-hours

questions.explanation: E = (a + 4m + b) / 6 = (20 + 4 × 26 + 50) / 6 = 29 and SD = (b − a) / 6 = (50 − 20) / 6 = 5. The estimate is therefore 29 ± 5 person-hours, that is between 24 and 34. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.1.4 (p. 49); FL-5.1.4 (K3).

questions.prompt: A tester estimates the exploratory testing of a redesigned search page. The estimates are: optimistic 5 person-hours, most likely 8 person-hours, pessimistic 17 person-hours. The team uses three-point estimation, where the standard deviation is (b − a) / 6. How should the result be reported as E ± SD?

options.text: 9 ± 2 person-hours
8 ± 3 person-hours
9 ± 6 person-hours
10 ± 2 person-hours

questions.explanation: E = (a + 4m + b) / 6 = (5 + 4 × 8 + 17) / 6 = 9 and SD = (b − a) / 6 = (17 − 5) / 6 = 2. The estimate is therefore 9 ± 2 person-hours, that is between 7 and 11. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.1.4 (p. 49); FL-5.1.4 (K3).

questions.prompt: A company plans a new customer portal. In comparable finished projects the ratio of development effort to test effort was 5:3. The development effort for the new project is estimated at 450 person-days. Using estimation based on ratios, what is the estimated test effort?

options.text: 168.8 person-days
281.2 person-days
750 person-days
270 person-days

questions.explanation: The ratio 5:3 means 3 person-days of test for every 5 person-days of development. 450 × 3 / 5 = 270 person-days. Turning the ratio upside down would give 750. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.1.4 (p. 49); FL-5.1.4 (K3).

questions.prompt: A supplier plans the next release of a billing system. In comparable finished projects the ratio of development effort to test effort was 7:2. The development effort for the new project is estimated at 840 person-days. Using estimation based on ratios, what is the estimated test effort?

options.text: 240 person-days
653.3 person-days
2940 person-days
186.7 person-days

questions.explanation: The ratio 7:2 means 2 person-days of test for every 7 person-days of development. 840 × 2 / 7 = 240 person-days. Turning the ratio upside down would give 2940. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.1.4 (p. 49); FL-5.1.4 (K3).

questions.prompt: An Agile team has finished five iterations. The test effort in the completed iterations was 52, 40, 44, 46, 48 person-hours, in that order. The team extrapolates the test effort of the next iteration as the average of the last three iterations. What is the estimate?

options.text: 48 person-hours
46 person-hours
45.3 person-hours
52 person-hours

questions.explanation: The last three iterations took 44, 46, 48 person-hours. Their average is (44 + 46 + 48) / 3 = 46 person-hours. Earlier iterations are left out because extrapolation here uses the most recent measurements. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.1.4 (p. 49); FL-5.1.4 (K3).

questions.prompt: A team is testing the requirements of a tax calculator. So far 60 of the 200 requirements have been tested, which took 45 person-days. Assuming the remaining requirements need the same effort each, what is the extrapolated effort for the remaining testing?

options.text: 64.3 person-days
150 person-days
31.5 person-days
105 person-days

questions.explanation: The measured rate is 45 person-days for 60 requirements. 140 requirements remain, so the remaining effort is 45 ÷ 60 × 140 = 105 person-days. 150 person-days would be the effort for all 200 requirements, including the work already done. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.1.4 (p. 49); FL-5.1.4 (K3).

questions.prompt: Four testers must estimate the effort to test a data migration. Each writes down an estimate without talking to the others: 30, 34, 36 and 70 person-hours. The team uses the Wideband Delphi technique. What should happen next?

options.text: The testers discuss why the estimates differ, in particular the outlier, and then each makes a new estimate alone
The four estimates are averaged and the result of 42.5 person-hours is entered into the test plan
The test manager picks the estimate of the most experienced tester and closes the discussion
The highest estimate is chosen, because it is the safest value when experts disagree

questions.explanation: In Wideband Delphi, experts first estimate in isolation. If the results deviate beyond an agreed range, they discuss their reasons and then estimate again on their own, and this repeats until consensus is reached. Averaging or picking one value skips the discussion that reveals the missing information. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.1.4 (p. 49); FL-5.1.4 (K3).

questions.prompt: A team estimates a user story with Planning Poker. In the first round the cards show 3, 3, 5 and 13. What does the technique require the team to do before it records an estimate?

options.text: Let the people with the lowest and the highest card explain their reasoning, then play another round
Record 13, because the most cautious estimate protects the team from overcommitment
Drop the outlier card 13 and record 3, the value most of the team members chose
Record 6, the average of the four cards, because a second round would only cost time

questions.explanation: Planning Poker is a variant of Wideband Delphi. When the cards differ widely, the estimators explain their views, typically starting with the extremes, and then estimate again. The rounds repeat until the estimates converge, so averaging, taking the maximum or dropping the outlier is not part of the technique. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.1.4 (p. 49); FL-5.1.4 (K3).

questions.prompt: A tester estimates the effort to automate a set of API checks. The optimistic estimate is 3 person-days, the most likely estimate is 5 person-days and the pessimistic estimate is 13 person-days. Using three-point estimation, what is the estimated effort in person-days? Enter a whole number only.
questions.explanation: Three-point estimation weights the most likely value four times: E = (a + 4m + b) / 6 = (3 + 4 × 5 + 13) / 6 = 6 person-days. A plain average of the three values would give 7, which ignores the weighting. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.1.4 (p. 49); FL-5.1.4 (K3).

questions.prompt: A team estimates the performance test of a ticket shop. The optimistic estimate is 8 person-hours, the most likely estimate is 11 person-hours and the pessimistic estimate is 20 person-hours. Using three-point estimation, what is the estimated effort in person-hours? Enter a whole number only.
questions.explanation: Three-point estimation weights the most likely value four times: E = (a + 4m + b) / 6 = (8 + 4 × 11 + 20) / 6 = 12 person-hours. A plain average of the three values would give 13, which ignores the weighting. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.1.4 (p. 49); FL-5.1.4 (K3).

questions.prompt: A tester estimates the usability test sessions for a mobile app. The optimistic estimate is 2 person-days, the most likely estimate is 5 person-days and the pessimistic estimate is 14 person-days. Using three-point estimation, what is the estimated effort in person-days? Enter a whole number only.
questions.explanation: Three-point estimation weights the most likely value four times: E = (a + 4m + b) / 6 = (2 + 4 × 5 + 14) / 6 = 6 person-days. A plain average of the three values would give 7, which ignores the weighting. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.1.4 (p. 49); FL-5.1.4 (K3).

questions.prompt: A team estimates the security test of a login service. The estimates are: optimistic 12 person-hours, most likely 18 person-hours, pessimistic 30 person-hours. The team uses three-point estimation, where the standard deviation is (b − a) / 6. What is the standard deviation of the estimate in person-hours? Enter a whole number only.
questions.explanation: SD = (b − a) / 6 = (30 − 12) / 6 = 3 person-hours. The most likely value does not enter the standard deviation; it only affects the estimate E = 19. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.1.4 (p. 49); FL-5.1.4 (K3).

questions.prompt: A team estimates the installation tests for a desktop client. The estimates are: optimistic 4 person-hours, most likely 7 person-hours, pessimistic 16 person-hours. The team uses three-point estimation, where the standard deviation is (b − a) / 6. The result is reported as E ± SD. What is the upper end of that range in person-hours? Enter a whole number only.
questions.explanation: E = (4 + 4 × 7 + 16) / 6 = 8 and SD = (16 − 4) / 6 = 2, so the range is 6 to 10 person-hours. The upper end is 10. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.1.4 (p. 49); FL-5.1.4 (K3).

questions.prompt: An integrator plans a project for a hospital. In comparable finished projects the ratio of development effort to test effort was 4:1. The development effort for the new project is estimated at 1200 person-days. Using estimation based on ratios, what is the estimated test effort in person-days? Enter a whole number only.
questions.explanation: The ratio 4:1 means 1 person-days of test for every 4 person-days of development. 1200 × 1 / 4 = 300 person-days. Turning the ratio upside down would give 4800. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.1.4 (p. 49); FL-5.1.4 (K3).

questions.prompt: A start-up plans a new mobile banking feature. In comparable finished projects the ratio of test effort to development effort was 3:5. The test effort for the new project is estimated at 90 person-days. Using estimation based on ratios, what is the estimated development effort in person-days? Enter a whole number only.
questions.explanation: The ratio 3:5 means 5 person-days of development for every 3 person-days of test. 90 × 5 / 3 = 150 person-days. Turning the ratio upside down would give 54. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.1.4 (p. 49); FL-5.1.4 (K3).

questions.prompt: A team has finished four iterations of a logistics product. The test effort in the completed iterations was 30, 36, 42, 45 person-hours, in that order. The team extrapolates the test effort of the next iteration as the average of the last three iterations. What is the estimate in person-hours? Enter a whole number only.
questions.explanation: The last three iterations took 36, 42, 45 person-hours. Their average is (36 + 42 + 45) / 3 = 41 person-hours. Earlier iterations are left out because extrapolation here uses the most recent measurements. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.1.4 (p. 49); FL-5.1.4 (K3).

questions.prompt: A team is running a suite of manual test cases for a release. So far 120 of the 300 test cases have been tested, which took 80 person-hours. Assuming the remaining test cases need the same effort each, what is the extrapolated effort for the remaining testing in person-hours? Enter a whole number only.
questions.explanation: The measured rate is 80 person-hours for 120 test cases. 180 test cases remain, so the remaining effort is 80 ÷ 120 × 180 = 120 person-hours. 200 person-hours would be the effort for all 300 test cases, including the work already done. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.1.4 (p. 49); FL-5.1.4 (K3).

questions.prompt:
A team must order four test cases for a payment service. Each test case covers one product risk. Likelihood and impact are rated from 1 (low) to 5 (high), and the risk level is likelihood × impact.
TC1: likelihood 2, impact 5
TC2: likelihood 4, impact 4
TC3: likelihood 3, impact 2
TC4: likelihood 5, impact 1

Using risk-based prioritization, in which order should the test cases be executed?

options.text: TC1, TC2, TC3, TC4
TC4, TC2, TC3, TC1
TC4, TC3, TC1, TC2
TC2, TC1, TC3, TC4

questions.explanation: Risk-based prioritization runs the tests for the highest risk level first. The levels are TC1 = 10, TC2 = 16, TC3 = 6, TC4 = 5, so the order is TC2, TC1, TC3, TC4. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.1.5 (p. 50); FL-5.1.5 (K3).

questions.prompt:
A team must order five test cases for a hospital booking system. Each test case covers one product risk. Likelihood and impact are rated from 1 (low) to 5 (high), and the risk level is likelihood × impact.
TC1: likelihood 3, impact 3
TC2: likelihood 1, impact 5
TC3: likelihood 4, impact 5
TC4: likelihood 2, impact 4
TC5: likelihood 5, impact 3

Using risk-based prioritization, in which order should the test cases be executed?

options.text: TC3, TC2, TC4, TC5, TC1
TC3, TC5, TC1, TC4, TC2
TC2, TC4, TC1, TC5, TC3
TC5, TC3, TC1, TC4, TC2

questions.explanation: Risk-based prioritization runs the tests for the highest risk level first. The levels are TC1 = 9, TC2 = 5, TC3 = 20, TC4 = 8, TC5 = 15, so the order is TC3, TC5, TC1, TC4, TC2. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.1.5 (p. 50); FL-5.1.5 (K3).

questions.prompt:
A team must order four test cases for a car rental app. Each test case covers one product risk. Likelihood and impact are rated from 1 (low) to 5 (high), and the risk level is likelihood × impact.
TC1: likelihood 5, impact 2
TC2: likelihood 2, impact 2
TC3: likelihood 3, impact 5
TC4: likelihood 4, impact 3

Using risk-based prioritization, in which order should the test cases be executed?

options.text: TC1, TC4, TC3, TC2
TC3, TC4, TC1, TC2
TC2, TC1, TC4, TC3
TC4, TC3, TC1, TC2

questions.explanation: Risk-based prioritization runs the tests for the highest risk level first. The levels are TC1 = 10, TC2 = 4, TC3 = 15, TC4 = 12, so the order is TC3, TC4, TC1, TC2. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.1.5 (p. 50); FL-5.1.5 (K3).

questions.prompt:
A team prioritizes four test cases for a tax form. The table shows which requirements each test case covers.
TC1: covers 1, 2, 3, 4
TC2: covers 5, 6, 7, 8, 10
TC3: covers 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 11
TC4: covers 1, 2, 9

Using additional coverage prioritization, in which order should the test cases be executed?

options.text: TC1, TC2, TC3, TC4
TC3, TC1, TC2, TC4
TC4, TC2, TC1, TC3
TC3, TC2, TC1, TC4

questions.explanation: Additional coverage prioritization first takes the test with the highest coverage (TC3), then always the test that adds the most requirements not yet covered. That gives TC3, TC1, TC2, TC4. Ordering only by the total number of requirements per test would give TC3, TC2, TC1, TC4. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.1.5 (p. 50); FL-5.1.5 (K3).

questions.prompt:
A team orders four test cases for an online shop by the priority of the requirements they cover. Priority 1 is the highest. Some test cases depend on others.
TC1: priority 3
TC2: priority 1, can only run after TC3
TC3: priority 4
TC4: priority 2

In which order should the test cases be executed?

options.text: TC2, TC3, TC4, TC1
TC1, TC4, TC2, TC3
TC3, TC2, TC4, TC1
TC2, TC4, TC1, TC3

questions.explanation: Tests run in priority order, but a test that another one depends on must run first, even if its own priority is lower. Pure priority order would be TC2, TC4, TC1, TC3; moving each prerequisite directly before the test that needs it gives TC3, TC2, TC4, TC1. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.1.5 (p. 50); FL-5.1.5 (K3).

TC3
TC1

A team prioritizes four test cases for a tax form. There are 12 branches in total, numbered 1 to 12. The table shows which branches each test case covers.

The team uses additional coverage prioritization but only has time for the first two test cases in that order. How many branches remain uncovered? Enter a whole number only.
questions.explanation: The first test is TC1 with the highest coverage, and the second is TC4, which adds the most new branches. Together they cover 11 of the 12 branches, so 1 remain uncovered. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.1.5 (p. 50); FL-5.1.5 (K3).

The test cases are executed by priority while respecting the dependencies. At which position (1 to 5) is TC2 executed? Enter a whole number only.
questions.explanation: TC2 has the lowest priority, but TC1 can only run after it. The resulting order is TC4, TC3, TC2, TC1, TC5, so TC2 is pulled forward to directly before TC1. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.1.5 (p. 50); FL-5.1.5 (K3).

questions.prompt: Match each situation to the test case prioritization strategy that is being used. One strategy is left over.

options.text: Additional coverage prioritization
Requirements-based prioritization
Prioritization by the date on which each test case was written
Risk-based prioritization

slots.text: The tests for the feature whose failure would cost the most money are run first
The test that exercises the most statements is run first, then the one adding the most new statements
Stakeholders rank the requirements, and tests for the top-ranked requirements are run first

questions.explanation: Running tests for the most important risks first is risk-based. Ordering by coverage gained, counting only what is not yet covered, is additional coverage prioritization. Ordering by the stakeholder priority of the related requirements is requirements-based. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.1.5 (p. 50); FL-5.1.5 (K3).

questions.prompt: A test schedule must respect more than priorities. Match each observation to its effect on the execution order. One effect is left over.

options.text: The high-priority test is removed from the test suite
Either may run first without breaking the prioritization
The affected tests wait until the resource is available
The low-priority test must be executed first

slots.text: A high-priority test needs data created by a low-priority test
The only test environment with the payment simulator is free on Thursday
Two tests have equal priority and no dependencies

questions.explanation: Dependencies override priority: a prerequisite runs first even when its own priority is low. The availability of resources such as environments or people can also force a different order. Tests of equal priority without dependencies can run in either order. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.1.5 (p. 50); FL-5.1.5 (K3).

questions.prompt: During system testing of a hotel booking site, a tester notes: "Booking test TC-118, test environment ST-2, build 4.7.1, Chrome 126. Steps: search for 2 nights in Lisbon, pick the first hotel, pay with a saved card. The confirmation page shows a total of €180. Screenshot attached." The tester is about to submit this as a defect report. Which missing information is MOST important to add so that the developers can analyse the problem?

options.text: The number of test cases that passed in the same test run
The name of the developer who wrote the price calculation
The expected result, so that the deviation becomes visible
An estimate of how long the correction will take to implement

questions.explanation: A defect report must state the expected result and the actual result, because the failure is the difference between them. The note gives the actual total but not what the total should have been. Who wrote the code, how many tests passed and how long a fix takes are not part of the failure description. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.5 (p. 56); FL-5.5.1 (K3).

questions.prompt: A tester found that a mobile banking app closes silently when a transfer amount contains a comma, for example "12,50". Which title is the BEST choice for the defect report?

options.text: Problem with the app that closes, found in release 3.2 on Tuesday
App closes without error message when transfer amount contains a comma
Developer forgot to validate what the amount field contains again
Transfer with a comma in the amount does not work, please fix soon

questions.explanation: A good title is a short summary of the anomaly: what happens and under which condition. The chosen title names the failure and its trigger. The others are vague, describe when the test was run rather than what went wrong, or blame a person, which a defect report should avoid. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.5 (p. 56); FL-5.5.1 (K3).

questions.prompt: An online shop rounds the VAT on every invoice down instead of to the nearest cent. Each invoice is wrong by less than one cent, the shop keeps working and customers do not notice. The tax authority requires correct VAT amounts, and an audit starts in two weeks. How should severity and priority be set in the defect report?

options.text: High severity and low priority, because the audit is still two weeks away
Low severity and low priority, because each invoice is wrong by less than one cent
Low severity for the operation of the shop, but high priority to fix because of the audit
Severity and priority are the same thing, so both are set to medium

questions.explanation: Severity is the degree of impact of the defect, and priority is the urgency of fixing it. Here the functional impact is small, but the legal deadline makes the fix urgent. The example shows that the two values are set independently and may differ. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.5 (p. 56); FL-5.5.1 (K3).

questions.prompt: A tester writes in a defect report: "Clicking Export on the Orders page with more than 1,000 rows shows a spinner that never ends (waited 10 minutes, see video). Expected: file download starts within 30 seconds, as stated in requirement R-88. This module is always sloppy and the developer clearly never tests anything." Which change improves the report MOST?

options.text: Remove the number of rows, because the defect should be reported for every table size
Remove the last sentence, because it is an opinion about people and not information about the defect
Remove the reference to requirement R-88, because developers know the requirements
Remove the waiting time and the video, because they make the report too long

questions.explanation: A defect report should be factual and give those who must resolve the defect what they need: steps, data, expected and actual results, evidence and references. Blame does not help the analysis and harms cooperation. The requirement reference, the evidence and the row count all help to reproduce and judge the defect. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.5 (p. 56); FL-5.5.1 (K3).

questions.prompt: A defect report for a train ticket app contains: an identifier, a title, the date and author, the test object and version, the test environment, numbered steps to reproduce, the actual result with a screenshot, the severity, the priority and the status "open". The developer returns it with the comment "Cannot tell whether this is wrong." Which element was missing?

options.text: The name of the test manager
The planned release date
The result of the last regression run
The expected result

questions.explanation: Without the expected result the reader cannot judge whether the actual result is a failure. The report has to state both, ideally with the source of the expectation, such as a requirement. The other items are not needed to decide whether the observed behaviour is wrong. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.5 (p. 56); FL-5.5.1 (K3).

questions.prompt: During acceptance testing, a user reports: "The monthly report is wrong." The tester who receives this must turn it into a defect report. Which action is the BEST next step?

options.text: Reproduce the problem and record steps, data, expected and actual figures
Set the status to "rejected", because the user did not supply any evidence
Raise the severity to the highest value, so that the report gets attention
Forward the sentence to the developers unchanged, so that no time is lost

questions.explanation: A defect report must describe the failure well enough to reproduce and resolve it: steps, data, expected and actual results and supporting evidence. Forwarding a vague sentence pushes the investigation onto the developers, rejecting it ignores a possible defect, and inflating severity misstates the impact. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.5 (p. 56); FL-5.5.1 (K3).

questions.prompt: A tester reports that a pharmacy system prints the wrong dosage on a label when the prescription was edited twice. The report states the test object, build, environment, steps, test data, expected and actual label text, and has photos of both labels. Which further item should the tester add to help the team decide how quickly to act?

options.text: The amount of time the tester spent on writing the report
The tester's opinion about which programmer should correct the code
The severity of the defect, describing its impact on patients and staff
A list of all test cases the tester plans to run next week

questions.explanation: A defect report includes the severity, the degree of impact on the interests of stakeholders or on requirements, and the priority to fix. For a wrong dosage the impact is serious, and stating it lets the team prioritize. The other items say nothing about the defect or its consequences. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.5 (p. 56); FL-5.5.1 (K3).

questions.prompt: A defect in a payroll system was corrected by the developers and delivered in build 9.3. The tester has not yet checked the correction. Which status should the defect report have now?

options.text: Awaiting confirmation testing
Duplicate of the original report
Closed, because a correction was delivered
Rejected, because the code has changed

questions.explanation: After a fix is delivered, the defect waits for confirmation testing, which checks that the failure no longer occurs. Only then is it closed, or re-opened if the test still fails. "Rejected" is for reports that are not defects and "duplicate" for reports of an already known defect. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.5 (p. 56); FL-5.5.1 (K3).

questions.prompt: A tester observes that a weather app shows temperatures in Fahrenheit for users in Germany, although the requirement says Celsius. The same failure was reported last week by a colleague and is still open. What should the tester do with the new finding?

options.text: Link it to the existing report and add any new information there
Do nothing, because a failure that has been seen before is no longer a defect
Create a second independent report with a higher severity to speed up the fix
Close the colleague's report and replace it with a new one under the tester's own name

questions.explanation: A defect should be tracked once. If the same defect is reported again, the new report gets the status "duplicate" and refers to the original, and useful extra information is added there. Raising severity artificially, ignoring the failure or replacing a colleague's report all damage the tracking. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.5 (p. 56); FL-5.5.1 (K3).

questions.prompt: A tester writes a defect report for a failure seen in a fuel pump controller: "Display froze during test." A developer asks for more context. Which addition gives the MOST useful context of the defect?

options.text: The total number of defects that were reported against the controller in earlier projects
The test case that was running, the test level, the firmware version and the test data used
The tester's length of experience with fuel pump controllers and with testing in general
The names of all the stakeholders who attended the most recent project status meeting

questions.explanation: The context of a defect includes the test case being run, the test activity or level, the version of the test object and relevant data such as test data. This lets the developer recreate the situation. Experience, historic defect counts and meeting attendance do not describe the circumstances of the failure. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.5 (p. 56); FL-5.5.1 (K3).

questions.prompt: A tester reports a defect in a parking app: "ID DR-431. Title: Payment fails. Author: J. Ortiz, tester, 12 May. Test object: ParkNow Android app 2.4.0. Actual result: after tapping Pay, the message 'Payment failed' appears. Severity: high. Priority: high. Status: open." Which TWO pieces of information are missing and needed to reproduce the failure? Select TWO options.

options.text: The names of the developers responsible for the payment module
The steps performed and the test data used before the payment attempt
The budget that remains for correcting defects in this release
The number of users who are likely to pay for parking each day
The test environment, such as the device, operating system and payment sandbox

questions.explanation: To reproduce a failure, the reader needs the steps and data that led to it and the environment in which it occurred. The report gives the result but neither of these. Developer names, usage figures and budgets are not part of the description of a failure. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.5 (p. 56); FL-5.5.1 (K3).

questions.prompt: Which TWO statements describe objectives of a defect report written during testing? Select TWO options.

options.text: To provide a means of tracking the quality of the work product
To record which developer was responsible, for use in performance reviews
To prove that the testers found more defects than in the previous release
To replace the test completion report at the end of the project
To give those who must resolve the defect enough information to do so

questions.explanation: Defect reports aim to provide sufficient information to resolve the issue, a means of tracking the quality of the work product, and ideas for improving the development and test process. They are not a tool for assigning blame, a competition metric, or a substitute for the test completion report. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.5 (p. 56); FL-5.5.1 (K3).

questions.prompt: A tester prepares a defect report for a food delivery app. Match each note to the part of the defect report where it belongs. One part is left over.

options.text: Severity (impact)
Test environment
Expected result
Status of the defect report
Actual result

slots.text: "Order total should be €23.40 according to the price list"
"Customers are charged €9 too much on every such order"

questions.explanation: The price that should appear is the expected result and the price that does appear is the actual result. The overcharge describes the impact, which belongs to severity. Device, operating system and server identify the test environment. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.5 (p. 56); FL-5.5.1 (K3).

questions.prompt: Match each situation to the status the defect report should receive. One status is left over.

options.text: Re-opened
Rejected
Closed
Deferred
Duplicate

slots.text: The team decides to correct the defect in a later release
Analysis shows that the software behaves as specified
Confirmation testing shows that the failure still occurs
Confirmation testing passes and nothing else is outstanding

questions.explanation: A defect postponed to a later release is deferred. A report that turns out not to describe a defect is rejected. If the failure is still present after a fix, the report is re-opened, and if confirmation testing passes it is closed. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.5 (p. 56); FL-5.5.1 (K3).

questions.prompt: Match each element of a defect report to the question it answers for the reader. One question is left over.

options.text: Who will pay for the correction?
Which test case or requirement is this related to?
What exactly do I have to do to see the failure myself?
How bad are the consequences for stakeholders?
How urgently should this be fixed?

questions.explanation: The steps enable reproduction, severity states the degree of impact, priority states the urgency of the fix, and references link the report to items such as the test case that revealed the failure. Cost allocation is not an element of a defect report. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.5 (p. 56); FL-5.5.1 (K3).

questions.prompt: A draft defect report for a web shop contains these two entries. Severity: "Must be corrected before the trade fair on Friday." Priority: "Customers cannot pay, so no order can be completed." What should the tester correct?

options.text: Move both entries into the title, since a title has to state the Friday deadline
Keep both entries, since severity and priority are two names for the same thing
Swap the two entries, since blocked payments are impact and the Friday date is urgency
Delete both entries, since severity and priority are decided by the developers alone

questions.explanation: Severity is the degree of impact of the defect, here that no customer can pay. Priority is the urgency of the fix, here the deadline before the trade fair. The two entries have been filled in the wrong way round. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.5 (p. 56); FL-5.5.1 (K3).

questions.prompt: A defect report contains exactly these items: a unique identifier, a title, the author and date, the test object and its version, the steps to reproduce, the actual result and the status. A review checklist asks for six items: unique identifier, test environment, expected result, actual result, severity and priority. How many of the six checklist items are missing from the report? Enter a whole number only.
questions.explanation: The report has the identifier and the actual result. It names no test environment, no expected result, no severity and no priority, so four of the six checklist items are missing. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.5 (p. 56); FL-5.5.1 (K3).

questions.prompt: A tester reviews a colleague's draft defect report with five sentences: (1) "Search for 'red shoes' returns 0 results." (2) "Expected at least 14 results, the number of matching products in the test database." (3) "Environment: staging, build 6.1.2, Firefox 128." (4) "The search team never tests properly." (5) "Steps: open the home page, type 'red shoes', press Enter." How many of the five sentences should be removed because they do not belong in a factual defect report? Enter a whole number only.
questions.explanation: Sentences 1, 2, 3 and 5 give the actual result, the expected result, the environment and the steps. Only sentence 4 is an opinion about people and should be removed, so the answer is 1. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.5 (p. 56); FL-5.5.1 (K3).

questions.prompt: In one week, a tester submitted 12 defect reports. After analysis, 2 were rejected as not being defects, 1 was marked as a duplicate, 3 were fixed and closed after confirmation testing, and 1 was fixed but re-opened because the failure still occurred. The rest are still open and waiting to be fixed. How many reports are waiting to be fixed, not counting the re-opened one? Enter a whole number only.
questions.explanation: Of the 12 reports, 2 were rejected, 1 is a duplicate, 3 are closed and 1 is re-opened. That accounts for 7 reports, so 12 − 7 = 5 reports are still open and waiting to be fixed. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.5 (p. 56); FL-5.5.1 (K3).

questions.prompt: A tester found that a video conferencing tool loses the audio of a participant who joins from the waiting room while screen sharing is active. The failure occurs about once in every four attempts. How should the tester describe this in the defect report?

options.text: Leave out how often it happens, because finding the frequency is the developers' task
Describe it as fully reproducible, so that the developers take the report seriously
Report it once it fails on each attempt, since an intermittent failure is hard to prove
Give the steps, state that it failed in about one of four attempts, and attach logs

questions.explanation: The description of a failure should enable reproduction and resolution. For an intermittent failure this includes how often it occurred under which steps, with supporting evidence such as logs. Waiting, overstating reproducibility or omitting the frequency all make the analysis harder or mislead the reader. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.5 (p. 56); FL-5.5.1 (K3).

questions.prompt: A team is discussing why it tests a new booking service at all. Which of the following is a typical test objective?

options.text: Providing information to stakeholders so that they can make informed decisions
Proving that the test object contains no remaining defects before release
Removing the defects that cause the failures observed during test execution
Deciding which features of the product are included in the next release

questions.explanation: Providing information for decisions is one of the typical test objectives. Removing defects is debugging, testing cannot prove the absence of defects, and deciding the release content is a product management task that testing only informs. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 1.1.1 (p. 15); FL-1.1.1 (K1).

questions.prompt: A team lists its goals for the system testing of a payroll product. Which goal is NOT a typical test objective?

options.text: Verifying compliance with legal and regulatory requirements
Building confidence in the quality of the test object
Ensuring the required coverage of the test object
Locating and repairing the faulty code behind each failure

questions.explanation: Locating and repairing faulty code is debugging, a separate activity from testing. Verifying compliance, building confidence and ensuring required coverage are all listed among the typical test objectives. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 1.1.1 (p. 15); FL-1.1.1 (K1).

questions.prompt: Which TWO of the following are typical test objectives? Select TWO options.

options.text: Evaluating work products such as requirements and user stories
Correcting the lines of code that caused an observed failure
Showing that the delivered software is free of any remaining defects
Negotiating the budget of the project with the paying customer
Reducing the risk level of inadequate software quality

questions.explanation: Reducing the risk level of inadequate quality and evaluating work products such as requirements, user stories, designs and code are typical test objectives. Testing cannot show freedom from defects, correcting code is debugging, and budget negotiation is project management. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 1.1.1 (p. 15); FL-1.1.1 (K1).

questions.prompt: A tester runs a test and the invoice total is wrong. A programmer reproduces the failure, finds a rounding mistake in the code and corrects it. The tester then repeats the test, which now passes. Which part of this story is debugging?

options.text: Repeating the test after the correction to see whether it now passes
Locating and correcting the cause of the wrong total
Comparing the invoice total that was shown with the expected total
Running the test that showed the wrong invoice total for the first time

questions.explanation: Debugging is concerned with finding the causes of a failure, analysing them and eliminating them: reproduction, diagnosis and fixing. Running the original test and comparing results is testing, and repeating the test after the fix is confirmation testing. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 1.1.2 (p. 16); FL-1.1.2 (K2).

questions.prompt: A code review finds that a variable is never initialised. No test has been executed and no failure has been observed. What does debugging involve in this situation?

options.text: Executing the code repeatedly until the variable causes a failure that the developer can diagnose
Reproducing a failure first, because a defect has to be seen as a failure before it can be corrected
Nothing at all, because the reviewers correct the defects they find during the review meeting itself
Removing the defect, with no reproduction or diagnosis, because static testing found the defect directly

questions.explanation: When static testing identifies a defect, debugging is concerned with removing it. Reproduction and diagnosis are unnecessary, since static testing finds defects directly and cannot cause failures. The author, not the review meeting, fixes the defect. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 1.1.2 (p. 16); FL-1.1.2 (K2).

questions.prompt: A start-up has no budget to involve a representative group of real users in its development project. How does testing contribute to the product's success in this situation?

options.text: Testing removes the need to think about users until the acceptance test level is reached
Testers correct usability defects in the code themselves so that users are satisfied
Testers take over from the product owner and decide which features users will receive
Testers stand in for users by keeping their needs in view throughout the lifecycle

questions.explanation: Testing provides users with indirect representation on the project: testers ensure that their understanding of users' needs is considered throughout the lifecycle. Involving real users is often too costly. Testers neither replace the product owner nor fix the code. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 1.2.1 (p. 16); FL-1.2.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: The release decision for a ticketing system is due next week, and the steering group asks what testing can contribute. Which contribution of testing is MOST relevant to this decision?

options.text: The transfer of responsibility for quality from developers to testers
A direct evaluation of the quality of the test object at this phase of the lifecycle
A shorter development schedule, because reviews are no longer needed
Evidence that the system contains no further defects of any kind

questions.explanation: Testing provides a means of directly evaluating the quality of a test object at various phases, and these measures contribute to decisions such as the release decision. Testing cannot show that no defects remain, does not replace reviews and does not move responsibility for quality. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 1.2.1 (p. 16); FL-1.2.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly describes the relation between testing and quality assurance (QA)?

options.text: Testing is product-oriented quality control, while QA is process-oriented and preventive
Testing and QA are two different names for the same quality activities
QA is product-oriented and corrective, while testing improves the processes
QA is the task of the test team, while testing is a task for everyone

questions.explanation: Testing is a product-oriented, corrective approach and a major form of quality control. QA is a process-oriented, preventive approach that focuses on implementing and improving processes and is the responsibility of everyone on a project. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 1.2.2 (p. 17); FL-1.2.2 (K1).

questions.prompt: A developer, tired after a long shift, misreads a requirement and codes a discount of 15% instead of 5%. A customer later receives an invoice that is too low. The team finds that requirements are often handed over late in the evening without any review. Match each part of the story to the correct term. One term is left over.

options.text: Test condition
Root cause
Error
Failure
Defect

slots.text: The wrong discount value in the code
The invoice that is too low
Handing over unreviewed requirements late in the evening

questions.explanation: A human error (mistake) produces a defect in a work product, here the wrong value in the code. When the defective code is executed, it causes a failure, the wrong invoice. The root cause is the fundamental reason that led to the error, here the late, unreviewed handover. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 1.2.3 (p. 17); FL-1.2.3 (K2).

questions.prompt: A regression test suite has been run unchanged for two years. It passes every night, yet users keep reporting new defects in the areas the suite covers. Which testing principle explains this BEST, and what follows from it?

options.text: Defects cluster together: the suite should be cut down to the modules with the most defects
Absence-of-defects fallacy: the passing suite shows that the users' reports are mistaken
Tests wear out: the tests and test data should be revised and new tests added
Exhaustive testing is impossible: the suite should be run less often than every night

questions.explanation: If the same tests are repeated many times, they become increasingly ineffective at detecting new defects. To overcome this, existing tests and test data may need to be modified and new tests written. The other principles are real, but the conclusions attached to them do not follow. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 1.3 (p. 17); FL-1.3.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: A team verified every specified requirement of a route planner and fixed all the defects it found. After release, cyclists, the main user group, abandon the product because the routes it proposes are impractical for them. Which testing principle does this illustrate?

options.text: Early testing saves time and money
Testing shows the presence, not the absence of defects
Testing is context dependent
Absence-of-defects fallacy

questions.explanation: It is a fallacy to expect that verification alone ensures success. A system whose specified requirements were tested thoroughly can still fail to fulfil users' needs and expectations, which is why validation must be carried out in addition to verification. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 1.3 (p. 17); FL-1.3.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: A tester studies the user stories for a loyalty scheme, identifies the features that can be tested, defines and prioritises test conditions, and reports two ambiguous acceptance criteria. Which test activity is the tester performing?

options.text: Test planning
Test implementation
Test design
Test analysis

questions.explanation: Test analysis examines the test basis to identify testable features, defines and prioritises test conditions and evaluates the test basis for defects. It answers the question "what to test?". Test design then turns the test conditions into test cases. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 1.4.1 (p. 18); FL-1.4.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: Match each test activity to a task that belongs to it. One task is left over.

options.text: Archiving useful testware and reporting at a project milestone
Elaborating test conditions into test cases and identifying coverage items
Running tests and comparing actual results with expected results
Organising test cases into test procedures and building the test environment
Comparing actual progress against the plan on an ongoing basis

questions.explanation: Test design produces test cases and coverage items, test implementation prepares procedures, scripts and the environment, test execution runs the tests and compares results, and test completion archives testware and reports. Comparing progress with the plan is test monitoring. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 1.4.1 (p. 18); FL-1.4.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: At the end of an iteration, a team creates product backlog items for the unresolved defects, hands the automated test scripts to the maintenance team and discusses what to improve next time. During which test activity do these tasks take place?

options.text: Test execution
Test implementation
Test completion
Test monitoring and test control

questions.explanation: Test completion usually occurs at milestones such as the end of an iteration. Change requests or backlog items are created for unresolved defects, useful testware is archived or handed over, and lessons learned are identified for future iterations. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 1.4.1 (p. 18); FL-1.4.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: A company develops both a mobile game and the software for an insulin pump. The test process for the pump uses more formal documentation, higher coverage and more independent testing. Which contextual factor explains this difference BEST?

options.text: The project constraints, because projects for medical devices are given larger budgets and more time
The business domain, in particular the criticality of the test object and the regulations that apply
The tools, because the software of medical devices has to be tested with licensed commercial tools
The team members, because the testers of a game lack the skills needed to write documentation

questions.explanation: The business domain, including the criticality of the test object, identified risks and specific legal regulations, is a contextual factor that shapes the test process. A safety-critical, regulated product calls for more rigour than a game. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 1.4.2 (p. 19); FL-1.4.2 (K2).

questions.prompt: Which TWO of the following are contextual factors that influence how the test process is carried out? Select TWO options.

options.text: The number of defects that test execution will reveal
The software development lifecycle that the organisation follows
The skills, experience and availability of the team members
The names that were chosen for the test cases
The order in which the testing principles are listed

questions.explanation: The syllabus lists stakeholders, team members, business domain, technical factors, project constraints, organisational factors, the software development lifecycle and tools as contextual factors. The other options are outcomes or details of the testing, and do not shape the process. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 1.4.2 (p. 19); FL-1.4.2 (K2).

questions.prompt: A team moves from a sequential lifecycle with one release a year to Agile development with a release every two weeks. Which change to the test process is the MOST likely consequence?

options.text: A separate test phase after all the iterations, with full documentation of each test case
More test automation and lighter documentation, with test activities repeated in each iteration
An unchanged test process, because the test process is independent of the lifecycle
No test planning, because Agile teams respond to change instead of following a plan

questions.explanation: The software development lifecycle is a contextual factor that affects, among other things, the degree of test automation, the level of detail of testware and when test activities occur. Frequent releases favour automation and lightweight documentation, but planning still takes place. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 1.4.2 (p. 19); FL-1.4.2 (K2).

questions.prompt: Which of the following lists contains work products of test implementation?

options.text: Test conditions, test charters, coverage items and test data requirements
Test logs, defect reports and a test completion report for stakeholders
Test procedures, automated test scripts, test suites and a test execution schedule
Test plan, test schedule, risk register, entry criteria and exit criteria

questions.explanation: Test implementation produces test procedures, manual and automated test scripts, test suites, test data, the test execution schedule and test environment items. Test charters and coverage items come from test design, the test plan and risk register from test planning, and test logs from test execution. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 1.4.3 (p. 20); FL-1.4.3 (K2).

questions.prompt: Match each work product to the test activity that produces it. One activity is left over.

options.text: Test analysis
Test execution
Test design
Test completion
Test planning

questions.explanation: The risk register is a test planning work product, often part of the test plan. Test charters come from test design, test logs are written during test execution, and documented lessons learned are an output of test completion. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 1.4.3 (p. 20); FL-1.4.3 (K2).

questions.prompt: A requirement for a tax calculation changes late in a project. The team needs to know which test cases must be updated and which earlier test results are no longer valid. What makes it possible to answer this quickly?

options.text: Configuration of the test environment by the developers themselves
The test completion report that was written for the previous release
Traceability across the test basis, testware and outcomes
A higher level of independence of the people who execute the tests

questions.explanation: Good traceability between test basis elements, testware, test results and defects makes it possible to determine the impact of changes. The team can follow the links from the changed requirement to the affected test cases and results. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 1.4.4 (p. 20); FL-1.4.4 (K2).

questions.prompt: A test manager reports that 38 of 40 requirements have at least one passed test case, and that the two remaining requirements relate to a high product risk. Which benefit of traceability does this report demonstrate?

options.text: Test cases need no review any more, because they are linked to the requirements
Coverage and residual risk can be evaluated and explained in terms stakeholders understand
Defects can be assigned automatically to the developer who introduced each of them
Test execution can be skipped for requirements that already have a test case

questions.explanation: Traceability of test cases to requirements shows whether requirements are covered, and traceability of test results to risks helps to evaluate residual risk. Including the status of test basis elements makes reports easier for stakeholders to understand. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 1.4.4 (p. 20); FL-1.4.4 (K2).

questions.prompt: Which TWO are benefits of maintaining good traceability between the test basis and the testware? Select TWO options.

options.text: It replaces the test plan in Agile software development
It shows that the test object is free of defects
It facilitates audits and helps to meet IT governance criteria
It makes it possible to determine the impact of changes
It removes the need for regression testing after a change

questions.explanation: Besides supporting coverage evaluation, good traceability makes it possible to determine the impact of changes, facilitates audits and helps to meet IT governance criteria. It does not replace regression testing or planning, and it cannot show freedom from defects. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 1.4.4 (p. 20); FL-1.4.4 (K2).

questions.prompt: In a small Agile team, Dana designs and executes the tests for the user stories. The team as a whole decides the test approach for each iteration and follows progress on a board. A manager outside the team coordinates the test environments shared by five teams. Which statement describes the roles correctly?

options.text: Dana has both roles, because whoever executes tests is the test manager as well
Nobody has the test management role, because Agile teams have no test management
The outside manager has the testing role, because environments are a technical matter
Dana has the testing role, and test management tasks are split between the team and the outside manager

questions.explanation: The testing role focuses on test analysis, design, implementation and execution. In Agile development some test management tasks may be handled by the team, while tasks spanning several teams may be performed by test managers outside the team. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 1.4.5 (p. 21); FL-1.4.5 (K2).

questions.prompt: A project assigns the two principal roles in testing to different people. Which pair of activities is mainly the focus of the test management role?

options.text: Test analysis, and test design with test techniques
Test planning, and test monitoring and test control
Test implementation, and test execution of test runs
Test design, and test implementation of test scripts

questions.explanation: The test management role takes overall responsibility for the test process and focuses mainly on test planning, test monitoring, test control and test completion. Test analysis, design, implementation and execution are the focus of the testing role. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 1.4.5 (p. 21); FL-1.4.5 (K2).

questions.prompt: A tester must tell a developer that the feature she has just finished fails four important tests. Which generic skill is MOST important for doing this well, and why?

options.text: Technical knowledge, because the tester should correct the code before reporting the failures
Domain knowledge, because the developer does not understand the business behind the feature
Creativity, because the tester should present the four failures as ideas for new features
Communication skills, because test results may be perceived as criticism of the product and its author

questions.explanation: Testers are often the bearers of bad news, and communicating test results may be perceived as criticism of the product and of its author. Good communication skills let the tester convey information about defects and failures in a constructive way. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 1.5.1 (p. 21); FL-1.5.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: A tester on an insurance project can explain the claim-handling rules to the developers and understands the vocabulary that the business representatives use. Which generic skill does this show?

options.text: Testing knowledge
Analytical thinking
Domain knowledge
Technical knowledge

questions.explanation: Domain knowledge enables a tester to understand and to communicate with end users and business representatives. Technical knowledge concerns tools and technology, and testing knowledge concerns the craft of testing, such as test techniques. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 1.5.1 (p. 21); FL-1.5.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: Match each generic skill of a tester to the reason the syllabus gives for it. One reason is left over.

options.text: Increases the effectiveness of testing, for example by using test techniques
Helps to identify defects, especially those that are difficult to find
Removes the need for testers to report defects
Increases the efficiency of testing, for example by using suitable test tools
Helps to interact effectively with all stakeholders

slots.text: Active listening and being a team player

questions.explanation: Testing knowledge raises effectiveness and technical knowledge raises efficiency. Thoroughness, carefulness and attention to detail help to find difficult defects, and communication skills such as active listening support interaction with stakeholders. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 1.5.1 (p. 21); FL-1.5.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: Which statement describes the whole team approach?

options.text: The whole team reports to the test manager, who has to approve every single release
Testers alone are responsible for quality, while developers are responsible for delivery
Anyone with the necessary skills can perform any task, and everyone is responsible for quality
Each task belongs to a fixed specialist, and work is handed over between departments

questions.explanation: In the whole team approach, any team member with the necessary knowledge and skills can perform any task, and everyone is responsible for quality. Team members share a physical or virtual workspace, which helps communication and interaction. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 1.5.2 (p. 22); FL-1.5.2 (K1).

questions.prompt: Which of the following is an advantage of the whole team approach?

options.text: It improves team dynamics and communication and lets the team use its varied skills
It lets the developers hand over all of the testing tasks to the testers in the team
It gives the testers the highest possible level of independence from the developers
It removes the need for testers to work together with business representatives

questions.explanation: The whole team approach improves team dynamics, enhances communication and collaboration, and creates synergy by letting the various skill sets be used for the benefit of the project. It reduces rather than maximises independence, and testers work closely with business representatives. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 1.5.2 (p. 22); FL-1.5.2 (K1).

questions.prompt: In which situation might the whole team approach be inappropriate?

options.text: A safety-critical product for which a high level of test independence is needed
A web shop that is developed by a co-located team of six people
A project in which testers help to create the acceptance tests
A product whose team members share a single virtual workspace

questions.explanation: Depending on the context, the whole team approach may not always be appropriate. In some situations, such as safety-critical systems, a high level of test independence may be needed, which conflicts with everyone sharing every task. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 1.5.2 (p. 22); FL-1.5.2 (K1).

questions.prompt: Put these ways of testing a work product in order of independence, from the lowest level to the highest level.

options.text: Testers from another team in the same organisation test it
Testers from outside the organisation test it
The author tests the work product
A peer from the author's team tests it

questions.explanation: Testing by the author gives no independence, testing by peers from the same team gives some, testing by testers outside the author's team but inside the organisation gives high independence, and testing by people outside the organisation gives very high independence. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 1.5.3 (p. 22); FL-1.5.3 (K2).

questions.prompt: A bank lets an external company do all its system testing. The developers stop writing component tests, saying "the test company will find the defects", and releases are delayed while the external testers wait for information. Which statement describes this situation BEST?

options.text: It shows drawbacks of independence: developers feel less responsible for quality and testers are isolated
It shows that the whole team approach has been applied too strictly by the external test company
