It shows that independent testing should be replaced completely by testing done by the developers
It shows benefits of independence: external testers recognise different failures than developers do

questions.explanation: Independent testers may be isolated from the development team, which can cause communication problems, and developers may lose a sense of responsibility for quality. Independent testers may also be seen as a bottleneck. For most projects, several levels of independence work best. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 1.5.3 (p. 22); FL-1.5.3 (K2).

questions.prompt: A supplier builds a billing system with a V-model. The code will only exist in month nine of a twelve-month project. What can the testers typically do in the first months?

options.text: Run system tests against a prototype that is delivered in each of the iterations
Take part in requirement reviews and carry out test analysis and test design
Wait until the code exists, because testing starts with the first executable build
Execute the automated regression tests that were written for earlier increments

questions.explanation: In sequential development models, testers typically participate in requirement reviews, test analysis and test design in the initial phases. Executable code is usually created later, so dynamic testing cannot be performed early. Iterations and increments belong to other lifecycle models. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 2.1.1 (p. 25); FL-2.1.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: A team delivers a working increment of a travel app every two weeks. Which consequence for testing follows MOST directly from this iterative and incremental way of working?

options.text: Test documentation becomes more detailed with each iteration, because each increment is formally handed over to the testers
Each increment is tested once at the acceptance test level, and no lower test levels are required for it at any time
Fast feedback and extensive regression testing are needed, and static and dynamic testing take place in each iteration
Dynamic testing is postponed until the final increment has been delivered, when the whole product is finally available

questions.explanation: When each iteration delivers a working increment, static and dynamic testing may be performed at all test levels in each iteration. Frequent delivery requires fast feedback and extensive regression testing, since earlier increments must keep working. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 2.1.1 (p. 25); FL-2.1.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: Which TWO aspects of testing are affected by the choice of software development lifecycle? Select TWO options.

options.text: The extent of test automation
The seven testing principles
The level of detail of the test documentation
The definition of what a failure is
The meaning of a test condition

questions.explanation: The lifecycle affects the scope and timing of test activities, the level of detail of test documentation, the choice of test techniques and test approach, the extent of test automation, and the role and responsibilities of a tester. Definitions and principles stay the same. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 2.1.1 (p. 25); FL-2.1.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: Which of the following is a good testing practice that applies whatever software development lifecycle is chosen?

options.text: Test analysis for a test level starts after the development of its code
For each development activity there is a corresponding test activity
Testers review a work product once its final version is approved
All of the test levels share the same test objectives to save effort

questions.explanation: Independent of the lifecycle, every development activity has a corresponding test activity, test levels have specific and different objectives, test analysis and design begin during the corresponding development phase, and testers review work products as soon as drafts are available. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 2.1.2 (p. 25); FL-2.1.2 (K1).

questions.prompt: A project wants to follow good testing practices. When should testers start to review a requirements specification?

options.text: When the first component built from it has been delivered
As soon as a draft of the specification is available
After the specification has been approved by the customer
During the test execution of the system test level

questions.explanation: Testers should be involved in reviewing work products as soon as drafts are available. This earlier testing and defect detection supports shift left and follows the principle of early testing. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 2.1.2 (p. 25); FL-2.1.2 (K1).

questions.prompt: Why is it good practice for different test levels to have specific and different test objectives?

options.text: Defects are then reported once per level to raise the defect counts
The lower test levels can be dropped once acceptance testing exists
Each test level can then be given to a different external supplier
Testing can be comprehensive while redundancy between the levels is avoided

questions.explanation: Different test levels have specific and different test objectives, which allows testing to be appropriately comprehensive while avoiding redundancy. The practice says nothing about suppliers, and it does not make lower levels dispensable. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 2.1.2 (p. 25); FL-2.1.2 (K1).

questions.prompt: Match each test-first approach to its characteristic. One characteristic is left over.

options.text: Expresses desired behaviour in simple natural language, usually Given/When/Then
Directs the coding through test cases; then the tests and the code are refactored
Derives tests from the code structure after the code has been written
Derives tests from acceptance criteria as part of the system design process

questions.explanation: TDD directs coding through test cases written first, followed by refactoring. ATDD derives tests from acceptance criteria during system design. BDD expresses the desired behaviour in a simple natural-language form that stakeholders can read. All three define tests before the code. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 2.1.3 (p. 26); FL-2.1.3 (K1).

questions.prompt: Which statement is true of TDD, ATDD and BDD alike?

options.text: The tests are defined before the code is written, which implements early testing
The tests are discarded as soon as the code has passed them for the first time
The tests are derived from acceptance criteria during the system design
The tests are written in the Given/When/Then format to suit stakeholders

questions.explanation: In all three approaches tests direct development and are defined before the code is written, so each implements the principle of early testing and follows shift left. Given/When/Then is typical of BDD only, acceptance criteria of ATDD, and the tests may persist as automated tests. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 2.1.3 (p. 26); FL-2.1.3 (K1).

questions.prompt: Put the steps of test-driven development (TDD) for one small piece of functionality in order.

options.text: Refactor the test and the code
Write code that satisfies the test
Write a test for the functionality

questions.explanation: In TDD the tests are written first, then the code is written to satisfy the tests, and then the tests and code are refactored. The cycle then repeats for the next small piece of functionality. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 2.1.3 (p. 26); FL-2.1.3 (K1).

questions.prompt: A company introduces DevOps with a delivery pipeline that builds, tests and deploys each change without manual steps. Which statement summarises the impact on testing BEST?

options.text: Non-functional quality characteristics become less visible, because the pipeline checks only functional behaviour
Feedback on code quality becomes fast and regression risk falls, but the pipeline and automation must be built and maintained
Testing moves to the operations team, because development and operations are merged into a single department
Manual testing from the user's perspective becomes unnecessary, because the pipeline runs all of the tests that matter

questions.explanation: DevOps gives fast feedback on code quality and minimises regression risk through automated regression tests, and it increases the visibility of non-functional characteristics. Its challenges include establishing the pipeline, maintaining CI/CD tools and resourcing test automation. Manual testing is still needed. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 2.1.4 (p. 26); FL-2.1.4 (K2).

questions.prompt: A team wants to "shift left". Which of the following actions is an example of this?

options.text: Starting static analysis after the dynamic tests have been run
Dropping the acceptance tests because defects are found earlier
Running non-functional tests at the component test level where this is possible
Moving all the system tests to the week before the release date

questions.explanation: Shift left means testing earlier in the lifecycle. Performing non-functional testing from the component level, reviewing specifications from a tester's perspective, writing tests before the code and running static analysis before dynamic testing are examples. Later testing is not neglected. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 2.1.5 (p. 27); FL-2.1.5 (K2).

questions.prompt: A manager objects to shift left: "Training the team to review specifications costs money now." Which reply reflects the idea of shift left correctly?

options.text: The cost is repaid because testing late in the lifecycle can then be dropped
Shift left costs nothing, because it only moves existing work to an earlier date
Stakeholder support is unimportant, because shift left is a purely technical step
Extra effort early is expected to save effort and cost later in the lifecycle

questions.explanation: Shift left might result in extra training, effort or costs earlier in the process but is expected to save effort or costs later. It does not mean that later testing is neglected, and it is important that stakeholders are convinced of the concept. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 2.1.5 (p. 27); FL-2.1.5 (K2).

questions.prompt: At the end of an iteration a team holds a retrospective. Developers, the product owner and testers agree that unclear acceptance criteria caused most rework, and decide to review criteria together before each iteration. Which typical benefit of retrospectives for testing does this show?

options.text: Improved quality of the test basis
Automatic archiving of the testware
Fewer test levels in later iterations
Higher independence of the testers

questions.explanation: Retrospectives can improve the quality of the test basis, because deficiencies in the extent and quality of the requirements can be addressed and solved. Other benefits are greater test effectiveness and efficiency, better testware, team bonding and better cooperation. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 2.1.6 (p. 28); FL-2.1.6 (K2).

questions.prompt: A team holds a retrospective after every release and writes down good ideas, but the same problems return each time. What is MOST likely missing?

options.text: A longer list of what was successful
Attendance of the testers only
A formal inspection of the meeting notes
Follow-up of the recommended improvements

questions.explanation: Retrospectives are critical for continuous improvement, and it is important that recommended improvements are followed up. Recording results is not enough if nobody implements them. Participants are not only testers but also developers, architects, product owners and others. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 2.1.6 (p. 28); FL-2.1.6 (K2).

questions.prompt: Which TWO questions are typically discussed in a retrospective? Select TWO options.

options.text: Which team member caused the most defects?
Which requirements should be removed from the contract?
What was successful and should be retained?
What could be improved, and how do we make the improvements happen?
Which testers should move to another team?

questions.explanation: Participants discuss what was successful and should be retained, what was not successful and could be improved, and how to incorporate the improvements and retain the successes. A retrospective is not about blaming people or renegotiating contracts. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 2.1.6 (p. 28); FL-2.1.6 (K2).

questions.prompt: A tester checks that an order service and a separate payment component exchange messages in the agreed format. Both were built by the same team and are parts of one system. Which test level is this?

options.text: System integration testing
Acceptance testing
Component testing
Component integration testing

questions.explanation: Component integration testing focuses on the interfaces and interactions between components of one system. Component testing looks at components in isolation, and system integration testing looks at interfaces to other systems and external services. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 2.2.1 (p. 28); FL-2.2.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: Match each test level to its focus. One focus is left over.

options.text: Evaluation of a work product without executing code
Components in isolation, often with a unit test framework
Overall behaviour and capabilities of an entire system or product
Interfaces between the system under test and other systems or external services
Validation and demonstrating readiness for deployment

questions.explanation: Component testing isolates components, system testing looks at the whole system, system integration testing covers interfaces to other systems and external services, and acceptance testing validates that the system fulfils business needs and is ready for deployment. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 2.2.1 (p. 28); FL-2.2.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: A tester reuses a functional test that books a flight and adds a check that the booking completes within three seconds. Which test type does the added check belong to?

options.text: Confirmation testing
Functional testing
Non-functional testing
White-box testing

questions.explanation: Non-functional testing evaluates how well the system behaves, for example its performance efficiency. Many non-functional tests are derived from functional tests: they perform the same function but check that a non-functional constraint, such as a response time, is satisfied. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 2.2.2 (p. 29); FL-2.2.2 (K2).

questions.prompt: A defect in a discount calculation was fixed. The tester first re-runs the test that had failed, then runs a suite of existing tests for the basket, checkout and invoice functions. What are these two activities called, in this order?

options.text: Confirmation testing, then exploratory testing
Maintenance testing, then acceptance testing
Regression testing, then confirmation testing
Confirmation testing, then regression testing

questions.explanation: Confirmation testing confirms that the original defect has been fixed, typically by executing the tests that failed because of it. Regression testing confirms that the change has caused no adverse consequences elsewhere. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 2.2.3 (p. 30); FL-2.2.3 (K2).

questions.prompt: A team must decide how much regression testing a change to a tax module needs. Which step is advisable first?

options.text: A retrospective to see why the tax module needed to be changed
An impact analysis to see which parts of the software could be affected
A confirmation test of each defect closed in the last release
A full manual run of each test case that exists for the system

questions.explanation: It is advisable first to perform an impact analysis to recognise the extent of the regression testing. Impact analysis shows which parts of the software could be affected by the change, so the regression tests can be chosen accordingly. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 2.2.3 (p. 30); FL-2.2.3 (K2).

questions.prompt: A hospital moves its patient records system from its own servers to a cloud platform. The software itself is unchanged. Which trigger for maintenance testing is this?

options.text: A corrective modification of the system
A migration of the operational environment
A planned functional enhancement
The retirement of the application

questions.explanation: Upgrades or migrations of the operational environment, such as from one platform to another, are a trigger for maintenance testing. They can require tests associated with the new environment as well as of the changed software. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 2.3 (p. 31); FL-2.3.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: An insurer retires a policy system after 25 years. The law requires policy data to be kept for ten more years. Which testing is MOST relevant?

options.text: Testing of the performance of the retired system under peak load
Testing of each function of the retired system at system test level
Testing of hot fixes that were deployed during the last year of use
Testing of data archiving and of the restore and retrieval procedures

questions.explanation: When a system is retired, testing of data archiving can be required if long data retention periods apply. Testing of restore and retrieval procedures after archiving may also be needed in case data is required during the archiving period. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 2.3 (p. 31); FL-2.3.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: Which TWO factors typically determine the scope of maintenance testing? Select TWO options.

options.text: The degree of risk of the change
The size of the existing system
The number of testers who know the system
The lifecycle used when the system was first built
The age of the test team

questions.explanation: The scope of maintenance testing typically depends on the degree of risk of the change, the size of the existing system and the size of the change. Testing a change to an operational system covers both the change itself and possible regressions in unchanged parts. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 2.3 (p. 31); FL-2.3.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: Which of the following work products is LEAST suitable for static testing?

options.text: A test charter for an exploratory testing session
A draft contract with a supplier of test environments
Third-party executable code under a restrictive licence
A product backlog item with its acceptance criteria

questions.explanation: Almost any work product that can be read and understood can be reviewed, including contracts, backlog items and test charters. Work products that are difficult for humans to interpret and should not be analysed by tools, such as third-party executable code for legal reasons, are not appropriate. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 3.1.1 (p. 33); FL-3.1.1 (K1).

questions.prompt: A team wants to run a static analysis tool over several work products. Which property must a work product have for static analysis to be possible?

options.text: A natural-language text that at least two reviewers have read
An executable form, so that the tool is able to run it step by step
An approval by the manager who decides what is to be reviewed
A structure against which it can be checked, such as a formal syntax

questions.explanation: Any work product that can be read and understood can be reviewed, but for static analysis the work product needs a structure against which it can be checked, for example models, code or text with a formal syntax. Execution is not needed for static testing. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 3.1.1 (p. 33); FL-3.1.1 (K1).

questions.prompt: A project manager says: "Reviews of the requirements cost us two days per sprint. We should stop them." Which answer explains the value of static testing BEST?

options.text: Reviews replace dynamic testing of the requirements, so the two days are saved again during test execution
Reviews are required by the syllabus for each work product, whatever they cost and whatever they find
Overall costs are lower with reviews, because less effort goes into fixing defects later
Reviews cost nothing overall, because the reviewers do them alongside their normal work in the sprint

questions.explanation: Even though reviews can be costly to implement, overall project costs are usually much lower than without reviews, because less time and effort is spent on fixing defects later. Static testing detects defects in the earliest phases and complements, but does not replace, dynamic testing. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 3.1.2 (p. 33); FL-3.1.2 (K2).

questions.prompt: A static analysis tool reports a block of code that no path through the program can ever reach. Why is this finding a good example of the value of static testing?

options.text: Static analysis has repaired the defect, since tools of this kind rewrite the code they check
Dynamic testing would detect the same defect faster by executing the block with boundary values
Static analysis has shown that the remaining code is correct, since no other report was produced
Dynamic testing cannot detect such a defect, since the unreachable code is never executed

questions.explanation: Static testing can identify defects that cannot be detected by dynamic testing, such as unreachable code, design patterns that were not implemented as desired and defects in non-executable work products. Unreachable code never runs, so no test can make it fail. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 3.1.2 (p. 33); FL-3.1.2 (K2).

questions.prompt: A team invites business analysts, developers, testers and an operations engineer to review a draft specification early in the project. Which TWO benefits of static testing does this practice aim at? Select TWO options.

options.text: Improved communication between the stakeholders involved
A measurement of the response time of the system
Proof that the specification contains no defects
A shared understanding among the stakeholders involved
Removal of the need for acceptance testing

questions.explanation: Because static testing can be performed early, a shared understanding can be created among the involved stakeholders and communication between them improves, which is why a wide variety of stakeholders should be involved. Response times need dynamic testing, and no review proves the absence of defects. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 3.1.2 (p. 33); FL-3.1.2 (K2).

questions.prompt: Which statement compares static testing and dynamic testing correctly?

options.text: Static testing causes failures in the work product, while dynamic testing finds the defects without executing any code
Static testing measures performance efficiency, while dynamic testing measures the maintainability of the code
Static testing applies to executable work products, while dynamic testing applies to documents such as requirements
Static testing finds defects directly, while dynamic testing causes failures that are then analysed to find the defects

questions.explanation: Static testing finds defects directly, whereas dynamic testing causes failures from which the associated defects are determined through analysis. Static testing can be applied to non-executable work products and can measure characteristics such as maintainability that do not depend on executing code. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 3.1.3 (p. 34); FL-3.1.3 (K2).

questions.prompt: Which TWO defects are typically easier or cheaper to find through static testing than through dynamic testing? Select TWO options.

options.text: A memory leak that appears after six hours of operation
A variable name that breaks the coding standard's naming convention
A requirement that contradicts another requirement
A response time that exceeds two seconds under load
A wrong total on an invoice printed by the system

questions.explanation: Defects in requirements, such as contradictions, and deviations from standards, such as naming conventions, are typical findings of static testing. Response times, memory leaks and wrong outputs appear when the software is executed, which is dynamic testing. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 3.1.3 (p. 34); FL-3.1.3 (K2).

questions.prompt: A team shows its customer a working increment every two weeks and collects comments. Which benefit of early and frequent stakeholder feedback does this give?

options.text: Misunderstandings about requirements are prevented or noticed sooner
Requirements are frozen once the first increment has been shown
Testers can stop reviewing the user stories before each iteration
Stakeholders no longer need to take part in acceptance testing

questions.explanation: Frequent stakeholder feedback throughout the lifecycle can prevent misunderstandings about requirements and ensures that changes to requirements are understood and implemented earlier. It does not freeze requirements or replace other test activities. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 3.2.1 (p. 35); FL-3.2.1 (K1).

questions.prompt: A product was developed for a year with almost no contact with its future users. At delivery it does not match what they wanted. Which consequence does the syllabus associate with such little stakeholder involvement?

options.text: Fewer defects, since the requirements stayed stable for a whole year
Higher test independence, since users did not influence the testers
Costly rework, missed deadlines, blame games and possibly project failure
Lower development costs, since fewer meetings were needed in the year

questions.explanation: If there is little stakeholder involvement, the product might not meet the stakeholders' original or current vision. A failure to deliver what the stakeholder wants can result in costly rework, missed deadlines, blame games and even complete project failure. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 3.2.1 (p. 35); FL-3.2.1 (K1).

questions.prompt: Why does early and frequent feedback help a development team to decide what to build next?

options.text: The team can build the features in the order in which they were first written
The team can leave risk analysis out, because stakeholders accept the risks
The team can replace its backlog refinement sessions with a final demonstration
The team can focus on the features that deliver the most value and reduce identified risks

questions.explanation: Frequent feedback improves the team's understanding of what it is building. It allows the team to focus on those features that deliver the most value to the stakeholders and that have the most positive impact on identified risks. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 3.2.1 (p. 35); FL-3.2.1 (K1).

questions.prompt: Put the activities of the generic review process in the order in which they take place.

options.text: Communication and analysis
Review initiation
Planning
Individual review
Fixing and reporting

questions.explanation: The review process starts with planning, which defines the scope. Review initiation makes sure everyone and everything is prepared. Reviewers then perform the individual review, the anomalies are discussed in communication and analysis, and finally defects are fixed and results reported. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 3.2.2 (p. 35); FL-3.2.2 (K2).

questions.prompt: Match each review role to its responsibility. One responsibility is left over.

options.text: Ensures the effective running of review meetings, including mediation and time management
Takes overall responsibility, such as deciding who is involved and when the review takes place
Collates anomalies from reviewers and records decisions
Decides what is to be reviewed and provides staff and time
Creates and fixes the work product under review

questions.explanation: The manager decides what is reviewed and provides resources. The moderator, or facilitator, runs the meetings. The scribe, or recorder, collates anomalies and records review information. The review leader has overall responsibility. Creating and fixing the work product is the author's responsibility. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 3.2.3 (p. 36); FL-3.2.3 (K1).

questions.prompt: During a review meeting two reviewers start to argue loudly, and a junior colleague stops contributing. Which role is responsible for dealing with this?

options.text: The moderator
The scribe
The manager
The author

questions.explanation: The moderator, also known as the facilitator, ensures the effective running of review meetings, including mediation, time management and a safe review environment in which everyone can speak freely. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 3.2.3 (p. 36); FL-3.2.3 (K1).

questions.prompt: A medical device company must review a safety requirement specification. It needs the maximum number of anomalies to be found, an audit trail, and metrics to improve its process. Which review type fits BEST?

options.text: Informal review
Technical review
Inspection
Walkthrough

questions.explanation: Inspections are the most formal review type and follow the complete generic process. Their main objective is to find the maximum number of anomalies, and metrics are collected and used to improve the lifecycle, including the inspection process itself. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 3.2.4 (p. 36); FL-3.2.4 (K2).

questions.prompt: An architect presents her design for a new messaging layer to colleagues. She leads the session herself, explains the design step by step so that the others learn it, and collects their ideas. Individual preparation was optional. Which review type is this?

options.text: Walkthrough
Informal review
Inspection
Technical review

questions.explanation: A walkthrough is led by the author and can serve many objectives, such as educating reviewers, gaining consensus, generating new ideas and detecting anomalies. Reviewers might perform an individual review beforehand, but this is not required. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 3.2.4 (p. 36); FL-3.2.4 (K2).

questions.prompt: Match each review type to a distinguishing feature. One feature is left over.

options.text: Performed by technically qualified reviewers and led by a moderator, to gain consensus on a technical problem
The author cannot act as the review leader or scribe
Carried out by executing the work product with test data
Follows no defined process and needs no formal documented output

questions.explanation: Informal reviews have no defined process. Technical reviews are done by technically qualified reviewers, led by a moderator, with consensus and decisions on technical problems among the objectives. In inspections, the most formal type, the author cannot be review leader or scribe. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 3.2.4 (p. 36); FL-3.2.4 (K2).

questions.prompt: A team plans to review a 90-page design document in one three-hour meeting, and the manager wants to use the number of anomalies found per reviewer in the annual appraisals. Which change would contribute MOST to a successful review?

options.text: Reviewing the document in small chunks and dropping the evaluation of participants
Extending the meeting to six hours so that the document is covered in one session
Sending the document to the reviewers at the start of the meeting to keep it confidential
Letting the manager moderate the meeting so that the appraisal figures are accurate

questions.explanation: Success factors include performing reviews on small chunks, so that reviewers do not lose concentration, and defining clear objectives; evaluation of participants should never be an objective. Participants also need adequate time to prepare. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 3.2.5 (p. 37); FL-3.2.5 (K1).

questions.prompt: Which TWO of the following are success factors for reviews? Select TWO options.

options.text: Keeping review results away from the author
Support from management for the review process
Limiting training to the moderator
Using the same review type for each work product
Providing adequate time for participants to prepare

questions.explanation: Success factors include clear objectives and measurable exit criteria, an appropriate review type, small chunks, feedback to stakeholders and authors, adequate preparation time, management support, a review culture, training for all participants and facilitated meetings. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 3.2.5 (p. 37); FL-3.2.5 (K1).

questions.prompt: A tester derives test cases for a pricing component in three ways: (1) from the pricing rules in the specification, (2) from the control flow of the source code, and (3) from her memory of rounding defects in earlier pricing projects. Which families of test techniques are these, in this order?

options.text: Black-box, white-box, experience-based
Black-box, experience-based, white-box
White-box, black-box, experience-based
Experience-based, white-box, black-box

questions.explanation: Black-box techniques analyse the specified behaviour without reference to internal structure. White-box techniques analyse the internal structure and processing. Experience-based techniques use the knowledge and experience of testers. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.1 (p. 39); FL-4.1.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: A component is rewritten in another programming language, but its required behaviour stays the same. What happens to the test cases that were designed with black-box test techniques?

options.text: They must be redesigned, because they depend on the structure of the old source code
They can be created again only after the design of the new implementation is finished
They lose their value, because black-box techniques rely on the tester's past experience
They remain useful, because they are independent of how the software is implemented

questions.explanation: Black-box test cases are based on the specified behaviour, so they are independent of the implementation. If the implementation changes but the required behaviour stays the same, the test cases are still useful. White-box test cases depend on the design and code. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.1 (p. 39); FL-4.1.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: A test suite achieves 100% statement coverage of a function that divides a total by a count. In production the function fails when the count is zero. How is this possible?

options.text: Exercising a statement does not detect defects that depend on particular data
Statement coverage of 100% is impossible to reach for functions that divide
Statement coverage counts the comments, which hid the faulty statement
Statement coverage of 100% leaves some executable statements unexercised

questions.explanation: With 100% statement coverage every executable statement has been exercised at least once, but exercising a statement will not detect defects in all cases. Data-dependent defects, such as a division that only fails when the denominator is zero, may remain undetected. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.3.1 (p. 42); FL-4.3.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: A tester measures the coverage of a set of component tests for a parser. The code has 60 executable statements, and the test cases exercise 45 of them. What percentage of statement coverage has been achieved? Enter a whole number only.
questions.explanation: Statement coverage is the number of executable statements exercised by the test cases divided by the total number of executable statements: 45 / 60 = 75%. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.3.1 (p. 42); FL-4.3.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: A set of test cases achieves 100% branch coverage of a module. What can be concluded about its statement coverage?

options.text: It is lower than 100%, because some statements lie outside all the branches
It is 50%, because each decision has a true branch and a false branch
It is 100% as well, because branch coverage subsumes statement coverage
It is unknown, because the two kinds of coverage are measured independently

questions.explanation: Branch coverage subsumes statement coverage: any set of test cases achieving 100% branch coverage also achieves 100% statement coverage, but not the other way round. Branches include unconditional transfers of control, so straight-line code is covered too. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.3.2 (p. 43); FL-4.3.2 (K2).

questions.prompt: A tester measures the coverage of a set of component tests for a discount module. The code has 12 branches, and the test cases exercise 9 of them. What percentage of branch coverage has been achieved? Enter a whole number only.
questions.explanation: Branch coverage is the number of branches exercised by the test cases divided by the total number of branches: 9 / 12 = 75%. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.3.2 (p. 43); FL-4.3.2 (K2).

questions.prompt: The specification of a legacy billing module is outdated and incomplete, but its source code is available. Why are white-box test techniques valuable here?

options.text: They replace the specification, since the code defines what the customer actually wanted
They take the entire implementation into account, so defects can be found despite the weak specification
They need no access to the code, so they work even when the specification has been lost
They reveal the requirements that were never implemented, since the missing code is easy to see

questions.explanation: A fundamental strength of white-box techniques is that the entire software implementation is taken into account, which facilitates defect detection even when the specification is vague, outdated or incomplete. Their weakness is that they may miss requirements that were not implemented. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.3.3 (p. 43); FL-4.3.3 (K2).

questions.prompt: A requirement says that orders above £500 need a second approval. The developer forgot to implement it, and no code for it exists. The team reaches 100% branch coverage. Why did white-box testing miss the defect?

options.text: White-box testing derives tests from existing code, and here there is no code to cover
White-box testing is restricted to static testing, and the defect needs execution
White-box testing covers statements only, and the approval would have been a branch
White-box testing had too little coverage, and 100% path coverage finds each omission

questions.explanation: If the software does not implement one or more requirements, white-box testing may not detect the resulting defects of omission: tests derived from the structure cannot cover code that does not exist. Black-box tests derived from the requirement would reveal the gap. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.3.3 (p. 43); FL-4.3.3 (K2).

questions.prompt: A team performs only black-box testing and reports that all planned test cases passed. A reviewer asks how much of the code these tests exercised. What does the syllabus say about this situation?

options.text: Code coverage can be measured only in safety-critical projects, where the necessary white-box tools are permitted
Black-box testing measures code coverage through its coverage items, so the reviewer can read it from the test report
Code coverage is irrelevant once the black-box tests have passed, because passing tests show the code is exercised
Black-box testing alone gives no measure of actual code coverage; white-box coverage measures provide it objectively

questions.explanation: Performing only black-box testing does not provide a measure of actual code coverage. White-box coverage measures give an objective measurement and the information needed to generate additional tests that increase coverage and, with it, confidence in the code. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.3.3 (p. 43); FL-4.3.3 (K2).

questions.prompt: A tester knows that the developers of a date library have often confused the 12-hour and 24-hour formats, and that similar libraries failed on 29 February. She designs tests for exactly these situations. Which test technique is she using?

options.text: Statement testing
Error guessing
Checklist-based testing
Boundary value analysis

questions.explanation: Error guessing anticipates errors, defects and failures based on the tester's knowledge, including how the application worked in the past, the errors developers tend to make and the failures that occurred in similar applications. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.4.1 (p. 43); FL-4.4.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: Before testing a file-upload feature, a tester takes a catalogue of typical upload problems, such as oversized files, wrong extensions and interrupted transfers, and designs one test to provoke each of them. How is error guessing being applied here?

options.text: As branch testing, driven by the decision outcomes found in the code
As a fault attack, driven by a list of possible defects and failures
As state transition testing, driven by a model of the valid transitions
As session-based testing, driven by a charter inside a fixed time box

questions.explanation: Fault attacks are a methodical way to implement error guessing. The tester creates or acquires a list of possible errors, defects and failures, and designs tests that will identify the associated defects, expose them or cause the failures. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.4.1 (p. 43); FL-4.4.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: Error guessing looks for typical problems in several areas. Match each anticipated problem to its area. One area is left over.

options.text: Test planning
Output
Logic
Input
Interfaces

slots.text: A correct value typed by the user is rejected
A report shows the date in the wrong format
A condition uses the wrong comparison operator
Two modules disagree about the type of a parameter

questions.explanation: The syllabus relates errors, defects and failures to input, output, logic, computation, interfaces and data. A rejected correct value is an input problem, a wrong format an output problem, a wrong operator a logic problem and a parameter mismatch an interface problem. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.4.1 (p. 43); FL-4.4.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: A team receives a new reporting tool with almost no specification and has two days before the demo. Which technique is MOST suitable, and why?

options.text: Decision table testing, because it systematically derives each combination of conditions from the specification
Exploratory testing, because it is useful when specifications are inadequate and time pressure is significant
Branch testing, because 100% branch coverage can be reached without a specification or the source code
Inspection, because the most formal review type finds the maximum number of anomalies within two days

questions.explanation: Exploratory testing is useful when there are few or inadequate specifications or when there is significant time pressure. Tests are designed, executed and evaluated simultaneously while the tester learns about the test object. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.4.2 (p. 44); FL-4.4.2 (K2).

questions.prompt: A tester performs exploratory testing in a 90-minute time box, guided by a document that states the test objectives. Afterwards she discusses the results with the product owner. Which terms describe the document and the discussion?

options.text: A test procedure and an inspection
A checklist and a walkthrough
A test charter and a debriefing
A test plan and a retrospective

questions.explanation: In session-based testing, exploratory testing is performed within a defined time box. The tester uses a test charter containing test objectives to guide the testing, and the session is usually followed by a debriefing with interested stakeholders. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.4.2 (p. 44); FL-4.4.2 (K2).

questions.prompt: Which TWO statements about exploratory testing are correct? Select TWO options.

options.text: It can incorporate other test techniques, such as equivalence partitioning
It is suitable only when a complete specification exists
It requires detailed test cases to be written before the session
It is more effective when the tester is experienced and has domain knowledge
It cannot be combined with more formal test techniques

questions.explanation: Exploratory testing can incorporate other test techniques and complements more formal techniques. It is more effective if the tester is experienced, has domain knowledge and strong essential skills such as analytical skills, curiosity and creativeness. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.4.2 (p. 44); FL-4.4.2 (K2).

questions.prompt: A team maintains a checklist for testing web forms. Which item should be removed from the checklist?

options.text: "Does each mandatory field show an error message when left empty?"
"Is the entered data kept when the user returns from the preview page?"
"Is the application of good quality?"
"Can the form be completed using the keyboard alone?"

questions.explanation: Checklists should not contain items that are too general, items that can be checked automatically, or items better suited as entry or exit criteria. It should be possible to check each item separately and directly, which a general question about quality does not allow. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.4.3 (p. 44); FL-4.4.3 (K2).

questions.prompt: A checklist for code changes has been used unchanged for three years. Developers have learned to avoid most of the errors it lists, while two new kinds of high-severity defect have appeared. What should the team do?

options.text: Update the checklist based on defect analysis, while keeping it from growing too long
Add each defect ever found to the checklist, so that nothing is missed again
Keep the checklist as it is, because a stable checklist makes testing repeatable
Replace the checklist by detailed test cases, because checklists wear out fully

questions.explanation: Some checklist entries become less effective over time as developers learn to avoid the same errors, and new entries may be needed for newly found high-severity defects. Checklists should be regularly updated based on defect analysis, without becoming too long. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.4.3 (p. 44); FL-4.4.3 (K2).

questions.prompt: Two testers use the same high-level checklist to test a registration page and end up running rather different tests. What is the consequence of using a high-level checklist?

options.text: Identical results, since the items are fixed
No coverage, since no test cases exist
Greater repeatability, but less coverage
Potentially greater coverage, but less repeatability

questions.explanation: In the absence of detailed test cases, checklist-based testing provides guidelines and some consistency. If the checklists are high-level, some variability in the actual testing is likely, resulting in potentially greater coverage but less repeatability. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.4.3 (p. 44); FL-4.4.3 (K2).

questions.prompt: Match each of the "3 C's" of a user story to its meaning. One meaning is left over.

options.text: The acceptance criteria
The medium that describes the user story, such as an entry on an electronic board
The explanation of how the software will be used, documented or verbal
The code that implements the user story

questions.explanation: The card is the medium describing the story, the conversation explains how the software will be used, and the confirmation consists of the acceptance criteria. Together they are called the 3 C's. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.5.1 (p. 45); FL-4.5.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: A product owner, a developer and a tester write a user story together using a mind map. What does this collaboration achieve?

options.text: A complete set of automated tests, so that no acceptance criteria are needed for the story
A transfer of testing tasks to the developer, who then delivers the story without tests
A fixed scope that cannot be negotiated later, since all three roles have signed the story
A shared vision of what should be delivered, from the business, development and testing perspectives

questions.explanation: Collaborative authorship, using techniques such as brainstorming and mind mapping, allows the team to obtain a shared vision of what should be delivered by taking into account three perspectives: business, development and testing. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.5.1 (p. 45); FL-4.5.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: During refinement a stakeholder says: "I have no idea how I would test this user story." According to INVEST, what might this indicate?

options.text: The story is not clear enough, or it does not reflect something valuable to the stakeholder
The story is finished, and the stakeholder can accept it without change
The story is independent, and so it needs no acceptance criteria to be written
The story is too small, and it should be merged with several others in the backlog

questions.explanation: Good user stories are Independent, Negotiable, Valuable, Estimable, Small and Testable. If a stakeholder does not know how to test a story, it may not be clear enough, may not reflect something valuable to them, or the stakeholder may simply need help with testing. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.5.1 (p. 45); FL-4.5.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: A team writes this acceptance criterion: "Given a basket worth £60, when the customer chooses standard delivery, then delivery is free." Which format is this?

options.text: Structure-oriented
Scenario-oriented
Risk-oriented
Rule-oriented

questions.explanation: The two most common formats are scenario-oriented, such as the Given/When/Then format used in BDD, and rule-oriented, such as a bullet-point verification list or a table mapping inputs to outputs. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.5.2 (p. 45); FL-4.5.2 (K2).

questions.prompt: A team writes acceptance criteria as a table that maps basket values to delivery charges. A new colleague says criteria must be in Given/When/Then form. Which reply is correct?

options.text: A rule-oriented table is a common format; any format works if the criteria are well-defined and unambiguous
The colleague is right, because the scenario-oriented format is the single one that the syllabus permits
Neither format is needed, because acceptance criteria are replaced by the conversation about the story
The table is acceptable for non-functional criteria, but functional criteria need the scenario form

questions.explanation: Rule-oriented criteria, such as a bullet-point verification list or a tabulated input-output mapping, are one of the two most common formats. A team may also use a custom format, as long as the acceptance criteria are well-defined and unambiguous. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.5.2 (p. 45); FL-4.5.2 (K2).

questions.prompt: What are acceptance criteria used for? Select TWO options.

options.text: To record who implemented the user story
To describe positive scenarios and leave out negative ones
To postpone acceptance of the user story until release
To serve as a basis for the acceptance testing of the user story
To define the scope of the user story

questions.explanation: Acceptance criteria define the scope of the user story, help to reach consensus among stakeholders, describe both positive and negative scenarios, serve as a basis for acceptance testing, and allow accurate planning and estimation. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 4.5.2 (p. 45); FL-4.5.2 (K2).

questions.prompt: A new tester asks why the team spends time on writing a test plan for a three-month project. Which answer gives a purpose of a test plan?

options.text: It replaces the test strategy of the organisation, so that the project can choose its own test policy
It lists the detailed steps of each test case, so that test execution needs no further preparation at all
It documents the means and schedule for achieving the test objectives and serves as a means of communication
It records the defects that are found during test execution, together with their severity and priority

questions.explanation: A test plan documents the means and schedule for achieving test objectives, helps to ensure that test activities meet the established criteria, serves as a means of communication, and shows that testing adheres to the test policy and test strategy or explains deviations. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.1.1 (p. 48); FL-5.1.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: A test plan for a logistics system names the test levels and test types, the test techniques, the entry and exit criteria, the degree of independence and the metrics to be collected. Under which typical part of a test plan do these items belong?

options.text: Test approach
Assumptions and constraints
Budget and schedule
Risk register

questions.explanation: The test approach covers test levels, test types, test techniques, test deliverables, entry and exit criteria, independence of testing, metrics, test data and environment requirements, and deviations from the test policy and strategy. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.1.1 (p. 48); FL-5.1.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: Which TWO items are typical content of a test plan? Select TWO options.

options.text: The source code of the automated test scripts
The stakeholders, with their roles and responsibilities
The lessons learned after the release
The forms and frequency of communication
The log of each executed test run

questions.explanation: Typical content includes the context of testing, assumptions and constraints, stakeholders, communication, the risk register, the test approach, and budget and schedule. Scripts, test logs and lessons learned are other testware, created later in the test process. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.1.1 (p. 48); FL-5.1.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: How does a tester add value during iteration planning?

options.text: By determining the testability of user stories and estimating the effort for the testing tasks
By defining and re-defining the product backlog for the releases of the coming year
By writing the test completion report for the iteration that is about to be planned
By approving the budget of the iteration and assigning developers to the user stories

questions.explanation: In iteration planning, testers take part in the detailed risk analysis of user stories, determine their testability, break stories down into tasks, estimate the test effort for testing tasks, and identify and refine functional and non-functional aspects of the test object. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.1.2 (p. 48); FL-5.1.2 (K1).

questions.prompt: Match each contribution of a tester to the kind of planning in which it is made. One kind of planning is left over.

options.text: Retirement planning
Iteration planning
Release planning

slots.text: Taking part in writing testable user stories and acceptance criteria for the product backlog
Breaking the user stories selected for the next two weeks into testing tasks

questions.explanation: Release planning looks ahead to the release, defines the product backlog and is the basis for the test approach across iterations; testers help to write testable stories there. Iteration planning concerns a single iteration backlog, where testers break stories into tasks. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.1.2 (p. 48); FL-5.1.2 (K1).

questions.prompt: A team agrees that system testing of a build may start only if the test environment is available and all smoke tests have passed, and that it ends when 95% of requirements are covered and no critical defect is open. Which statement classifies these conditions correctly?

options.text: The environment and the smoke tests are entry criteria; the coverage and the open defects are exit criteria
The environment and the coverage are entry criteria; the smoke tests and the open defects are exit criteria
All four conditions are entry criteria, because they are agreed before the test level has been started
All four conditions are exit criteria, because they are checked by the test manager during the test level

questions.explanation: Entry criteria define the preconditions for an activity, such as availability of resources and the initial quality level of the test object. Exit criteria define what must be achieved to declare the activity completed, such as coverage levels and the number of unresolved defects. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.1.3 (p. 49); FL-5.1.3 (K2).

questions.prompt: The budget for testing a campaign website is used up before the planned coverage is reached. Under which condition is it acceptable to end testing?

options.text: The testers have accepted among themselves that the remaining testing is unimportant
The test plan is rewritten afterwards so that the reached coverage matches the target
The developers have promised to correct any defect that the users report afterwards
The stakeholders have reviewed and accepted the risk of going live without further testing

questions.explanation: Running out of time or budget can be viewed as a valid exit criterion. Even without other exit criteria being satisfied, it can be acceptable to end testing if the stakeholders have reviewed and accepted the risk to go live without further testing. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.1.3 (p. 49); FL-5.1.3 (K2).

questions.prompt: In Agile software development, entry and exit criteria often have other names. Match each statement to the correct term. One term is left over.

options.text: Definition of Ready
Definition of Scope
Definition of Done

slots.text: The criteria a user story must fulfil before development and testing of it can start
The team's objective metrics for a releasable item

questions.explanation: Entry criteria that a user story must fulfil to start development or testing activities are called the Definition of Ready. Exit criteria are often called the Definition of Done, which defines the team's objective metrics for a releasable item. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.1.3 (p. 49); FL-5.1.3 (K2).

questions.prompt: Which statement about the layers of the test pyramid is correct?

options.text: Tests in the top layer are the fastest, so most of the tests should be placed there
Tests in the bottom layer are small, isolated and fast, so many of them are needed
Tests in the bottom layer are slow end-to-end tests, so few of them are needed
Tests in each layer have the same granularity, so the layers hold equal numbers

questions.explanation: The test pyramid shows that tests have different granularity. Bottom-layer tests are small, isolated, fast and check a small piece of functionality, so many are needed. Top-layer tests are complex, high-level, end-to-end tests that are slower, so only a few are needed. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.1.6 (p. 50); FL-5.1.6 (K1).

questions.prompt: What does the test pyramid model support a team in?

options.text: The choice between scenario-oriented and rule-oriented criteria
Test automation and the allocation of test effort across groups of tests
The assignment of severity and priority to the defect reports
The calculation of the risk level from likelihood and impact

questions.explanation: The test pyramid supports the team in test automation and in test effort allocation by showing that different test objectives are supported by different levels of test automation. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.1.6 (p. 50); FL-5.1.6 (K1).

questions.prompt: The original test pyramid model defines three layers. Put them in order from the bottom of the pyramid to the top.

options.text: UI tests
Unit tests
Service tests

questions.explanation: The original model defines unit tests at the bottom, service tests in the middle and UI tests at the top. The higher the layer, the lower the granularity and isolation and the longer the execution time. Other models name the layers differently. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.1.6 (p. 50); FL-5.1.6 (K1).

questions.prompt: Match each testing quadrant to the tests it contains. One group of tests is left over.

options.text: Reviews of the test plan by the steering group
Component tests and component integration tests
Exploratory testing, usability testing and user acceptance testing
Functional tests, examples and user story tests
Smoke tests and non-functional tests other than usability tests

slots.text: Q1: technology facing, supports the team
Q2: business facing, supports the team
Q3: business facing, critiques the product
Q4: technology facing, critiques the product

questions.explanation: Q1 holds component and component integration tests, Q2 functional tests, examples and user story tests, Q3 exploratory, usability and user acceptance testing, and Q4 smoke tests and non-functional tests except usability tests. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.1.7 (p. 51); FL-5.1.7 (K2).

questions.prompt: A team runs sessions in which real users try a new checkout while a tester observes where they hesitate. In which testing quadrant does this activity belong, and how is it typically performed?

options.text: Q1, technology facing and supporting the team; these tests are automated and part of CI
Q4, technology facing and critiquing the product; these tests are often automated
Q3, business facing and critiquing the product; these tests are user-oriented and often manual
Q2, business facing and supporting the team; these tests check the acceptance criteria

questions.explanation: Usability testing belongs to quadrant Q3, together with exploratory testing and user acceptance testing. Q3 tests are business facing, critique the product, are user-oriented and are often manual. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.1.7 (p. 51); FL-5.1.7 (K2).

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of the testing quadrants model for test management?

options.text: To calculate how many test cases each of the test levels must contain before a release
To visualise test levels and test types so that all appropriate ones are included in the lifecycle
To assign each tester to exactly one quadrant for the duration of the whole project
To replace the test levels by four phases that are carried out one after the other

questions.explanation: The testing quadrants group the test levels with the appropriate test types, activities, techniques and work products in Agile development. The model helps test management to ensure that all appropriate test types and levels are included, and to describe the test types to stakeholders. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.1.7 (p. 51); FL-5.1.7 (K2).

questions.prompt: Which two factors characterise a risk and together express its risk level?

options.text: Risk identification and risk mitigation
Risk acceptance and risk transfer
Risk severity and risk priority
Risk likelihood and risk impact

questions.explanation: A risk is characterised by its likelihood, the probability of occurrence, and its impact, the consequences of the occurrence. Together these two factors express the risk level, a measure for the risk. The higher the level, the more important its treatment. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.2.1 (p. 52); FL-5.2.1 (K1).

questions.prompt: A team rates each product risk on a scale from 1 to 5 for likelihood and from 1 to 5 for impact, and calculates the risk level by multiplying the two. A risk of wrong tax totals has likelihood 3 and impact 5. What is its risk level? Enter a whole number only.
questions.explanation: In the quantitative approach, the risk level is calculated as the multiplication of risk likelihood and risk impact: 3 × 5 = 15. Adding the two values would give 8, which is a different, non-standard scale. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.2.1 (p. 52); FL-5.2.1 (K1).

questions.prompt: A project to build a pharmacy app has these risks: (1) the supplier of the barcode library may go bankrupt; (2) the dosage calculation may be wrong for children; (3) two testers may leave the team; (4) pages may load too slowly on old phones. Which of them are product risks?

options.text: Risks 2 and 4
Risks 1 and 2
Risks 1 and 3
Risks 3 and 4

questions.explanation: Product risks relate to product quality characteristics, such as incorrect calculations and inadequate response time. Supplier issues and people issues, such as bankruptcy of a supplier or a shortage of staff, are project risks that affect schedule, budget or scope. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.2.2 (p. 52); FL-5.2.2 (K2).

questions.prompt: The estimate for the test effort of a migration turns out to be far too low, and the release date is in danger. What type of risk has occurred, and what does it affect?

options.text: A project risk, which affects the schedule, budget or scope of the project
A product risk, which affects the satisfaction and the trust of the end users
A project risk, which affects the functional correctness of the test object
A product risk, which affects the quality characteristics of the test object

questions.explanation: Inaccurate estimates are an organisational issue and therefore a project risk. Project risks relate to the management and control of the project and, when they occur, may have an impact on the project schedule, budget or scope. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.2.2 (p. 52); FL-5.2.2 (K2).

questions.prompt: Which TWO are possible negative consequences when a product risk occurs? Select TWO options.

options.text: Scope creep during the project
Loss of revenue, trust or reputation
Conflicts between the team members
High maintenance costs and an overloaded help desk
Delays in the delivery of work products

questions.explanation: When product risks occur, consequences include user dissatisfaction, loss of revenue, trust or reputation, damage to third parties, high maintenance costs and an overloaded help desk, criminal penalties and, in extreme cases, physical harm. The other options are project risks. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.2.2 (p. 52); FL-5.2.2 (K2).

questions.prompt: A product risk analysis for a banking app rates "wrong transfer amount" as a very high risk and "unattractive colours in the settings page" as a low risk. How should this influence the testing?

options.text: Transfers are left to the developers, since very high risks cannot be reduced by testing
The settings page is tested first, since low risks are quick to remove from the list
Transfers are tested more thoroughly and earlier, with stronger test techniques and higher coverage
Both areas receive the same test effort, so that the test coverage is evenly balanced

questions.explanation: The results of product risk analysis are used to determine the test scope, test levels and types, the test techniques and coverage, to estimate effort and to prioritise testing in an attempt to find critical defects as early as possible. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.2.3 (p. 52); FL-5.2.3 (K2).

questions.prompt: Product risk analysis consists of two activities. Match each task to the activity it belongs to. One activity is left over.

options.text: Risk identification
Risk monitoring
Risk assessment

slots.text: Generating a comprehensive list of risks in a brainstorming workshop
Determining likelihood, impact and level of each risk and prioritising the risks

questions.explanation: Risk identification generates a comprehensive list of risks, for example through brainstorming, workshops or interviews. Risk assessment categorises the risks, determines their likelihood, impact and level, prioritises them and proposes ways to handle them. Risk monitoring is part of risk control. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.2.3 (p. 52); FL-5.2.3 (K2).

questions.prompt: What is the goal of product risk analysis from a testing perspective?

options.text: To provide the project manager with a list of the staff who caused the risks
To provide awareness of product risk so that test effort is focused to minimise residual risk
To provide evidence that each identified product risk has been fully removed
To provide a reason to postpone testing until each risk has been accepted

questions.explanation: From a testing perspective, the goal of product risk analysis is to provide an awareness of product risk in order to focus the test effort in a way that minimises the residual level of product risk. Ideally it begins early in the lifecycle. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.2.3 (p. 52); FL-5.2.3 (K2).

questions.prompt: A product risk analysis shows a high risk that a flight-booking engine calculates fares wrongly. Which response is an example of risk mitigation by testing?

options.text: Assigning testers experienced in fare rules and applying decision table testing with high coverage
Buying an insurance policy that covers the financial loss caused by wrong fares
Preparing a manual fare desk that takes over if the engine fails in production
Informing the stakeholders and deciding to live with the risk without more testing

questions.explanation: Risks can be mitigated by testing, for example by selecting testers with the right experience and skills and applying appropriate test techniques and coverage levels. Insurance is risk transfer, living with the risk is risk acceptance, and a fallback procedure is a contingency plan. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.2.4 (p. 53); FL-5.2.4 (K2).

questions.prompt: After mitigation actions for a security risk have been carried out, a team keeps checking whether the actions work and whether new risks are appearing. What is this activity called?

options.text: Risk identification
Risk assessment
Risk monitoring
Risk transfer

questions.explanation: Product risk control consists of risk mitigation and risk monitoring. The aim of risk monitoring is to ensure that the mitigation actions are effective, to obtain further information to improve risk assessment, and to identify emerging risks. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.2.4 (p. 53); FL-5.2.4 (K2).

questions.prompt: Match each metric to its category of test metrics. One category is left over.

options.text: Coverage metrics
Test progress metrics
Product quality metrics
Defect metrics
Cost metrics

slots.text: Number of test cases run and passed

questions.explanation: Test cases run, passed and failed are test progress metrics. Defect density and numbers of defects found and fixed are defect metrics. Availability, response time and mean time to failure are product quality metrics, and requirements or code coverage are coverage metrics. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.3.1 (p. 54); FL-5.3.1 (K1).

questions.prompt: Why are test metrics gathered during test monitoring?

options.text: To show that the test object contains no further defects once the planned test cases are passed
To show progress against the plan, the quality of the test object and the effectiveness of the test activities
To replace the test completion report with numbers that need no further explanation to anyone
To rank the testers by the number of defect reports each of them has written during the project

questions.explanation: Test metrics are gathered to show progress against the planned schedule and budget, the current quality of the test object, and the effectiveness of the test activities with respect to the test objectives or an iteration goal. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.3.1 (p. 54); FL-5.3.1 (K1).

questions.prompt: A test manager writes a report every Friday that states the testing period, whether testing is ahead of or behind schedule, the impediments, the current metrics, new risks and the testing planned for next week. Which report is this, and what is it for?

options.text: A defect report, which gives the information to resolve a defect
A test progress report, which supports the ongoing test control
A test completion report, which summarises a finished test level
A test plan, which documents the means of achieving test objectives

questions.explanation: Test progress reports are generated regularly and include the testing period, progress and deviations, impediments, metrics, new and changed risks, and testing planned for the next period. They support ongoing test control by enabling changes to schedule, resources or plan. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.3.2 (p. 54); FL-5.3.2 (K2).

questions.prompt: Which TWO items are typically found in a test completion report but NOT in a test progress report? Select TWO options.

options.text: Lessons learned that are relevant to the testing
The impediments for testing and their workarounds
The testing planned for the next period
An evaluation of testing and product quality against the original test plan
The test metrics

questions.explanation: A test completion report contains a test summary, an evaluation against the original test plan, deviations, impediments, metrics, unmitigated risks and unfixed defects, and lessons learned. Testing planned for the next period belongs to a progress report, and impediments and metrics appear in both. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.3.2 (p. 54); FL-5.3.2 (K2).

questions.prompt: How do the reports for the team and for a steering committee at the end of a project typically differ?

options.text: Both kinds of reporting have the same content and formality, because the audience does not influence how tests are reported
Progress reporting within the team follows a fixed template, while completion reporting is given verbally at each daily meeting
Progress reporting within the team is frequent and informal, while completion reporting follows a set template and occurs once
Completion reporting is written daily for the testers, while progress reporting is written once for the steering committee

questions.explanation: Different audiences require different information and influence the formality and frequency of reporting. Test progress reporting to others in the same team is often frequent and informal, while test completion reporting follows a set template and occurs only once. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.3.2 (p. 54); FL-5.3.2 (K2).

questions.prompt: A test team is spread over three time zones, and the members rarely meet face to face. Which way of communicating test status is MOST appropriate, according to the syllabus?

options.text: No regular communication, since each site tests on its own
A single meeting at the end of the project for all three sites
Verbal updates in the corridor, such as short talks after lunch
More formal communication, such as written reports and shared dashboards

questions.explanation: More formal communication may be more appropriate for distributed teams, where direct face-to-face communication is not always possible because of geographical distance or time differences. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.3.3 (p. 55); FL-5.3.3 (K2).

questions.prompt: A tester must report the same test status to the developers in her team and to the finance director who pays for the project. What should she do?

options.text: Tailor the communication, because different stakeholders are interested in different types of information
Report to the developers only, because test status is too technical for management
Send both the same detailed test log, because equal treatment avoids misunderstandings
Wait for the test completion report, because status is communicated once at the end

questions.explanation: Typically, different stakeholders are interested in different types of information, so communication should be tailored accordingly. Developers may need details of failures, while a finance director needs progress, risks and cost in summary. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.3.3 (p. 55); FL-5.3.3 (K2).

questions.prompt: Which TWO are options for communicating the status of testing? Select TWO options.

options.text: Decision tables in which several rules have been merged
Dashboards, such as task boards and burn-down charts
Verbal exchanges with team members and other stakeholders
Stubs and drivers that are part of the test environment
Equivalence partitions of the input data of a test object

questions.explanation: The options include verbal communication, dashboards such as CI/CD dashboards, task boards and burn-down charts, electronic channels such as email and chat, online documentation and formal test reports. One or more can be used. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.3.3 (p. 55); FL-5.3.3 (K2).

questions.prompt: A failure that was seen in last month's release cannot be reproduced on the current build. How does configuration management help the tester?

options.text: It guarantees that the failure was caused by the test environment and not the code
It is possible to revert to the previous baseline and repeat the earlier tests on it
It rewrites the test cases automatically so that they pass on the current build
It removes the need for defect reports, because each change is already recorded

questions.explanation: Configuration management keeps a record of changed configuration items when a new baseline is created. It is possible to revert to a previous baseline to reproduce previous test results. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.4 (p. 56); FL-5.4.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: A test environment has been approved for testing and recorded as a baseline. A developer wants to upgrade its database version to try something out. What does configuration management require?

options.text: The change is forbidden until the project has been completed
The change is made by the tester who uses the environment most
The change goes through a formal change control process
The change is made at once and noted in the next test report

questions.explanation: For a complex configuration item such as a test environment, CM records its parts, their relationships and versions. Once approved for testing, the item becomes a baseline and can only be changed through a formal change control process. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.4 (p. 56); FL-5.4.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: What does configuration management ensure in order to support testing? Select TWO options.

options.text: Documentation and software items are referenced unambiguously in testware
Test effort for each baseline is estimated with three-point estimation
Test cases are prioritised by the risk level of each configuration item
Configuration items, including test items, are uniquely identified and version controlled
Defects are fixed in the order of their severity after each change

questions.explanation: CM ensures that all configuration items, including test items, are uniquely identified, version controlled, tracked for changes and related to each other so that traceability is maintained, and that all identified documentation and software items are referenced unambiguously in testware. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 5.4 (p. 56); FL-5.4.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: Match each kind of test tool to what it does. One description is left over.

options.text: Facilitate automated test execution and coverage measurement
Support the tester in performing reviews and static analysis
Facilitate communication
Decide which defects are fixed before the release
Facilitate management of requirements, tests, defects and configuration

slots.text: Test execution and test coverage tools

questions.explanation: Test management tools increase process efficiency by managing requirements, tests, defects and configuration. Static testing tools support reviews and static analysis, test execution and coverage tools automate execution and measure coverage, and collaboration tools facilitate communication. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 6.1 (p. 59); FL-6.1.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: A team needs to check how a web shop behaves when 20,000 users order at the same time. Which category of test tool is needed?

options.text: Test management tools
