Collaboration tools
Non-functional testing tools
Static testing tools

questions.explanation: Non-functional testing tools allow the tester to perform non-functional testing that is difficult or impossible to perform manually, such as generating the load of thousands of simultaneous users. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 6.1 (p. 59); FL-6.1.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: A tester keeps the test data for a pricing engine in a spreadsheet and uses formulas to calculate the expected results. Is the spreadsheet a test tool?

options.text: Yes, because any tool that assists in testing is a test tool in that context
Yes, but only while it is stored inside the test management system
No, because test tools must execute the test cases without human action
No, because test tools have to be bought from a specialised testing vendor

questions.explanation: The syllabus lists, besides the named categories, any other tool that assists in testing, and gives the example that a spreadsheet is a test tool in the context of testing. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 6.1 (p. 59); FL-6.1.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: A team wants every code change to be built automatically, tested and tracked through its workflow up to deployment. Which category of tool supports this?

options.text: Test design tools
DevOps tools
Non-functional testing tools
Static testing tools

questions.explanation: DevOps tools support the DevOps delivery pipeline, workflow tracking, automated build processes and continuous integration and delivery. Test design and implementation tools, by contrast, facilitate the generation of test cases, test data and test procedures. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 6.1 (p. 59); FL-6.1.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: A company automates its regression tests. Which outcome is a potential benefit of the test automation?

options.text: More time for testers to design new, deeper and more effective tests
No further cost for maintaining the automated tests
Independence from the vendor of the automation tool
No further need for testers to think critically about results

questions.explanation: Benefits include time saved on repetitive manual work, greater consistency, more objective assessment, easier access to information, reduced execution times and more time for testers to design new, deeper and more effective tests. The other options contradict known risks. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 6.2 (p. 59); FL-6.2.1 (K1).

questions.prompt: A manager buys a test automation tool after a sales demonstration and announces that manual testing will end next month. No effort was planned for training or for maintaining scripts. Which risk of test automation does this illustrate BEST?

options.text: Incompatibility of the tool with the development platform
Non-compliance of the tool with safety standards
Unrealistic expectations about the benefits of the tool
Abandonment of an open-source tool by its community

questions.explanation: Simply acquiring a tool does not guarantee success: each new tool requires effort for introduction, maintenance and training. Unrealistic expectations about the benefits of a tool, and inaccurate estimates of the time, cost and effort needed, are typical risks. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 6.2 (p. 59); FL-6.2.1 (K1).

questions.prompt: Which TWO are potential risks of using test automation? Select TWO options.

options.text: Easier access to statistics and graphs about the test progress
Greater consistency and repeatability of the tests that are executed
Dependency on a tool vendor that may go out of business or give poor support
Using a test tool when manual testing would be more appropriate
Earlier defect detection through shorter test execution times

questions.explanation: Risks include unrealistic expectations, inaccurate estimates, using a tool where manual testing is more appropriate, relying on a tool too much, vendor dependency, abandoned open-source software, platform incompatibility and unsuitable tools. The other options are benefits. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 6.2 (p. 59); FL-6.2.1 (K1).

questions.prompt: An automated suite reports "all 600 tests passed" every night. Nobody reads the results in detail, and a serious usability problem reaches the customers. Which risk of test automation occurred?

options.text: Using a tool that is incompatible with the platform used for development
Estimating the cost of introducing the tool inaccurately at the project start
Relying on the tool too much and ignoring the need for human critical thinking
Choosing an open-source tool whose components need very frequent updates

questions.explanation: Relying on a tool too much, for example by ignoring the need for human critical thinking, is a risk of test automation. Passing automated checks do not replace human evaluation, especially for characteristics such as usability. Syllabus reference: CTFL v4.0.1, section 6.2 (p. 59); FL-6.2.1 (K1).

notes.back: The degree, as a percentage, to which the specified items have been exercised by a test suite.
Finding, analysing and removing the causes of failures. A separate activity from testing.
An imperfection in a work product, where it does not meet its requirements. Also called fault or bug.
A human action that produces an incorrect result. Also called mistake.
An event in which a component or system does not do what it should, or does what it should not.
A fundamental reason for a problem, for example the situation that led to an error.
The degree to which a work product satisfies the stated and implied needs of its stakeholders.
A process-oriented, preventive approach: follow and improve good processes so that they yield good products.
A set of activities to discover defects and evaluate the quality of work products.
The work product being tested.
The reason or purpose of testing, such as finding defects or building confidence.
Checking whether the system meets the needs of users and other stakeholders in its operational environment.
Checking whether the system meets its specified requirements.
The set of related test activities: planning, monitoring and control, analysis, design, implementation, execution and completion.
Defining the test objectives and choosing the approach that best achieves them within the constraints.
Ongoing checking of all test activities and comparison of actual progress against the plan.
Taking the actions needed to meet the test objectives, based on monitoring information.
Analysing the test basis to identify testable features and define test conditions. Answers "what to test?"
Elaborating test conditions into test cases and other testware. Answers "how to test?"
Creating or acquiring the testware needed for execution: procedures, scripts, suites, data and environment.
Running tests according to the schedule, comparing actual with expected results and logging the outcome.
Activities at a milestone: archive testware, shut down the environment, capture lessons learned, write the completion report.
The body of knowledge used as the basis for test analysis and design, such as requirements or user stories.
A testable aspect of a component or system, identified as a basis for testing.
A set of preconditions, inputs, actions, expected results and postconditions, developed from test conditions.
A sequence of test cases in execution order, with any actions needed to set up and wrap up.
Data needed for test execution.
The consequence or outcome of executing a test.
Work products produced during the test process for use in planning, designing, executing, evaluating and reporting on testing.
The ability to establish explicit relationships between work products, such as requirements, test cases, results and defects.
A group of test activities organised and managed together, performed at a given stage of development.
A group of test activities related to specific quality characteristics; most can be performed at every test level.
A test level that focuses on components in isolation. Also called unit testing.
A test level that focuses on interfaces and interactions between components.
Testing that focuses on interactions between components or systems.
A test level that focuses on the overall behaviour and capabilities of an entire system or product.
A test level that focuses on interfaces between the system under test and other systems or external services.
A test level that focuses on validation and on demonstrating readiness for deployment.
Testing that evaluates the functions a component or system should perform: "what" it does.
Testing that evaluates attributes other than functional ones: "how well" the system behaves.
Specification-based testing that derives tests from documentation, without reference to internal structure.
Structure-based testing that derives tests from the implementation or internal structure.
Testing that confirms an original defect has been successfully fixed.
Testing that confirms a change has caused no adverse consequences.
Testing the changes to an operational system, and checking for regressions in its unchanged parts.
An approach in which testing is performed earlier in the lifecycle.
Testing in which the work product is examined without executing the software.
Testing that involves executing the software.
Evaluating a work product with a tool, without executing it.
A type of static testing in which people evaluate a work product to detect anomalies or improve it.
A condition that deviates from expectation. It is not necessarily a defect.
A review that follows no defined process and needs no formal documented output.
A review that follows a defined process and produces formally documented output.
A review led by the author, with objectives such as educating reviewers and gaining consensus.
A review by technically qualified reviewers, led by a moderator, to gain consensus and decide on a technical problem.
The most formal review type: follows the complete process, aims to find the maximum number of anomalies, collects metrics.
A procedure used to define test conditions, identify coverage items and derive test cases.
A technique based on analysing the specified behaviour of the test object, without reference to its internal structure.
A technique based on analysing the internal structure and processing of the test object.
A technique that uses the knowledge and experience of testers to design and implement test cases.
An attribute or combination of attributes derived from test conditions with a test technique, such as a partition or a branch.
A black-box technique that divides data into partitions whose members are expected to be processed in the same way.
A black-box technique based on exercising the boundaries of ordered equivalence partitions.
A black-box technique for requirements in which combinations of conditions result in different outcomes.
A black-box technique that derives test cases from a model of states and the transitions between them.
Executable statements exercised by the tests, divided by all executable statements, as a percentage.
Branches exercised by the tests, divided by all branches, as a percentage.
An experience-based technique that anticipates errors, defects and failures from the tester's knowledge.
An experience-based technique in which tests are designed, executed and evaluated at the same time while the tester learns.
An experience-based technique in which tests are designed and executed to cover the conditions of a checklist.
An approach that focuses on avoiding defects through collaboration and communication.
The conditions an implementation of a user story must meet to be accepted by stakeholders.
A test-first approach in which a team derives test cases from acceptance criteria before the story is implemented.
A document describing the test objectives, resources and processes for a test project.
The way testing will be done for a project: levels, types, techniques, criteria, independence and so on.
A description of how testing is performed in general, in line with the test policy of the organisation.
The preconditions for undertaking a given activity.
What must be achieved to declare an activity completed.
A model showing that different tests have different granularity, with many small fast tests below and few end-to-end tests on top.
A model grouping tests as business or technology facing, and as supporting the team or critiquing the product.
A potential event, hazard, threat or situation whose occurrence causes an adverse effect.
A measure of a risk, expressed by its likelihood and its impact.
A risk related to the management and control of the project, affecting schedule, budget or scope.
A risk related to the quality characteristics of the product.
Risk analysis together with risk control.
Risk identification followed by risk assessment.
Generating a comprehensive list of risks.
Categorising risks, determining likelihood, impact and level, prioritising, and proposing how to handle them.
Risk mitigation together with risk monitoring.
Carrying out the actions proposed in risk assessment to reduce the risk level.
Checking that mitigation is effective, improving the assessment and identifying emerging risks.
A test approach in which test activities are selected, prioritised and managed on the basis of risk analysis and control.
A regular report during testing that supports ongoing test control.
A report that summarises a finished test activity, such as a test level or an iteration.
The process of logging, analysing, classifying, responding to and closing reported anomalies.
Documentation of an anomaly, giving those who handle it enough information to resolve it.
The use of software to perform or support test activities.

notes.text: A typical test objective: providing {{c1::information to stakeholders::what, to whom}} so that they can make informed decisions.
A typical test objective: reducing the {{c1::risk level::what}} of inadequate software quality.
Debugging after a failure involves {{c1::reproduction}} of the failure, {{c2::diagnosis}} (finding the defect) and {{c3::fixing}} the defect.
When static testing finds a defect, debugging only removes it: there is no need for {{c1::reproduction or diagnosis}}.
Testing gives users {{c1::indirect representation::kind of presence}} on the development project.
Testing evaluates quality directly, which contributes to decisions such as the {{c1::release decision}}.
Testing is {{c1::product}}-oriented and corrective; quality assurance is {{c2::process}}-oriented and preventive.
A person makes an {{c1::error}}, which produces a {{c2::defect}}, which may result in a {{c3::failure}}.
Principle 1: testing shows the {{c1::presence}}, not the {{c2::absence}}, of defects.
Principle 2: {{c1::exhaustive}} testing is impossible.
Principle 3: {{c1::early}} testing saves time and money.
Principle 4: defects {{c1::cluster together}}. This illustrates the {{c2::Pareto}} principle.
Principle 5: tests {{c1::wear out}}. Repeated tests become less effective at finding new defects.
Principle 6: testing is {{c1::context dependent}}.
Principle 7: the {{c1::absence-of-defects}} fallacy. Verification alone does not ensure that users' needs are met.
Test analysis answers "{{c1::what to test}}?"; test design answers "{{c2::how to test}}?"

Contextual factors of the test process include stakeholders, team members, {{c1::business domain}}, technical factors, project constraints, organisational factors, the {{c2::software development lifecycle}} and tools.
Test planning work products: test plan, test schedule, {{c1::risk register}}, entry criteria and exit criteria.
Test design work products: test cases, {{c1::test charters}}, coverage items, test data requirements and test environment requirements.
Test implementation work products: test procedures, test scripts, {{c1::test suites}}, test data, the test execution schedule and test environment items.
Good traceability supports coverage evaluation, shows the {{c1::impact of changes}}, facilitates {{c2::audits}} and helps to meet IT governance criteria.
The {{c1::test management}} role focuses on planning, monitoring, control and completion; the {{c2::testing}} role on analysis, design, implementation and execution.
Testing knowledge increases the {{c1::effectiveness}} of testing; technical knowledge increases its {{c2::efficiency}}.
In the whole team approach, any team member with the necessary skills can perform any task, and {{c1::everyone}} is responsible for quality.
Levels of independence: the author (none), {{c1::peers from the same team}} (some), testers outside the team but inside the organisation (high), testers {{c2::outside the organisation}} (very high).
A drawback of independent testing: developers may lose a sense of {{c1::responsibility for quality}}.

The lifecycle affects the scope and timing of test activities, the level of detail of {{c1::test documentation}}, the choice of techniques, the extent of {{c2::test automation}} and the role of the tester.
Good practice in any lifecycle: for every development activity there is a corresponding {{c1::test activity}}.
Good practice in any lifecycle: testers review work products as soon as {{c1::drafts}} are available.
In TDD, {{c1::tests}} are written first, then the {{c2::code}} to satisfy them, and then both are {{c3::refactored}}.
BDD expresses desired behaviour in natural language, usually in the {{c1::Given/When/Then}} format.
A testing benefit of DevOps: {{c1::fast feedback}} on code quality and on whether changes adversely affect existing code.
A challenge of DevOps: test automation needs additional {{c1::resources}} and may be difficult to establish and maintain. Manual testing is {{c2::still needed}}.
A shift-left practice: performing {{c1::non-functional}} testing starting at the component test level, where possible.
Shift left may cost extra effort {{c1::earlier}} in the process but is expected to save effort and cost {{c2::later}}.
A retrospective asks: what was {{c1::successful}} and should be retained, what could be {{c2::improved}}, and how to make the improvements happen.
Retrospective results are recorded and are normally part of the {{c1::test completion report}}.
The five test levels: component, {{c1::component integration}}, system, {{c2::system integration}} and acceptance testing.
Forms of acceptance testing: user acceptance, {{c1::operational}} acceptance, contractual and regulatory acceptance, {{c2::alpha}} testing and beta testing.
Non-functional characteristics (ISO/IEC 25010): performance efficiency, compatibility, {{c1::usability}}, reliability, {{c2::security}}, maintainability, portability and safety.
Functional testing checks functional completeness, functional {{c1::correctness}} and functional appropriateness.
Before regression testing, an {{c1::impact analysis}} shows which parts of the software could be affected.
Triggers for maintenance testing: {{c1::modifications}}, upgrades or {{c2::migrations}} of the operational environment, and {{c3::retirement}}.
The scope of maintenance testing depends on the degree of {{c1::risk}} of the change, the size of the existing system and the size of the {{c2::change}}.
Almost any work product can be reviewed. For static analysis, a work product needs a {{c1::structure}} against which it can be checked.
Static testing can find defects that dynamic testing cannot, such as {{c1::unreachable code}}.
Static testing finds {{c1::defects}} directly; dynamic testing causes {{c2::failures}}, from which defects are found by analysis.
Early and frequent stakeholder feedback prevents {{c1::misunderstandings}} about requirements and lets the team focus on the features of most {{c2::value}}.
Review process activities: planning, {{c1::review initiation}}, individual review, {{c2::communication and analysis}}, fixing and reporting.
The {{c1::moderator}} (facilitator) ensures the effective running of review meetings, including mediation and time management.
The {{c1::scribe}} (recorder) collates anomalies from reviewers and records review information.
The {{c1::manager}} decides what is to be reviewed and provides resources; the {{c2::review leader}} takes overall responsibility for the review.
In an inspection, the author cannot act as {{c1::review leader or scribe}}.
Review success factors include clear objectives and measurable exit criteria, reviewing in {{c1::small chunks}}, adequate preparation time and {{c2::management}} support.
Evaluation of {{c1::participants}} should never be an objective of a review.
The three families of test techniques: {{c1::black-box}}, {{c2::white-box}} and {{c3::experience-based}}.
Equivalence partitions must not {{c1::overlap}} and must be {{c2::non-empty}}.
{{c1::Each Choice}} coverage requires each partition from each set of partitions to be exercised at least once. It ignores combinations.
2-value BVA: for each boundary value, the coverage items are the boundary value and its {{c1::closest neighbour in the adjacent partition}}.
3-value BVA: for each boundary value, the coverage items are the boundary value and {{c1::both its neighbours}}.
Decision table notation: T and F for conditions, "{{c1::–}}" for an irrelevant condition, {{c2::N/A}} for an infeasible one, X for an action that occurs.
Decision table coverage = exercised columns ÷ total {{c1::feasible}} columns.
Transition label syntax: {{c1::event}} [{{c2::guard condition}}] / {{c3::action}}.
State transition coverage criteria, weakest first: {{c1::all states}}, {{c2::valid transitions}} (0-switch), {{c3::all transitions}}.
A state table shows invalid transitions as {{c1::empty cells}}. Test only {{c2::one}} invalid transition per test case, to avoid defect masking.
100% statement coverage does not ensure that all the {{c1::decision logic}} has been tested.
Branch coverage {{c1::subsumes}} statement coverage: 100% branch coverage implies 100% statement coverage, but not the reverse.
White-box testing may not detect defects of {{c1::omission}}: requirements that were never implemented.
Error guessing draws on how the application worked in the past, the errors developers tend to make, and failures in {{c1::similar applications}}.
A {{c1::fault attack}} implements error guessing with a list of possible errors, defects and failures.
Session-based exploratory testing uses a {{c1::time box}}, a {{c2::test charter}} with test objectives, and a {{c3::debriefing}} afterwards.
A checklist should not contain items that can be checked {{c1::automatically}}, items better suited as entry or exit criteria, or items that are too {{c2::general}}.
The 3 C's of a user story: {{c1::Card}}, {{c2::Conversation}} and {{c3::Confirmation}}.
INVEST: Independent, {{c1::Negotiable}}, Valuable, {{c2::Estimable}}, Small and {{c3::Testable}}.
The two most common formats for acceptance criteria: {{c1::scenario}}-oriented (Given/When/Then) and {{c2::rule}}-oriented (list or table).
ATDD test cases are typically written in this order: {{c1::positive}}, then {{c2::negative}}, then {{c3::non-functional}}.
The first step of ATDD is a {{c1::specification workshop}}, in which the user story and its acceptance criteria are analysed, discussed and written.
Typical test plan content: context of testing, assumptions and constraints, stakeholders, communication, {{c1::risk register}}, {{c2::test approach}}, budget and schedule.
{{c1::Release}} planning looks at the product backlog and the whole release; {{c2::iteration}} planning looks at a single iteration backlog.
In Agile, entry criteria for a user story are the Definition of {{c1::Ready}}; exit criteria for a releasable item are the Definition of {{c2::Done}}.
Three-point estimation: E = ({{c1::a + 4m + b}}) ÷ 6 and SD = ({{c2::b − a}}) ÷ 6.
Metrics-based estimation techniques: {{c1::ratios}} and {{c2::extrapolation}}. Expert-based: Wideband Delphi and three-point estimation.
In Wideband Delphi, experts estimate in {{c1::isolation}}, discuss deviations, and repeat until {{c2::consensus}}. {{c3::Planning Poker}} is a variant.
Test case prioritization strategies: {{c1::risk}}-based, {{c2::coverage}}-based and {{c3::requirements}}-based.
If a higher-priority test case depends on a lower-priority one, the {{c1::lower-priority}} test case must be executed first.
In the test pyramid, the higher the layer, the lower the test {{c1::granularity}} and isolation, and the longer the {{c2::execution time}}.
Quadrant Q1 ({{c1::technology}} facing, supports the team) contains component and component integration tests.
Quadrant Q3 ({{c1::business}} facing, critiques the product) contains exploratory testing, {{c2::usability}} testing and user acceptance testing.
Risk level is expressed by risk {{c1::likelihood}} and risk {{c2::impact}}.
Project risk categories: {{c1::organisational}} issues, people issues, technical issues and {{c2::supplier}} issues.
Product risk analysis helps to determine the test {{c1::scope}}, the test levels and types, the techniques and {{c2::coverage}}, the effort and the priorities.
Responses to an analysed product risk: mitigation by testing, risk {{c1::acceptance}}, risk {{c2::transfer}} or a contingency plan.
Test metric categories: project progress, test progress, product quality, {{c1::defect}}, risk, {{c2::coverage}} and cost metrics.
Only a test progress report contains the {{c1::testing planned for the next period}}.
Only a test completion report contains {{c1::lessons learned}} and an evaluation against the original test plan.
Options for communicating test status: verbal communication, {{c1::dashboards}}, electronic channels, online documentation and formal test reports.
More {{c1::formal}} communication may suit distributed teams, where face-to-face contact is not always possible.
A configuration item approved for testing becomes a {{c1::baseline}} and can only be changed through formal {{c2::change control}}.
Configuration management ensures that configuration items are uniquely {{c1::identified}}, {{c2::version}} controlled and tracked for changes.
{{c1::Severity}} is the degree of impact of a defect; {{c2::priority}} is the urgency of fixing it.
Objectives of a defect report: information to {{c1::resolve}} the issue, a means of tracking the {{c2::quality}} of the work product, and ideas for process improvement.
Tool categories include test management, static testing, test design and implementation, test execution and coverage, {{c1::non-functional}} testing, {{c2::DevOps}} and collaboration tools.
Any tool that assists in testing is a test tool: even a {{c1::spreadsheet}}, in the context of testing.
A benefit of test automation: time saved by reducing {{c1::repetitive manual work}}.
Risks of test automation include {{c1::unrealistic expectations}} of a tool and relying on a tool too much, ignoring human {{c2::critical thinking}}.
